Movement runs on Access Levels 0 through 9, and access is a social weapon as much as a technical one: it can be quietly lowered after a relative's bad audit, temporarily raised to bait someone into a room, or revoked mid-errand so a citizen discovers their new standing at a rank gate in front of witnesses. The Red Ledger Intake Office is where that machinery first shows a seam. Citizens arrive with travel-status problems, summons and record corrections, and a few of them are actually holding the edge of the disappearing-records scandal that runs to Red Ledger Prime in the Nivarek Compound. Names are going missing from the system entirely, and nobody in the intake queue is told that. The Victory Walk's edited conquest reliefs contradict the chronicle Maelra Dravon is supposed to be curating, and the vandalism that occasionally appears there is not random. Helvyra is absent from every route board: the Dravon Disconnection is absolute, and the city's one gate reaches Relstaris only.

The Command Spine.description: The elevated avenue running through inner Quilrath toward the Ascendant Keep - part parade route, part command artery, part surveillance corridor. It runs broad and hard underfoot, black star-glass panels set with gold lines marking where formation traffic takes priority, a red command-light grid burning overhead. Officers, couriers and approved citizens move along it beneath projection banners of approved Dravon history, and the patrol drones overhead never quite leave the edge of hearing. Most days it carries errands rather than parades: escorts collecting visitors, clerks crossing between compounds, a supply crew keeping to the outer lane. At the joins, the inlay is worn pale where couriers have cut the same corner for years.

The Inner Compliance Gate.description: The controlled entrance from the wider city into inner Quilrath. Every arrival is scanned, logged, ranked and assigned movement permissions before the checkpoint bridge releases them, and escorts are issued to anyone who cannot move alone. The approach is a long channel of black composite under white processing light, lined by a rail that keeps arrivals in single file, and the bridge extends only once a permission has cleared. The queue is orderly because everyone in it has watched a denial happen. Gate staff work from scripts and do not improvise; a question about a delay gets the same sentence each time. Past the barrier there is a waiting bay of fixed benches where the escorted sit until the officer assigned to them arrives.

The Rank Gates.description: Smaller inner checkpoints dividing movement by clearance, rank mark, escort authorization and loyalty standing. Each one reads a citizen silently and opens, or does not. They are set into ordinary walls at the ends of ordinary corridors, narrow enough for one person, a red reader plate at shoulder height and a light above it that changes without any sound. This is where people learn their status has changed: no announcement, no explanation, just a gate that used to work and a crowd pretending not to look. Anyone refused steps aside and waits, because arguing with a gate is a worse record than being refused by one. The plates are wiped down on a schedule, and the fingermarks accumulate again within the hour.

The High Civic Rings.description: Elite residential rings for command families, ranking administrators and officer households, terraced in black star-glass with gold status inlay. The terraces step back from the avenue behind their own rank gates, with private landings, quiet interior courts and windows that show a warm interior light rather than anything happening inside. Children are raised here to impossible standards, and reformist conversations happen at ordinary volume behind private doors. The comfort is genuine and entirely conditional. Household staff, tutors and couriers come and go on standing permissions of their own. The inlay along each frontage is renewed when a household's standing changes, which is how a street learns of a promotion before the family announces one.

The Victory Walk.description: A public avenue lined with red-lit star-glass reliefs, holographic conquest records and official history projections. The reliefs are cut deep into black glass and lit from within so the carved conquests read from the far side of the walk, and the projections between them cycle campaign records on a fixed loop. School tours pass through weekly and citizens can recite the approved account on request. What the displays leave out of the Dravon conflicts is more interesting than what they show. Guides move groups along at a measured pace, pausing at the same panels every time. Maintenance crews polish the lower panels often, because the lower panels are the ones people touch.

The Civic Watch Plazas.description: Open angular plazas fitted with surveillance pylons, rank scanners, public address systems and automated crowd-routing barriers. The paving is hard black composite, the barriers sit flush until they rise, and the pylons stand at the corners with their sensor heads turning slowly and continuously. Loyalty announcements and public corrections happen here, before crowds the barriers have already arranged. People choose their words carefully and praise promptly. Between announcements the plazas are simply the fastest way to cross between avenues, and they are used that way constantly. The address speakers carry a short tone before every message, and conversation drops on that tone before anyone decides to stop talking.

Red Ledger Intake Office.description: The public-facing branch of the Red Ledger. Travel-status problems, missing paperwork, summons and record corrections are handled at its counters by quiet Nivarek clerks who never hurry anyone. The hall is low-ceilinged and evenly lit, with a numbered waiting bank facing a run of counters and red data readouts recessed into the desk surfaces. It feels like ordinary bureaucracy, which is the point; the files that decide anything are not kept in this building. Citizens bring documents in folders, rehearse their question while they wait, and are answered in the same unhurried register whatever they ask. Nobody at the counters can say when a referral will come back, and they have been trained not to guess aloud.

The Gilt Setting.description: A formal restaurant in the High Civic Rings: an arrival-and-reservation room, the dining floor, small booked rooms, a serving passage and the preservation kitchen behind. Dark polished finishes, understated gold, seating and service order arranged by rank. Arrivals give a name at the front room and wait while it is confirmed; the dining floor beyond is quiet enough that cutlery is the loudest thing in it. Successive preparations come out on a timed service, and a booked room reduces interruption without promising privacy from anything else. A reservation buys a beautiful evening and no access whatsoever. Diners here do sincerely enjoy the food, and some of them are marking a family occasion.

The Ascendant Keep.name: The Ascendant Keep
The Ascendant Keep.basicInfo:
House Dravon's central seat is a command fortress rather than a palace: black star-glass walls, red tactical light, sealed elevators and holographic battle maps above panoramic windows overlooking the districts it controls. The approach is severe and deliberately legible, the interior a sequence of halls, chambers and courts connected by corridors that carry sound badly and sightlines well. War planning, ceremony, advancement and family power all converge in the same building. A declaration made in one chamber is recorded in another before the speaker has left the floor. Elite guards stand in exact formation and the corridors are quieter than they should be. Movement inside runs on sealed lifts and rank-gated doors, so most people who work here only ever see the part of it their standing reaches. Officers, adjutants, ceremonial staff, household attendants and Nivarek observers all keep to their own routes through it. Natural light reaches only the outer windows, and everything inward of them is lit red. Visitors are escorted throughout, held between appointments in bare anterooms, and told plainly that waiting is part of the process. The stonework equivalent is not here: nothing is carved, everything is cast, fitted and replaced when it wears.

Work on offer here: House Dravon — Walk the Gates Unknown (ask Orvane Dravon).
The Ascendant Keep.hiddenInfo: The Red War Room is where Dravon's next move actually lives — Ignivex pressure, Dustfall containment, Contair and Relstaris files, and the early shape of off-world expansion routes. Anything stolen from it is worth a house. Kaldor Dravon remains the active head, fully in command and dangerous; he delegates daily operations to Sorin and Vaelen deliberately, and permits the succession pressure between them because sharpened heirs and guessing rivals both serve him. Kaldor's War Gallery frames the First Dravon Conflict as noble resistance to disorder and stays quiet about Ark Genesis and the Castro power that ended the campaign; the Second Conflict's treatment is even more selective. The gaps between the gallery's version and the true chronology are traceable, and the Correction Archive across the city in the Nivarek Compound holds the revisions before release. The Oath Courts look ceremonial and function as surveillance: Nivarek observes every vow, and advancement trials are where loyalty is proven or quietly lost.

Ascendant Hall.description: The main command chamber of House Dravon: raised command platforms, tactical displays, house banners and rank stations under panoramic windows overlooking the controlled districts. The platforms step up toward the windows so that anyone addressing the room does it with the city behind them, and the rank stations line the floor in fixed positions nobody mistakes for interchangeable. Major decisions, command ceremonies and high-level negotiations happen here. Between them the hall is worked rather than admired: adjutants updating displays, couriers arriving at the lower stations, a duty officer holding the floor. The view is part of the argument, every single time. Delegations are brought in facing the windows, and never seated higher than the platform they are answering.

The Iron Assembly.description: A vast ceremonial chamber for declarations, rank advancements, loyalty ceremonies and state addresses. It is built as a bowl of tiered seating around a speaking floor, the tiers black and unornamented, the floor lit hard from above so whoever stands on it is the brightest thing in the room. It is not a senate; it is a performance of unity, and the seating quietly publishes who is currently trusted. Attendance is by summons, places are assigned, and everyone present reads the arrangement before the first word. Accusations delivered from its floor have ended families between one speech and the next. Ceremonial staff rehearse entries and exits beforehand, because the choreography is part of the message.

The Red War Room.description: The restricted strategic chamber where Dravon watches Ignivex, Dustfall, Contair and Relstaris on live campaign maps. The maps stand as projected volumes over a central table, updating continuously, and the walls carry secondary displays officers turn to without leaving their positions. Access is tightly held and the room is swept constantly. Officers speak in clipped ranges and timings, and the red light makes everyone in it look like they have already decided. Sessions run long and nothing leaves on paper. Entry is by name against a list held at the door, and a name can be on the list one week and absent the next without anyone in the room remarking on it.

Kaldor's War Gallery.description: A curated history chamber staging Dravon's official account of past wars in holographic relief. The reliefs stand in sequence along a walking route, each with its own lighting and commentary cue, the room kept cool and dim so the projections carry. Guides frame the First Dravon Conflict as noble resistance to disorder; the Second is handled more carefully still. Anyone who knows the real chronology can watch the edits happening in front of them. Officer candidates, visiting delegations and school groups are all brought through, each with a version of the tour pitched to them. One relief near the end of the route has a noticeably shorter commentary, and the guides move groups past it without pausing.

The Inner Obsidian Yard.description: The elite training yard for Dravon heirs, command candidates and approved officers, black composite underfoot and instrumented for measurement rather than spectacle. Sensor arrays ring the floor at waist height, readouts run along the wall for anyone qualified to read them, and there is seating only for assessors. This is command preparation, not sport: controlled duels, advancement trials and affinity demonstrations, watched by people whose job is to score them. Bouts are stopped on a called figure rather than on a finish, and the results go into a record before anyone has caught their breath. The composite is scuffed in a wide band through the centre of the floor and clean at the edges.

The Oath Courts.description: Formal courtyards used for vows, promotions, loyalty renewal and rank confirmation, open to the sky and ringed with recording positions. The paving is plain and the surrounding galleries are narrow, so a voice carries clean across the court and is captured from several angles at once. Obedience is proved in public here. Nivarek observers attend every session, and the pause before a vow is timed as carefully as the words that follow it. Families attend when invited and stand where they are placed. Ceremonies run back to back on busy days, with the next party waiting in the gallery while the previous one finishes. The wording of each oath is issued in advance so that nobody has an excuse for hesitating, and the ones who hesitate anyway do it in front of everybody who matters to them.

Private Dravon Strategy Suites.description: Restricted meeting rooms for Dravon family leadership: small, sealed, and unrecorded by anything the family does not control. Each is little more than a table, fixed seating, a single display surface and a door that reports only that it was opened. The light in them is lower than anywhere else in the Keep, which is deliberate and which visitors notice before they can say why. Succession friction, reform-versus-expansion arguments and emergency war planning all happen at these tables. Attendance is by summons and the summons carries no agenda. The sound damping is good enough that a raised voice never leaves the room, so a family argument ends with everyone walking out at the same measured pace.

Nivarek Compound.name: Nivarek Compound
Nivarek Compound.basicInfo: House Nivarek makes conquest permanent by recording it, and its compound is the legal-memory engine of Dravon rule: black archive towers, red data columns, glass-floor record chambers and sound-dampened corridors. The towers are narrow and windowless above their lower floors, and inside them the data columns stand floor to ceiling in ranks, shedding a red working light that never changes with the hour. Loyalty standing, family classification and citizenship status are all decided here. What arrives as a person's difficult year leaves as a classification, a grade and a file reference. Clerks move in exact routes and nobody raises their voice. Hearings run to timetable in chambers built for it, testimony is taken in sealed rooms, and gold-lined legal panels mark the doorways where a decision becomes binding. Citizens summoned here wait in corridors with benches along one wall and nothing else, and are called by reference rather than by name. The air is cool and dry throughout, kept that way for the records rather than the people. Nothing in the building hurries, and the effect of that on anyone waiting is well understood by the staff who designed the waiting.
Nivarek Compound.hiddenInfo: Nivarek is terrifying because it is precise. People are broken through procedure rather than violence: a loyalty audit can reduce a family's standing, a sealed testimony session can produce a confession nobody struck anyone for, and the Conquered-Family Registry Wing quietly assigns inherited suspicion marks to children who have done nothing. Red Ledger Prime holds the files that matter — elite family records, erased identities, military assignments, hidden political risk — and records are disappearing out of it. The Erased are the same mystery seen from the other end: people Dravon now claims never existed. The Unbroken Accord's Archive believes it has a friend inside this record system and does not know who; Myrra Nivarek quietly helps people in the intake queues and has never been confirmed as anything more. The Correction Archive stores altered records and revised histories before release, which makes it the one room in Quilrath where the official past and the real one are held side by side.

Nivarek Record Court.description: The central administrative hall of House Nivarek, a glass-floored chamber of red data columns where legal status, family classification and loyalty standing are processed. The columns rise in ranks from a floor that shows the working levels below, so the whole machinery of the place is visible and entirely inaudible. Disputes are heard without raised voices and settled in writing. A representative states a case from a fixed position, an adjudicating clerk answers from another, and the result is issued as a document rather than announced. Clerks cross the floor along fixed routes and do not look up as they pass. Family representatives wait at the margin for their reference to be called. The glass is cleaned nightly and still shows the faint tracks of the routes most used.

Red Ledger Prime.description: The restricted high-security branch of the Red Ledger, behind biometric archive gates. The gates open onto a short sealed passage and then a chamber of shelved data cores standing in their own field, with handling stations set at intervals and nothing on any wall that names what is held where. Elite family files, erased identities, military assignments and state secrets are held here. The air is cold, the light is red, and the number of people cleared to stand in the room is small enough to list by name. Retrieval is logged at the gate, at the station and on the core itself. Nobody works here alone, and nobody working here discusses the work outside. A single chair sits at the reading station and there is no second one.

Loyalty Audit Courts.description: Formal hearing chambers where citizens, officers, elite families and conquered-house members are reviewed. Each chamber is a plain room with a raised examiner's desk, a single seat facing it and recording positions along the side wall. No violence is used and none is required: an audit can lower a grade, strip an access level, or open a review of everyone the subject is related to. Proceedings run to a posted list, subjects are called in one at a time, and the finding is issued afterwards rather than delivered in the room. Families wait outside on benches designed to be uncomfortable. The corridor outside the chambers is the quietest part of the compound, and people who have waited there before bring nothing to read.

Conquered-Family Registry Wing.description: Record halls for absorbed minor families, relocated populations, work assignments and inherited suspicion marks, displayed as holographic family trees branching into classifications. The trees hang in the aisles at working height, pale red against the dark, and a clerk can rotate a whole lineage with one hand to find the branch that matters. Children appear on them already carrying a standing they were born into. Requests to view a line are taken at a desk at the head of the wing and answered in the order they were logged. Missing entries are commoner than the staff will admit. A gap in a branch is shown as a gap, unlabelled, and the display offers no explanation for it because the display has not been given one.

Sealed Testimony Rooms.description: Private deposition, interrogation and confession rooms where silence is part of the pressure. Sound-dampened walls, one table, a recording field and an examiner with unlimited time. The rooms are small and evenly lit, with no clock, no window and a door that closes without any sound at all. A session begins when the examiner begins it and continues through long stretches in which nothing is said. People walk out of these rooms having agreed to things they came in fully intending to deny, and cannot always say when that turned. Nothing is written by the subject; the record is made by the field and read back at the end. Water is provided on request, which is the only thing in the room that can be asked for.

The Correction Archive.description: A restricted archive holding altered records, revised histories and corrected public narratives before release. The shelving is ordinary and the handling is not: each item is stored in a pair, the version in circulation and the version replacing it, with the working copy issued only against a countersigned request. It is the one place in Quilrath where the official past and the real one sit on adjacent shelves. Staff work in silence at low tables under directed light, comparing, amending and closing files that will be public in a month. Access is severely limited, and the wing does not appear in the compound's public directories. Nothing here is destroyed, which is a working principle and not a mercy.

Balrath Bastion Barracks.name: Balrath Bastion Barracks
Balrath Bastion Barracks.basicInfo: House Balrath makes conquest physical. The compound - Balrath Barracks to most, the Gate-House to outsiders - builds and maintains the walls, gates, drones, transit locks and issued equipment that let Dravon control who moves through Quilrath. Armored machine halls, red-lit gate machinery, drone racks and heavy transit lifts run loud beneath a disciplined surface. The halls are stacked and connected by black alloy walkways, the repair bays seal for testing, and the maintenance pits below the floor line are open working spaces rather than hidden ones. Shifts change on a horn and the crews move in formation until they reach their stations. Engineers, wall technicians, gate operators, drone-line supervisors, quartermasters and rapid-response troops all work the same site and rarely mix outside their own halls. Gold-coded command lines run along the walls to mark authority and route, and the equipment depots issue nothing without a name attached. Above the upper tiers are the aerial patrol launch slots, which fire off at intervals all day. It is a working industrial compound first, and its discipline is visible in how quickly a mess is cleared rather than in how little mess is made.
Balrath Bastion Barracks.hiddenInfo: Everything that makes the city a cage is manufactured here, which means everything that makes it a cage can be reached here. Gate lockdowns, rank-gate behaviour and surveillance pylon coverage are all set from the Inner Wall Control Yards, and a single sabotage in the Gateworks changes what the Inner Compliance Gate will accept. The Labor Transit Systems Office is the uncomfortable one: it moves classified conquered-house populations out to the Camp Belt, and the engineers who route those transports know exactly what their work supplies. Lurani Balrath has begun asking about it. The Prototype Gate Lab exists because Dravon wants Lunar Gates of its own and cannot build them without Contair; Namar Balrath's admiration for the technology he is supposed to replace shades into illegal study of captured equipment, and the lab does not add a gate or change the city's one Relstaris link. Border Infrastructure Command's corridor plans are third-conflict preparation, not contingency.

Balrath Gateworks.description: The main engineering hall for Quilrath's gates, walls and access-control systems, full of red-lit gate machinery and heavy transit lifts. The hall runs tall, with gantries at two levels, test frames standing in the open floor and lifts hauling assemblies up through it continuously. Lockdown protocols are written and tested here, and repairs after unrest run around the clock. A test cycle is called, the frame drives a barrier through its full travel, and the whole hall hears it. Crews work in rotation with supervisors tracking faults on boards at the hall's end. The noise is constant, and the crews have learned to shout everything twice. Hand signals cover the rest, and a newcomer is taught them before being taught anything else.

Inner Wall Control Yards.description: The control center for inner walls, automated barriers, surveillance pylons and rank-gate systems, banked with wall-control stations and live district feeds. The stations face a wall of feeds in fixed grid order, each operator holding a set of sectors, and the room is kept dim so the displays read. A citywide lockdown begins as one confirmed instruction at one of these desks. Drone response launches from the slots overhead within seconds of it. Ordinary shifts are hours of watching nothing change, punctuated by barrier faults, a pylon losing a feed, or a rank gate reporting a reader error that someone has to go out and touch. Confirmations are spoken aloud and repeated back. The chairs are worn through at the armrests.

Drone Assembly Tiers.description: Stacked production and maintenance tiers turning out Dravon state drones: reliable, intimidating, ugly and completely standardized. The tiers run one above another with racks of frames along the outer wall, assembly benches down the middle and test cages at the end of each line where a finished unit is put through its paces before it is signed off. Shifts run against quotas under supervisors who count failures. Parts arrive in numbered crates and every unit leaves with the same profile as the one before it. Balrath engineers compare the output to Contair's elegance in private and defend it loudly in public. The scrap bins at the line ends are emptied twice a shift, and nobody on the floor is told where the contents go.

Military Equipment Depots.description: Storage and inspection halls for issued armor, weapons, field kits, gate hardware and rapid-response equipment, racked in numbered aisles under gold-coded command lines. The aisles run long and identical, the racking is heavy, and an inspection bench sits at the head of each run where kit is checked, logged and either passed back or pulled. Quartermasters check every item out against a name. Nothing leaves on a promise, and an item returned damaged generates a report before it generates a replacement. Dravon does not win through brilliance here; it wins through scale, and the aisles prove it. The end of one aisle carries a board of outstanding returns, and the names on it stay up until the items come back.

Border Infrastructure Command.description: The strategic engineering office for Ignivex pressure, Dustfall containment and the old Contair invasion scars, its walls carrying siege corridor plans and border maps. It is a working office rather than a command chamber: plan tables at standing height, map surfaces that can be marked and cleared, and engineers arguing over a corridor profile with the drawings between them. The planning assumes a third conflict rather than fearing one. Projects here are measured in seasons of construction and are revised constantly as the frontier situation changes. It is also where the reasons Dravon has not moved on Dustfall directly are written down. The oldest drawings in the room are the Contair scar surveys, and they are consulted more often than anyone here says aloud.

Labor Transit Systems Office.description: A restricted infrastructure office routing outer-city labor movement, conquered-family transport and work-camp logistics. It is a quiet room of scheduling stations, well away from the machine halls, with the whole system rendered as flows and timings on the wall displays. Transit schedules scroll past as abstract load figures on the wall displays. Staff work to clearing times and reroute around delays, and the work is genuinely difficult in the way any large scheduling problem is difficult. Engineers here can trace exactly how inner comfort is supplied by outer control, and some have started doing that arithmetic. The figures are held at a level of abstraction that makes the arithmetic possible only if somebody chooses to do it, and most of the time nobody does.

Prototype Gate Lab.description: A smaller experimental lab where Balrath tries to improve gate and access systems without Contair equipment. It is one room of test rigs behind a sealed bay door, with containment around the working frame and instrumentation banked along the wall to catch what happens in the fraction of a second that matters. Test rigs fail loudly and expensively; the successes are incremental and heavily reported. A working session is mostly waiting, then a burst of noise, then hours of reading what the instruments caught. Captured technology occasionally appears on the benches, and no paperwork explains where it came from. Nobody in the lab asks about it, and the pieces are gone again within a few days.

The Gray Rings.name: The Gray Rings
The Gray Rings.basicInfo:
Ring 2, the compliant middle city: administrative blocks, standard housing, state commerce and industry in gray composite instead of star-glass, under red command-lights older and dimmer than the Inner Circle's. The composite is patched where it has been repaired and the repairs do not quite match, which is the ring's most honest visual detail. Assigned work, standardized goods of famously adequate quality and civics instruction fill the day under the Civic Standing Grades. Mornings run on shift horns and queue boards; the streets fill twice a day and are unremarkable in between. This is where the regime looks most like a functioning state. Counters are staffed, permits issue, clinics treat people, classes are taught, and a household with clean paperwork can live an entire ordinary life inside the system as designed. Nivarek assesses Standing here and Kathvar administrators process what that Standing means at the counters, the queues and the gates. Many residents believe in the order they live under, keep decent and careful lives, and file honest reports. The pressure is procedural rather than dramatic: a grade that moves on a relative's audit, a permit that takes three days instead of one, a stock board that is shorter this week than last.

Work on offer here: Quilrath — A Day at the Permit Counter; Quilrath — The Corrected File (ask Odrin Kathvar).
The Gray Rings.hiddenInfo: Standing decides housing, work assignment, movement radius, queue speed and audit frequency, and Nivarek decides Standing — Kathvar administrators at the counters only process what has already been determined, which does not stop people begging the wrong clerk. Ferrik Nivarek audits from the Standing Office believing precision is mercy; his files are immaculate and his sleep is not. Torbek Karn works a Provision Hall counter and moves extras through the tolerated gray market with perfect paperwork, useful to the same officials who periodically raid it — everyone's quiet friend, nobody's informant so far. Merron Talvek teaches the official history in the Civics Classrooms, believes about half of it, and polices which half he says aloud; a pupil recently asked him about a name he remembers and the records do not. Olna Bresk runs a floor in the Works, files honest reports and has never been audited, which is the regime's best argument in one decent person. The horror here is procedural, not theatrical: what the ladder quietly does to people who love someone on a lower rung.

Standing Office.description: The Nivarek office where Civic Standing is assessed and audited for this ring: a waiting hall, numbered assessment rooms, and files that are always more current than the people sitting in front of them. The waiting hall has fixed bench seating facing a call board, and the assessment rooms open off it in a numbered run. Grades rise on service and fall on association. Sessions are scheduled and subjects attend at a stated time, sometimes with a relative, more often alone. Auditors work through a fixed sequence of questions and take down answers that have already been checked. The room where a result is delivered has no window. Outside, people who have finished tend to leave briskly, and the ones still waiting do not ask them anything.

Provision Hall.description: A state distribution hall issuing standardized goods against allocation records - adequate, reliable and famously uninspiring. It is a long room with a counter down one side, shelved stock behind it, a stock board above the counter and a queue rail marking the path from the door. Clerks work the counters at a measured pace while the queue reads the board for what is actually in stock today. Allocations are drawn against household records, checked and handed over in standard packaging. Extras move through here too, for households whose paperwork is perfect. Nobody names that arrangement out loud and nobody is surprised by it. The board is updated by hand at the start of each session, and the lines that have been wiped and rewritten most often are legible as faint marks.

The Works.description: The ring's industrial floor: production lines, shift boards and foremen who protect their crews by keeping the figures clean. The floor is loud, well lit and organized in lines, with a board at each line head carrying the shift's targets and the crew's names, and walkways marked in painted composite between them. Output, ownership and scale are not things anyone on the floor is told. Work is assigned, quotas are set elsewhere, and a good foreman's skill lies in keeping the reported figures honest and the crew out of a review. Shift change fills the surrounding streets twice a day with people too tired to say much to each other. At the line ends, the tool racks are labelled in handwriting rather than print, because the printed labels stopped matching the tools years ago.

The Administrative Blocks.description: Gray composite office blocks handling the ring's permits, records, work assignments and service routing, staffed largely by Kathvar administrators. The corridors run long and identical, every desk carrying a queue number above it. Rooms are divided by low partitions, terminals sit at every station, and the working sound is a steady low murmur of cases being taken and passed on. Things genuinely get done here, at precisely the pace the system intends. A file moves from one desk to the next in an order that is documented and unalterable, and the administrators know exactly which step is slow and cannot do anything about it. Residents come in with a reference number and leave with a different one. The floor outside the busiest doors is polished pale in a wide arc.

The Standard Housing Blocks.description: Assigned housing in uniform gray composite, allocated by Civic Standing, the command-light grids along its walkways older and dimmer than the Inner Circle's. The blocks step back from shared walkways with stairwells at fixed intervals, the units are identical in plan, and the differences between them are entirely what the households inside have made. Families keep their units carefully, because a maintenance complaint becomes a record. Small repairs are done quietly and well. Evenings bring children onto the walkways and cooking smells into the stairwells, and the blocks are sociable in a low-key, practised way. Neighbors know each other's grades without a number ever being said aloud. The walkway lights flicker in the same few places year after year, and nobody has reported them.

The Civics Classrooms.description: Instruction rooms for civics, trade training and the official history, their projection walls teaching what the Victory Walk teaches. The rooms are plain and bright, with fixed desks facing the wall, a teacher's station to one side and the day's lesson already loaded when the class arrives. The children recite well. Lessons run to a set sequence and are assessed on accuracy of recall, and trade training shares the same rooms in the afternoons with the benches folded out. Teachers learn quickly which questions to answer fully, which to redirect, and which to pretend they did not quite hear over the room. Most of them are competent and fond of their classes. The wall panel in each room carries a small scuffed patch where a decade of pupils have pressed the same control.

The Gray Ring Clinic.description: The ring's civilian clinic: adequately staffed, adequately supplied, and noticeably better than anything further out. It has a waiting room with a call board, treatment rooms off a central corridor, and a dispensary counter that closes for an hour in the middle of the day. Emergency care is officially promised and here it is mostly delivered. Permissions and Standing shape who gets an appointment and how quickly, which the staff process without ever discussing it. The clinicians are good and they work fast, because the appointment book is full every day it opens. Families bring their own record cards and hand them over at the desk. A notice by the door lists which services are currently referred elsewhere, and it is amended more often than it is reprinted.

The Ring Gate.description: A controlled crossing between rings, with scanners, movement-radius checks and lanes sorted by grade. The lanes are marked on the paving and funnel into separate reader positions, with a barrier line across the whole width and staff positions behind it. Gatefolk pass most days without incident; anyone whose radius has narrowed finds out at the barrier. There is a side bay for anyone held, and it is in full view of the lanes. Surveillance is heaviest at exactly this point, because the regime watches movement between rings above all else. Traffic peaks hard at the start and end of the working day and is thin the rest of the time. The reader plates here are newer than anything else in sight, and they are replaced on a schedule rather than when they fail.

The Civic Counters.description: The public service counters - permits, work orders, record corrections, service routing - where residents meet the administration face to face. It is a wide hall with the counters in a run, numbered tickets drawn at the door, and a seated waiting area that fills by mid-morning and empties slowly. Kathvar staff process consequences of decisions made elsewhere and cannot reverse any of them, which does not stop people from asking, at length, every day. The staff are patient about it, because patience is most of the job and because the asking is reasonable. Forms are checked, referred and stamped, and a completed case is handed back with a reference for the next stage. The ticket dispenser at the door jams often enough that someone keeps a tool behind the nearest counter.

The Measured Hour.description: A cafe in the Standard Housing Blocks with an order counter, shared front tables, smaller conversation tables and a wash recess behind. The fittings are standardized and maintained, the room clean and restrained, the service measured without being cold. Clerks, teachers and household members sit somewhere that is not their own kitchen. Cyrra comes light or standard with optional Selka, and the food is Terva bread, cooked Terva portions and whatever preserved fruit has been allocated. The small tables offer ordinary conversational distance and nothing more reliable than that. People trade household news, read, or mark a relative's achievement. The stock behind the counter is recorded, and what is not on the board is genuinely not available.

The Ashrings.name: The Ashrings
The Ashrings.basicInfo:
Ring 3, the outer residential and labor belts: patched prefab housing, work-order queues and curfew gates, where the city stops pretending. The prefab is repaired rather than replaced, in whatever material a household could legitimately obtain, and the command-lights along the rows are older still than the Gray Rings' and stand further apart. Grade 4 Half-lights live probationary and audited, and conquered-house lines mostly enter the ladder here. A day runs on the boards: present for assignment, wait, work, collect an allotment, be inside before the gates close. Clinic care has visibly thinned and the queues are longer than the ones two rings in. Kathvar administrators work the permit desks and the checkpoint documentation; Standing itself is determined elsewhere and arrives here already decided. The ring's defining fact is a gap rather than a presence: surveillance is total at the ring gates and threadbare in the deep interior, because the regime watches movement between rings more than life inside them. Households manage the difference between what the record says and what a family actually needs, and the management is practical rather than dramatic - shared cooking, watched children, a repair done quietly, a place held in a queue for a neighbour who is late.

Work on offer here: Corridor — Names That Hold (ask Edda Nhalor).
The Ashrings.hiddenInfo: The ring's defining fact is a gap rather than a presence. Surveillance is total at the ring gates and threadbare in the deep Ashrings, because the regime watches movement between rings far more closely than life inside them — so people keep their opinions for where the pylons do not reach, and illegal activity plausibly follows the same gap without belonging to anyone in particular. Audits weigh family association, so a relative's fall drags a whole household into review; Sedran Vaereth is raising two children under exactly that pressure, furious at Dravon and at the cousins in Dustfall whose gang name makes every Vaereth audit worse. When the Accord's Edge wing strikes a Standing Office or a checkpoint, the reprisal audits land here within days, on Archive families as often as anyone, which is the Archive's standing argument against the Edge and an argument with no clean winner. The Deep Shelves cell is somewhere in Quilrath and nobody has placed it.

The Prefab Rows.description: Patched prefab housing in long rows, repaired with whatever a household could legitimately obtain and some of what it could not. The units sit close, the walkways between them are narrow and swept, and the repairs are visible everywhere as mismatched panels, resealed joints and doors rehung by hand. Doors stay open in the evening until curfew closes them. Children run the length of the rows, cooking carries between units, and people sit on their own steps because that is where the space is. Community here is practical: shared cooking, watched children, and a careful silence about certain neighbors. Nothing is assumed about anyone's circumstances out loud. The row lighting fails in sections and is repaired unofficially, which is the kind of thing everybody knows and nobody reports.

The Work-Order Queues.description: Open-air queues where residents present for the day's assignments and wait for the boards to update. The boards stand at the head of the ground, the queue forms behind a painted line, and there is no shelter and nowhere provided to sit. A missed order costs standing; an unfilled one costs more. Clerks work from a hatch, reading names against orders and sending people on. Waits run long and the boards sometimes do not change for an hour at a time. People bring something to sit on, and the queue's own etiquette about holding a place is older than most of the clerks working it. A place held for someone who has gone to fetch a child is honoured; a place held for no stated reason is argued about, quietly, and usually conceded.

The Curfew Gates.description: Barriers closing the rows at curfew, scanned and logged, staffed by bored operators with total authority over a few minutes. The barrier drops across the walkway, a reader post stands beside it, and a single light above the post says whether it is open. A late arrival argues, or does not, and the record notes it either way. Traffic builds in the last stretch before closing, with people walking faster than they would admit to, and then the rows go quiet. Operators work a rota and most of them are neither cruel nor generous about the margin. The lights on these gates are among the newest equipment anywhere in the ring, and the contrast between them and the housing behind is noticed by everyone who passes under them.

The Ashring Clinic.description: A thinned clinic running on shortages, whose staff triage harder than they would two rings inward. The waiting room is larger than the treatment space behind it, the supply cupboards are logged and locked, and the call board moves slowly through the day. Care is competent and rationed, and permissions decide as much as symptoms do. Clinicians substitute constantly, stretch what they have, and write referrals that they know will take weeks. The waiting room is full of people who have already decided to endure it a while longer before coming in. Families wait together, bring their own record cards, and know the staff by sight. A hand-written note on the dispensary shutter lists what has not arrived this week, and it is rarely a short list.

The Deep Ashrings.description: The far interior of the ring, where surveillance coverage fails because the regime watches movement between rings rather than life inside them. It is the same patched prefab and broken-up ground as the rest, with the pylons thinning out and then simply not being there, and no marker anywhere that says where the coverage ends. People come here to say things they cannot say at home. Conversations happen walking rather than sitting, and they end when they end. Other business finds the same gap useful; nobody owns it, and nothing about it is guaranteed. The depth at which coverage actually fails is not fixed and not posted, and the people who use the ground read it by habit and by what has worked before rather than by anything they could explain.

The Permit Desk.description: A small counter issuing movement, work and visit permits against Standing and curfew terms, usually worked by a Kathvar administrator following rules written elsewhere. It is one window in a composite frontage with a rail outside it, a terminal behind, and a queue that starts before the desk opens. A Grade 4 applicant learns here exactly how far their life is allowed to reach this month, printed as a distance and a set of hours. Applications are checked against the record, granted, narrowed or refused, and the administrator explains the terms plainly because an applicant who misunderstands them is an applicant who comes back with a violation. Visit permits are the ones argued over most. The rail outside is worn smooth at the height of a resting forearm.

The Provision Counter.description: The ring's thin version of a Provision Hall: a counter, a stock board, and allotments measured against household records. The room is small, the shelving behind the counter is visible from the queue, and the board carries fewer lines than it has slots for. Availability and access are separate problems, and a household can be refused goods that are visibly on the shelf. The clerk reads the record, states what the allotment covers, and hands it across in standard packaging without further comment. Arguments happen, briefly, and change nothing. Trading between neighbors begins about three steps past the door, and it is conducted in the ordinary tone of people swapping what they have for what they need.

The Spare Room.description: A resident-kept common room with a shared food table, a cleared music floor, wall seating and a preparation corner. The furniture is ordinary and removable, the panels have been cleaned and repaired with visible pride, and the room is warm in a way the rows outside are not. Neighbors arrange sessions with voluntary cooks and performers, ending inside everyone's real curfew. Shared portions come from allotted Terva, cultured protein and preserved ingredients, and contributions toward ingredients are agreed in advance rather than assumed. An exhausted worker, a careful loyalist and a quiet dissenter share an evening without settling anything. A nervous first performer is applauded whether or not it went well.

The Camp Belt.name: The Camp Belt
The Camp Belt.basicInfo: Ring 4: relocation blocks and work camps for classified conquered-house populations, built as camp construction rather than city construction. The distinction is visible in everything: prefabricated blocks set in rows on prepared ground, service runs above the surface rather than buried, perimeter before amenity, and nothing built to outlast the arrangement it serves. Grade 5 Ashfeet live on restricted labor, ration allotments and movement by work order only, fed by the Labor Transit Systems Office in the Balrath compound. The day begins at a muster and ends when a crew is released; between those two points a resident's location is a matter of record rather than of choice. Healthcare is thin and family life is conducted under classification. Classification is Nivarek's, the transit system is Balrath's, and the work orders, allotments and clinic coordination are processed by Kathvar staff, so no single authority is present to appeal to. Crews formed by assignment often stay together for years and become something like neighbours. Meals are cooked, children are taught what their parents can teach them, and old work rhythms carry songs older than the camps. The conditions are uniform; the people living in them are not, and nothing here reads as a single mood.
The Camp Belt.hiddenInfo: No single House governs the ring and none is invented: classification is Nivarek's, the labor transit system is Balrath's, and ordinary paperwork and service routing are Kathvar's — which means a family can be crushed by three separate offices, none of which considers itself responsible. Nor does the ring carry one collective mood; residents are not uniformly exhausted, resigned or rebellious, and the procedurally dystopian rule applies here as everywhere. Maru Sorn keeps the old survey route-songs alive as work rhythms, and the Archive knows every verse is a map; lately the verses are reaching them incomplete, because someone in the camps is editing them. Varda Olm refused promotion to keep her posting and treats beyond her ration allotment, leaving the Standing Office to decide what that makes her. The Erased are not a camp population — erasure is removal from the records, not a lower rung, and the people here are still on the ladder.

The Relocation Blocks.description: Housing blocks built as camp construction rather than city construction, holding classified conquered-house families under assignment. The blocks run in rows on prepared ground, service lines carried above the roofline, entrances numbered rather than named, and the ground between them compacted hard by use. The units are small, identical and recorded. Occupancy is assigned and changes without consultation when a work order changes. Family life continues inside them anyway: meals, arguments, and children learning the difference between a visit and a transfer. Households make what they can of the space, and the small alterations that appear - a hung cloth, a shelf, a step swept clean - are the only way one unit is told from another from the outside.

The Work Camps.description: Camps where restricted labor is carried out under quota and supervision, with movement governed entirely by work order. The working ground is open and functional, marked out by task, with supervisors' positions raised enough to see the whole of it and a tally board where the quota is posted at the start of the shift. Crews form by assignment rather than choice and often stay together for years. That length of time makes them something more than crews: people know each other's families, cover a bad hour, and train the newcomers without being asked to. Old survey route-songs set the rhythm of a shift, and no supervisor has ever thought to ask what they are. The verses run long and the crews know where each one turns.

The Labor Transit Intake.description: The receiving end of Balrath's labor transit system: arrival platforms, manifest checks and assignment processing. The platforms are bare and functional, with a marshalling area beside them and a processing line under a long canopy, and the whole space is built for moving people through rather than holding them. Families learn their classification and their destination in the same few minutes. Names are read from a manifest, checked against a record, and answered with a block number and a work order. Belongings are carried, not stored. The transit crews work fast, because the schedule was written somewhere that has never seen this platform. When a run is finished the platforms are empty within minutes and stay that way until the next one.

The Camp Infirmary.description: The ring's medical room, running on ration allotments and the stubbornness of its physicians. It is one room with a treatment bay, a few beds behind a screen, a locked supply cabinet and a desk where everything is written down. Supplies decide treatment more often than diagnosis does, and the staff improvise constantly, substituting, rationing and deciding which of two people needs the last of something more. Anyone treated beyond their allotment becomes a small entry in a record that someone else will interpret later. The physicians write those entries anyway. Patients arrive after a shift rather than during one, because an hour missed is an hour that has to be explained, and the busiest part of the day is the one after the crews are released.

The Ration Allotment Post.description: The distribution point where food and supply allotments are issued against classification records. It is a counter under a canopy with a scale, a terminal and shelved stock behind, and a queue rail running out across open ground. The measure is exact and the calculation is never explained. Records are read, the allotment is weighed out, and the entry is closed. People arrive early, collect quietly, and share afterward in ways the post does not record and does not entirely fail to notice. The clerks work to the figures they are given and have no discretion to adjust them. Queue order is kept by the people in it rather than by anyone at the counter, and it holds because everyone has to come back tomorrow.

The Work-Order Muster.description: The assembly yard where crews form at shift call and work orders are read against names. It is an open expanse of compacted ground with a raised reading position at one end and painted crew marks on the surface, and there is nothing in it to stand under. Reassignments are announced with no preamble, and a changed order can separate a household by morning. Names are called, crews close up, and the yard empties in the order the orders were read. The yard is loud for ten minutes and then completely empty for the rest of the day. The painted marks are repainted when they wear, and the paint is the one thing on the ground that is maintained to a schedule.

The Camp Perimeter.description: The outer boundary of the camp ring: barriers, patrol tracks and monitored crossings that turn movement by work order into a physical fact. The crossings are gated and staffed, the patrol track runs worn and unsurfaced alongside the barrier line, and monitoring posts stand where the ground gives the best view rather than at regular intervals. Its form varies considerably along its length, and no stretch of it is a reliable guide to the next. Crews pass out and back through the same crossings on the same orders, and the checks at shift end are slower than the ones at shift start. What does not vary is that leaving requires a document, and documents are issued somewhere else entirely.

The Southreach.name: The Southreach
The Southreach.basicInfo:
Ring 5, the outermost southern approaches toward Dustfall: patrol roads, checkpoint chains and the smuggler country where Dravon's writ frays. The built part of it is thin and functional - hard surfacing, barrier posts, checkpoint housings, monitoring masts standing alone on open ground - and between those points the country is broken, unimproved and difficult. Redline sweep formations work this ground against smuggling, refugee movement and Accord traffic, deploying under the same red command-lights the corps is named for and moving in formation rather than as individuals. Checkpoint documentation is handled by outer-ring civic staff; the authority behind it is not theirs. Traffic is sparse and consists mostly of the things the state has authorized, which means anything unscheduled is conspicuous. Away from the roads, the ground rewards knowledge of it and punishes the lack, and the practical reach of any patrol is a matter of hours and terrain rather than of policy. Further out, competing claims along the shared frontier route exceed what anyone can actually control, and skirmishing keeps regular patrol off it. The writ is real and it frays, and both facts are the place.

Work on offer here: Quilrath — The Schedule That Changed (ask Cadi Selm); Corridor — Into the Outer Rings (ask Torbek Karn); Corridor — Past the Quiet Mile (ask Cadi Selm).
The Southreach.hiddenInfo: Underneath the patrols run the escape lines south. The Quiet Mile is a stretch of the Southreach where the patrol schedule has been quietly purchasable for years, and the Archive's routes use it — a standing arrangement, not a guarantee, and a new officer or a trap would look identical until someone walked it. Cadi Selm guides families through carrying Archive copies as memorized fragments and has never seen Dustfall in daylight. Beyond the Quiet Mile lies the Accord's Dustfall-facing outpost, the settlement the mutual-aid lists actually run through; Dustfall itself is not Accord. Captain Avrenna Volsk sweeps this ground as a true believer with one crack in her certainty: a childhood friend who exists in no record and whom she remembers anyway. Competing Dravon and Ignivex claims on the shared frontier route exceed what either can actually control, and ongoing skirmishes keep regular patrol off it — without removing a single checkpoint here.

The Patrol Roads.description: Hard-surfaced routes running south through open country, worked by Dravon patrols and Redline sweep formations. They run straight where the ground allows it, with barrier posts and monitoring masts set along them and nothing else in sight for long stretches. Traffic is sparse and heavily watched, and a vehicle off schedule draws attention within minutes. Movement is logged at the fixed points and inferred between them, so timing matters more here than documents do. Patrols run to a pattern that is varied deliberately, and the varying is something the people who use this country study. The roads are maintained better than anything in the Camp Belt, for reasons unconnected to the people living near them. Repair crews work them on a schedule and do not stay past their shift.

The Checkpoint Chains.description: Strings of checkpoints across the southern approaches, each logging documents, cargo and direction of travel. A checkpoint is a barrier, a reader post, a shelter for the staff and a search bay off to one side, set where the ground funnels traffic rather than at measured intervals. Kathvar staff process the paperwork; the authority behind it belongs to someone else. A vehicle is stopped, the manifest is read against the load, and the direction of travel is entered whether or not anything else is. Exact placement shifts, and the shifting is the point - a route that was clear last month may not be clear tonight. The staff learn a regular carrier's face and still check the documents, because the check itself is the thing being recorded.

Smuggler Country.description: The broken ground beyond reliable patrol coverage, where Dravon's writ frays into intermittent presence. It is unimproved country of cut ground, loose footing and cover that comes and goes, with no marked route through it and nothing built that was meant to last. Smugglers, families moving south and Accord runners all use it, sometimes on the same night without ever meeting. Movement here is slow, unlit and navigated by memory of the ground itself. Patrol presence is real but intermittent, and a sweep through one stretch says nothing about the next. The terrain rewards people who know it and punishes everyone else, which is the only law out here. The few usable water points are known to everyone who works the country, and they are approached carefully for exactly that reason.

The Quiet Mile.description: A stretch of the Southreach where the patrol schedule has been quietly purchasable for years, and the escape lines run. Nothing marks it and nothing about it looks different from the country on either side; it is ground like the rest of the Southreach, and its significance is entirely a matter of timing. Its length, course and endpoints are known only to the people who walk it. Passage is walked rather than driven, with guides carrying nothing that would identify them and families told only as much as they need for the next stage. The arrangement is standing rather than guaranteed, and in all those years it has never once been written down. A changed schedule and a trap look identical until somebody walks it.

The Quilrath Gate.name: The Quilrath Gate
The Quilrath Gate.basicInfo:
Quilrath's one Lunar Gate, with a single direct destination: Relstaris. It is old, Contair-built before the permanent bar, and kept barely functional by Dravon engineers working without Contair support. The structure stands at the centre of a working yard of staging areas, cargo lanes, escort stations and engineer positions, and the contrast between the original work and the Dravon patching laid over it is visible to anybody who looks at the foundations. Traffic moves under treaty-remnant inspection: cleared departures form up in the yard, arrivals are processed in an intake hall, and inspectors examine the legacy structure under escort because its foundations are Contair infrastructure Dravon cannot legally refuse to have inspected. Engineers monitor field readings, log faults and improvise repairs out of whatever is available, then document the improvisation carefully afterwards. The work never stops and it never gets ahead. Nothing here reaches anywhere but Relstaris, and no route board suggests otherwise. Every failure of this gate tightens the city, and everyone who works the yard knows it, which gives the whole place the particular carefulness of people maintaining something they could not replace.

Work on offer here: Quilrath — The Gate's Last Failure (ask Pelna Ostrek).
The Quilrath Gate.hiddenInfo: The inspections exist because the foundations are legacy Contair infrastructure Dravon cannot legally refuse to have examined and cannot afford to lose — inspectors enter under Access Level 2 as escorted inner visitors, and the escort is not courtesy. Pelna Ostrek, the Dravon engineer who liaises with them, dreads two things equally: the day the gate fails for good, and the inspectors noticing how close that day is. Her readings say the next failure may be the last one; filing the report would end her career and not filing it might end the gate. Nobody present knows how to build what they are maintaining, and Balrath's Prototype Gate Lab has not changed that. There is no Helvyra link and no Corsair Waypoint here — the Dravon Disconnection is absolute — so Relstaris political traffic is the city's one direct door, and everything else arrives indirectly or not at all. No route, corridor or transit sequence between this gate and anywhere else in Quilrath is fixed.

Quilrath Gate Yard.description: The working yard around the gate: staging areas, cargo lanes, escort stations and the constant traffic of engineers crossing between jobs. The surfacing is hard and marked out in lanes, cargo is held in numbered bays, and the escort stations sit where the lanes converge so that nothing reaches the structure unaccompanied. Departures for Relstaris form up here under inspection, called forward in order, checked once at the bay and again at the line. Engineers cut across the lanes all day carrying parts and readings between positions, and the yard crews have long since stopped moving out of their way. The yard has the atmosphere of a place where everyone is quietly aware the equipment is older than they are. Spare housings are stacked along one edge, salvaged rather than ordered.

The Legacy Gate Structure.description: The Contair-built gate itself, raised before the permanent bar and never replaced: foundations and field geometry nobody currently in Quilrath knows how to reproduce. The original work is precise in a way nothing around it is, its surfaces still true and its joins still tight, and the Dravon maintenance shows as patching laid over it - brackets, shunts and replacement housings fitted to an original they were not designed for. Access to the structure itself is controlled and every approach is logged. When it cycles, the sound is wrong in a way the older engineers recognize. They describe it to newer staff in terms of what it used to sound like, which is the only record of that anybody has. The patching is neat, and it is patching.

The Inspection Floor.description: Where treaty-remnant inspectors examine the legacy structure under escort, reading systems Dravon cannot legally refuse to have examined. It is a working floor rather than a chamber: instrument positions, a run of access points to the structure's lower systems, and an escort standing at each one for the duration. The sessions are formally polite and mutually resented. Inspectors state what they intend to examine, the escort confirms it, and the examination proceeds at whatever pace the inspectors choose. Every finding is recorded by both sides, and both sides read the other's face rather harder than the instruments. Sessions end on time regardless of what has been found, and the findings are exchanged as documents at the floor's edge before anyone leaves.

The Engineer Stations.description: Cluttered working stations where Dravon gate engineers monitor field readings, log faults and argue about what the drift means. The benches carry more instrumentation than surface, cabling is run and re-run overhead, and the fault log is open on a display at every position. Repairs are improvised from available parts and documented carefully afterward, because the documentation is the only thing that makes the next improvisation possible. Arguments here are technical, sustained and conducted in front of the readings. A shift is mostly watching numbers that should not move and noting the ones that do. The fault log is long enough now that newcomers are told not to read it end to end, and the older engineers can quote its worst entries from memory.

The Arrival Processing.description: The intake hall for travellers off the Relstaris run: identity checks, permission review, escort assignment, and a wait that is never short. The hall is plain and brightly lit, with a queue rail folded back on itself, processing positions along one wall and a holding area for anyone whose paperwork needs a second look. Cleared passengers still face local processing, because nothing about arriving in Quilrath is automatic. Documents are read, permissions confirmed against the record, and escorts issued to anyone who cannot move alone. Staff work steadily and answer questions with the same short formulations each time. First impressions of the city are formed standing in this queue, under a ceiling fitting that has been replaced and does not match its neighbours.

Relstaris City.name: Relstaris City
Relstaris City.basicInfo:
Relstaris City is the broad public hub of the planetary capital, where silver and white terraces run beneath the blue glow of the Core and no single house owns the street. Academy students, house delegates, traders, service workers, performers and minor-house families share the same crossings all day and most of the night. It is monumental without being empty, and it never entirely quiets down. The hub is built in layers that were never meant to match: pale star-glass frontages and light decking stand on ancient star-metal bracing, old energy conduits run inside modern lighting runs, and a single terrace can carry a foundation from one custodial era, a security corridor from another, expansion balconies from a third and Republic notices bolted over all of it. Colour changes from street to street rather than holding to one civic palette, so silver gives way to warm stone frontages and then to darker composite within a few crossings. Corelight is the hub's clock as much as its light; its intensity shifts with city demand, maintenance cycles and daily routing, and residents read the work period, the evening and the maintenance window off the strength in the roadbed. Food, transit fares, lodging and repairs all cost money here, desirable addresses cost a great deal, and much of the hub's daily conversation is about what can be afforded and who can be asked.

Work on offer here: Relstaris — A Shift at the Civic Desk.
Relstaris City.hiddenInfo: The hub is the city's earliest warning system. Announcements posted in the Public News Gallery are frequently the first public trace of a Republic decision still being argued over inside the Citadel, and gallery curators quietly control how long an inconvenient item stays visible. Hundred Banners Walk is a permanent low-grade dispute: banner placement is reviewed by shared-ground administrators, and a minor house raised or dropped a few metres along the processional reads as a political verdict to everyone who works here. Orientation staff in the Capitol Orientation Hall keep informal notes on which arrivals ask about house compounds rather than Academy directions, and transit coordinators at the Central Transit Ring can tell from lane loading when a compound is preparing to receive a delegation before any formal notice is issued. A small incident here becomes citywide news faster than officials can assemble a response, which is precisely why some people choose to start their trouble in the open.

Central Arrival Terrace.description: A broad civic landing platform of pale composite decking where local transit craft and escorted arrivals set down in rotation. Guidance markers light the walking lanes as each craft clears, and arrivals from eight cities spill into the same processing line. The air carries cold ozone from the lane emitters and the noise of a dozen accents trying to find the same exit. The decking is laid over older star-metal bracing that shows at the platform edges where newer surfacing has been cut back for repair, . Ground staff sort passengers by route rather than by house, hold escorted delegations in a separate lane, and refuse a setdown to any craft without a cleared slot. Someone is usually sitting on a case by the rail, waiting for a relative who has not arrived.

Corelight Avenue.description: The main avenue of the capital, carrying the visible blue glow of the Core uphill toward the Citadel between silver frontages that reflect it back. Delegations, commuters and street traffic share its width under standing flight restrictions. At dusk the light in the roadbed strengthens perceptibly, and residents still stop to watch it despite seeing it every day. The roadbed is a thick band of star-glass set over old energy conduits that were laid long before the present surface. Traffic wardens keep the pedestrian lanes clear when a house procession is expected, vendors work the crossings with permits they renew at civic desks, and the avenue's rents are high enough that a shopfront here is a claim in itself.

Every-House Plaza.description: A wide shared plaza with no house markings in its paving, used for festivals, demonstrations, speeches and public celebration by permit and by long custom. Movable stages and civic screens are stored beneath the surface and raised as needed. On an ordinary afternoon it holds food carts, arguing students and a tired protest that has been running for three days. The floor is laid in mixed pale stone and darker composite and the seams are kept deliberately plain so that nothing in the surface can be read as a house claim. Permit officers work from a booth at the edge, granting time slots and refusing overlapping events. The carts pay for their pitches, the screens are shared, and whoever speaks last is usually talking to people already packing up.

Hundred Banners Walk.description: A processional street displaying the symbols of the major houses and selected minor houses on suspended light-banners, none of which grants ownership of the road. Placement is reviewed on a public schedule and contested constantly. Visitors photograph it; residents read it like a ranking table and can name every house that moved this cycle. The banners hang from brackets fixed into old star-metal arches that carry newer light housings. Colour is deliberately unmatched along the walk, each house showing its own, and the effect at full brightness is a crowded corridor of competing light rather than a single civic scheme. A banner that dims is an immediate topic of argument, and the maintenance crews who replace the housings are careful to be seen doing it.

Public Flight Crossing.description: A controlled multi-level intersection where major flight lanes pass above pedestrian space, separated by lit lane fields and a cadence of clearance tones. Crossing wardens hold pedestrians for seconds at a time as delegation flights come through. Standing beneath it, the sound of passing fliers arrives slightly after their shadows do. The support columns are old work, star-metal cased in newer glass. Fast flight is restricted through the crossing, and the lanes are separated by use, with emergency routing, student traffic and formal approaches all holding different expectations. Wardens turn back fliers without clearance, argue with the same regular offenders, and keep a repair notice posted on the pedestrian rail about a field emitter that has been flickering for most of the cycle.

Capitol Orientation Hall.description: A high, quiet hall of interactive city maps, visitor guidance, plain-language legal information, Academy directions and civic service desks. Staff answer the same twenty questions in a dozen languages and keep a patient tone. The building smells faintly of warm machinery from the map tables, which run hot and are never quite switched off. The hall is older than its fittings. Arrivals queue for housing lists, work registration, Academy directions and the cost of a transit pass, and staff are direct about what is expensive and what is simply not available. A worn patch runs along the front edge of the largest map table where people lean while they argue about where they can afford to live.

Central Transit Ring.description: The hub's circular concourse of public lifts, shuttles and district transfer platforms, ringed by boards showing live routing to Low Relstaris, the Academy and the southern gates. Coordinators work from a raised platform at its center. It is the loudest civilised place in the district, and the only one where nobody apologises for pushing. The concourse floor is newer decking over an older structural ring. Fares are posted at every barrier, passes are checked, and the queues at the cheaper platforms are longer than at the express lanes for exactly that reason. Coordinators reroute lanes as loading changes, call closures over the concourse, and keep a handwritten list beside the main board of the transfers currently not running.

Public News Gallery.description: A long colonnade of civic display surfaces carrying citywide announcements, debate coverage, Academy results, market notices and cultural listings. People stop mid-commute to read, then argue with strangers about what they read. Curators rotate the panels on a set cycle, and everyone notices when an item vanishes early. The colonnade is old construction with newer panels set into the bays between its columns. Readers cluster by interest rather than by house, students at the results panels, traders at the market notices, and older residents at the civic announcements, and the arguments cross between groups constantly. A bench at the far end has been worn smooth by people who come to read the whole cycle through rather than pay for a private feed.

First Night Promenade.description: A popular evening route along a raised terrace where newcomers see the capital fully illuminated for the first time, the Core glow running under their feet. Vendors, buskers and guides work the railing side. Locals bring visitors here specifically to watch the moment the city registers on their face. The terrace is built out over older structure, its supports visible from beneath as star-metal work under newer glass decking. The light comes up as the evening activity period begins, brightening the roadbed below and the frontages across the gap in mismatched colours that belong to each street rather than to the promenade. The rail itself is polished dull along its whole length by the weight of people leaning on it.

City Overlook.description: A public terrace at the hub's high edge, open to anyone, revealing the Citadel above, the Academy towers west, the market levels below and the distant entertainment skyline. Fixed viewers name what is in sight from each angle. It is a favoured place for difficult conversations, because nobody here is watching anything but the view. The terrace is plain work, a broad slab of composite and glass anchored into far older bracing, its low parapet repaired in visibly different materials. From here the city's refusal of a single palette is obvious, silver and white in the central streets giving way to warm and dark frontages further out, all of it crossed by the blue of the Core running through the main roadbeds. Nobody collects a fee at the entrance, which is much of why it is always occupied.

The Citadel.name: The Citadel
The Citadel.basicInfo: The Citadel stands at the exact political center of Relstaris: Darkstar's residence, the meeting place of the Republic Council, the home of the advisor network, and the most protected descent toward the Core. It is not a palace but an immense working structure, ancient and restrained, that visibly preserves the architecture of previous Core holders rather than erasing them. Petitioners, staff, representatives and protesters move through its public levels every day under constant, polite observation. The building is a section cut through the city's whole history. Genesis-era foundations and challenge spaces carry Dravon security corridors, Corsair balconies open off later Castro restoration, and Republic fittings are bolted to all of it without pretending the layers match. Ancient star-metal bracing stands exposed where newer star-glass facing was cut back and never replaced, and old energy conduits run inside the lighting and signal runs that serve the modern offices. Corelight rises through the lower structure and is the building's clock as much as its light, strengthening with the opening of the work period, easing through the evening and dropping noticeably when maintenance routing takes hold.
