Access is the real currency here: entry costs nothing, an escort is not automatic, and a matter can take cycles of filings, travel and unpaid time that many petitioners cannot afford.
The Citadel.hiddenInfo: Nearly everything decided here is decided before it is announced. Council Deliberation Rooms handle the real negotiation; the Republic Council Chamber ratifies it, and the Petition Gallery receives the consequences weeks later. The Advisor Review Office currently has open work on conflicts of interest inside the administrative floors, which is why some advisors have become conspicuously cooperative. The Sealed Former-Holder Quarters and the Deep Citadel Archive hold records concerning old challenges, sabotage and emergency authority that several living houses would rather stayed classified rather than destroyed, and reclassification requests are a routine, quiet fight. Access matters more than rank: Castro Protection Wing personnel control the Secure Family Transit, the Core Descent is gated separately from everything above it, and a petitioner with the right advocate can reach a hearing faster than a representative with a grievance. Long-serving maintenance staff know passages the current security model does not fully account for, because previous governments built them.

Citadel Approach.description: A monumental shared avenue climbing from Corelight Avenue to the main structure, wide enough that a delegation and a protest can use it simultaneously without touching. Security markers are set into the paving rather than fenced. Arriving on foot takes long enough that the building has time to work on the person walking it. The paving is newer work laid over an older processional surface, and the seam is visible where the two meet part way up. Light rises through the joins with the strength of the Core routing, brightest when the work period opens and thinner during maintenance. Wardens keep the flight ban over the approach and know most of the regular protesters by sight. A worn line runs up one side where petitioners walk to stay clear of arriving delegations.

Coreward Steps.description: Broad public steps used for formal arrivals, petition queues, speeches and protests, with the Core glow rising faintly through their seams. Civic staff run the queue from portable desks near the top. On hearing days the steps are crowded by dawn and the arguments begin before the doors open. The stone is ancient and unevenly worn, patched in newer composite at the centre where the traffic is heaviest, so the repair reads as a pale stripe up the middle. Queue staff issue numbered marks, refuse places held for absent people, and send petitioners back down for filings that are not in order. The steps have no shelter and no seating, which is a constant complaint at the desks. People who have queued before bring their own cushions and share them with those who did not.

Public Entry Hall.description: The Citadel's controlled threshold: security screening, orientation, waiting benches and access routing to every public level. Staff assign escorts and issue temporary access marks that expire visibly. The hall is deliberately plain, and the wait is long enough that strangers with unrelated grievances end up comparing them. The hall is old defensive structure repurposed, its star-metal ribs bare above newer screening arches. The light is even and unsparing, dimming only when city routing tightens. Screening refuses weapons, unregistered recording gear and anyone whose filing reference does not resolve, and the refusals are handled quietly and without exception. The benches are scarred along their front edges by decades of people scraping them closer to the desks.

Petition Gallery.description: The public submission and hearing space where citizens, houses, businesses and institutions file matters and wait to be heard. Clerks triage, advocates coach, and the filing surfaces record everything submitted. Some petitioners have been coming for years and know the staff by name, which is not the same as being answered. The gallery is a long vaulted room with newer clerk stations built into bays that once held something else, the fixing scars still visible. Advocates charge for their help, and the difference between a filing written by one and a filing written alone is obvious to every clerk here. Matters are taken in order of filing rather than of standing, a rule enforced loudly and often. A bowl of spare styluses sits at the counter because people keep walking off with them.

Republic Hearing Chamber.description: A formal chamber for public testimony before representatives or appointed officials, with a raised bench, an open floor and recording surfaces that cannot be paused mid-session. Testimony here becomes citable record. Witnesses often discover that the hardest questions come from the official who is supposedly on their side. The chamber is Genesis-era work in its bones, a ribbed shell with Republic benches and recording columns fitted inside it and no attempt to disguise the difference. Light comes from the upper glass and the recording columns, steady and slightly cold. Attendance is public, seats are unassigned, and a crowded hearing is moved to a larger slot rather than closed. The floor before the bench is polished pale by people standing where they were told to stand.

Public Arbitration Court.description: Where major disputes over Relstaris law, housefront rights and shared civic property are heard and settled. Arbitrators sit without house insignia, a rule enforced at the door. Cases here frequently outlive the people who filed them, and the court keeps the running record of who inherited which argument. The chamber is plain, pale and acoustically dead, built inside older structure whose heavier arches are visible above the newer ceiling line. Parties pay for their own representation, and a long case can cost a small house more than the property it concerns. Clerks call matters in strict rota and hold both sides to the filed claim rather than the argument made in the room. The claimants' benches are fitted with narrow ledges worn smooth by generations of stacked documents.

Historical Custodian Walk.description: A public gallery recording every previous Core holder, including disputed, incomplete and deliberately unflattering eras. Panels state what is known and mark what is not. School groups pass through daily, and adults tend to slow at whichever era their own house would rather skip. The walk runs along an old structural corridor whose star-metal facing was left exposed during restoration, so the panels are mounted against the actual fabric of the periods they describe. Lighting is low and even, brightening panel by panel as people approach and settling again behind them. Entry is free and unescorted, guides work for tips at the lower end, and custodians correct visitors who read a gap as a hidden truth. One panel has been replaced so often that its frame no longer matches the others.

Core Observation Gallery.description: A protected public viewing level looking down onto the Corelight systems through layered shielding, with no direct access to the Core itself. The blue light moves slowly and unevenly. Visitors expect a machine and find something closer to weather, which is roughly the impression the Republic intends. The gallery floor is newer construction cantilevered into a much older shaft, and the joins where it meets the ancient wall are deliberately left visible. The light below shifts with demand and routing, flaring when the city pulls hard and thinning through maintenance windows, so the view is never the same twice. Numbers are capped and the queue is managed by staff who move people along firmly once their turn is done. The handrail nearest the glass is worn bright along its whole length.

Civic Memorial Court.description: A quiet open court memorialising city workers, protectors and civilians lost in earlier transitions and disasters, names cut into pale stone rather than projected. Families leave small objects at the base. It is the one public space in the Citadel where speaking loudly earns a look from strangers. The court is set into a gap between two older wings, its walls carrying the cut lines of structures that were taken down rather than restored. Light here is kept low and constant, deliberately held back from the shifts that run through the rest of the building. Custodians clear and store what is left rather than discarding it, and the storage is itself a record that families sometimes ask to see. A shallow groove runs along the base of the oldest panel where people have rested their hands.

Republic Council Chamber.description: The chamber where the Core Holder and the six major-house representatives meet, built as a ring so no seat leads. Votes and formal statements are recorded live to the Republic Records Office. The room is acoustically unforgiving, which means nobody can mutter something they are unwilling to have quoted. The ring sits inside a far older domed shell, and the difference between the ancient supports and the restored seating is visible at every junction. Each seat carries its house mark and nothing else, and the marks are refitted rather than rearranged when a house changes its representative. Staff are admitted only in fixed numbers, and the doors are held by Citadel personnel rather than house security. The floor between the seats is inlaid in a pale band that nobody crosses during a session.

Representative Hall.description: The working floor of the Republic: offices, preparation rooms, staff spaces and secure communication for each major-house seat, arranged along a shared corridor nobody can avoid. Aides trade information in passing. Six houses that dislike each other keep their filing clerks within thirty metres of one another. The corridor is a Dravon-era security spine reused as office access, its narrow sightlines now serving nothing more dramatic than paperwork. Each office is decorated to its own house taste, so the doors along one wall run through entirely different colours and materials. Space is allocated by the Republic rather than claimed, and requests for a larger suite are a standing source of complaint. The corridor carpet is worn through in a line between two particular doorways.

Council Deliberation Rooms.description: Smaller negotiation chambers used before public decisions, screened against recording and booked under neutral labels. Most Republic outcomes are actually settled here. Staff know a session went badly when representatives leave separately and none of them stops to speak in the corridor. The rooms are small, plain and identical, cut into older structure whose original divisions were replaced with uniform partitions. Light is flat and unchanging inside them, isolated from the routing shifts that mark the hour elsewhere in the building. Bookings run on a rota and are refused to anyone without a seat or a named delegation, which minor-house advocates raise as a grievance every petition season. Each room holds a jug of water and a stack of plain paper, and both are always used up.

Emergency Session Chamber.description: A hardened council space for citywide emergencies, with independent power, sealed doors and direct feeds from district and Core systems. It is tested monthly and used rarely. The seating is identical to the main chamber so that nobody has to renegotiate precedence during a crisis. The chamber is set deep in old defensive fabric, its star-metal shell reinforced under later governments and fitted with current systems. Its lighting is on a separate supply and does not follow the routing shifts that run through the public levels, which makes the room feel oddly detached from the city's hour. Entry is restricted to seat holders, named advisors and the technical staff who run the feeds. A supply locker by the door is inventoried after every test and never quite matches the list.

Republic Records Office.description: The current legal memory of the city: laws, decisions, appointments, votes and public directives, searchable by anyone with standing and a filing reference. Clerks are exacting about provenance. A request made here sometimes reveals more about the requester than the record reveals about the city. The office is a long hall of newer cabinetry inside a much older storage structure, the original heavy shelving still in place above and no longer used. Search access is free, certified copies are not, and the fees for a full case history are a real obstacle for a small house. Clerks refuse vague requests, insist on the exact reference, and will spend an hour helping someone who asks properly. The counter bell has been replaced with a written notice asking people not to ring it.

House Relations Office.description: The office that manages disputes arising from major-house activity inside Relstaris, from security boundary breaches to competing ceremonial claims. Staff work by de-escalation and precedent. Its corridor holds a permanent queue of aides who all insist their matter is urgent and none of whom are wrong. The office is converted older administrative rooms, its internal walls newer than its floor and its windows framed in star-metal older than every house complaining through them. Matters are logged, scheduled and answered in written form, which slows everything down and is entirely deliberate. Officers refuse to take a complaint verbally and refuse to discuss another house's filing. A map of marked boundary lines on the wall has been amended so often that the corrections are now layered.

Minor-House Petition Office.description: Advocacy, rotating hearings and representation requests for the smaller houses, staffed by officers who spend their days translating ambition into admissible filings. Cases are scheduled by rota, not influence. It is the busiest office in the Republic levels and the one with the fewest chairs. The room is small and low for this part of the building, fitted into space left over between larger offices, with pipes and conduit runs boxed in along the ceiling. Officers explain fees, advise on what a filing will actually cost in time and travel, and tell people plainly when a matter will not succeed. The rota is posted where everyone can see it and is the subject of constant, mostly good-natured suspicion. A second door was cut into the corridor because the queue kept blocking the first.

District Coordination Floor.description: The administrative floor connecting Central, North, East, South, West, Low and High Relstaris, with live district boards showing service, transit and protection status. District officers argue about allocation openly here. When a district drops off a board, everyone on the floor stops talking at once. The floor is one wide space carved from several older rooms, the removed walls still legible in the ceiling and the old conduits overhead. Board light is the brightest thing in the room and shifts constantly as reports come in. Allocation is fought over by officers who each have to go back and explain the outcome to their own district, and nobody leaves entirely satisfied. A repair request for one board's failing panel has been on the floor's own list for most of the cycle.

Planetary Affairs Chamber.description: Where the major houses negotiate shared declarations, external positions and coordinated responses without surrendering territorial authority. Dissent is formally recorded rather than suppressed. Drafting sessions run long because six houses can agree on an action and still fight over every clause describing it. The chamber is a restored older hall, its ancient ceiling left rough above newer pale composite and a long table that is the only recent thing in it. Light is steady and slightly warm, chosen to be unlike the council ring so that the two rooms are not confused in the record. Sessions are closed while drafting and opened for the reading, and the drafts themselves are filed whether or not they are adopted. The table carries a deep score along one edge that nobody will admit to.

Intercity Emergency Coordination Room.description: The room that requests, offers and tracks aid between Nexaran cities during crises reaching beyond Relstaris, with standing channels to each city's counterpart. Liaison officers keep a live ledger of what was given and what was owed. Nobody here pretends that generosity and leverage are separable. The room is compact and heavily fitted, its communication stacks built into an older wall whose conduit channels were reused. Arrangements are opt-in and negotiated case by case, and officers are careful to say so when a city assumes that preparation means obligation. Costs, transport and receiving capacity are settled before anything moves, which is where most of the delay actually happens. The ledger board keeps a column for aid promised and never sent, and it is not empty.

External Contact Office.description: A small, careful office maintaining procedures for future diplomatic contact without inventing governments or assigning representation to anyone who has not actually arrived. Its work is mostly protocol drafting and archival comparison. The staff are unusually relaxed, being responsible for something that has not happened yet. The office is two rooms at the end of a corridor, older work with newer shelving, the door still carrying the fixing holes of a previous function. Its light follows the building's routing, which the staff use as a cue to stop for the day. Requests to reserve space or standing for an unnamed party are refused outright and logged as refused. A shelf of blank protocol folders sits ready, labelled by procedure rather than by anyone's name.

Senior Advisor Hall.description: Offices for Darkstar's most trusted citywide advisors, plain rooms along a corridor with a single controlled entrance. Advisors here can reach him without a Council vote, which is exactly why access to the hall is watched. The atmosphere is quiet, fast and slightly under-slept. The corridor is old security fabric put to administrative use, its observation alcoves now holding chairs, files and a drinks station. The rooms are deliberately undecorated, and the only thing distinguishing one door from another is the name card slotted beside it. Entry is by standing appointment or summons, and staff without either are turned around at the head of the corridor without discussion. Someone has left a cold pot of tea on the station long enough that it has become a running joke.

City Operations Floor.description: Daily administration for infrastructure, staffing, service disruption and public works, run from a wide floor of shared consoles rather than private offices. Overnight faults are triaged here before dawn. The board of unresolved items is visible to everyone on the floor, which is both a tool and a punishment. The floor sits above a reused conduit run, and the low hum through the deck is a permanent feature new staff stop noticing. Work is priced as well as scheduled, and an item can sit on the board for cycles because the repair budget has gone elsewhere. Operations staff take calls from district officers, contractors and residents, and are blunt about who gets answered first. A spare console at the end of the row has been out of service so long it is used as a table.

Core Systems Coordination Office.description: The office connecting civic power demand to Core operations without holding any authority over the Core itself, a distinction its staff repeat constantly and mean. Load forecasts and district priorities are set here. During shortages this small room decides which neighbourhoods notice and which do not. The office is fitted into old machinery space, ancient conduit housings running behind the forecast boards with current cabling inside them. The maintenance windows that dim the city's light are planned here, so the staff know the hour by the schedule rather than the glow. Districts petition for priority, utilities are billed at local rates, and neither fact makes the choices easier. The forecast board carries a handwritten note reminding everyone which districts were cut last time.

Public Welfare Administration.description: Housing emergencies, shelter allocation, displacement cases, food access and civic support, handled by caseworkers with too many files and genuinely good systems. Applicants are seen in order of need, which is argued about daily. The waiting area is the warmest room on the administrative levels, deliberately. The offices are recent work inside an older civic shell, interview rooms partitioned out of a single hall with the original ceiling unbroken above. Caseworkers explain what is covered, what is subsidised and what must be paid, since nothing here is free and desirable housing is beyond most applicants. Refusals are given in writing with the grounds stated and can be appealed at the same counter. A shelf of children's toys near the benches is restocked from staff pockets.

Market and Labor Administration.description: Commercial regulation, labour disputes, public contracts and shortage management, conducted across long tables where employers and worker representatives sit within reach of each other. Rulings are posted publicly the same day. The office is loud in the mornings and unnervingly quiet whenever a large contract is under review. The hall is old trade-era construction with newer tables and recording fittings, heavy brackets from some earlier use still bolted along the upper walls. Permits, licences and contract filings all carry fees, and the posted fee schedule is read more carefully than any ruling. Officers refuse to hear a dispute until both sides have filed, which regularly leaves one party waiting alone. The posting board outside is overlapped three deep by the end of a busy day.

Academy Liaison Office.description: The channel between city government and the Academy's independent administration, staffed by people fluent in both bureaucracies and loyal to neither. It handles incidents, funding friction and student unrest. Everyone here understands that the Academy will cooperate precisely as far as its independence is left intact. The office is modest, two connected rooms of newer fitting inside older fabric, its window frame exposed star-metal left as the restoration found it. Tuition, housing support and student hardship come up constantly, since many families pay more for a place in the city than for the teaching. Officers refuse to intervene in academic decisions and say so early in most meetings. A stack of unclaimed student files waits on the desk for someone to come back for it.

Protection Coordination Chamber.description: Public protection planning, emergency response and cross-house security coordination, run from a chamber with district maps that update faster than the people reading them. House security liaisons attend by invitation. Joint planning works because every participant is aware of what the others are not saying. The chamber is hardened older work, a Dravon-era command space whose heavy doorframes and sightlines survived every subsequent restoration. Map light dominates the room and changes as reports arrive, the fixed lighting kept low so the boards stay readable. Liaisons are admitted without their own personnel, searched at the door like everyone else, and briefed only on what concerns them. A cabinet of outdated district plans is kept because arguments about boundaries keep needing them.

Advisor Review Office.description: The internal investigator of the advisor network, examining misconduct, conflicts of interest and administrative capture. It can compel records from any administrative floor. Staff work behind closed doors and are noticeably unpopular in corridors where their most recent requests have landed. The office is deliberately unremarkable, a short run of rooms in older fabric with newer locks, positioned where nobody passes on the way to anywhere else. Its lighting is kept even and slightly bright, which staff claim is practical and everyone else finds unpleasant. Investigators refuse to discuss open matters and are the only administrative staff who routinely eat at their desks. The corridor outside has a bench that was put there for waiting witnesses and is almost never used.

Darkstar's Working Chamber.description: A quiet, functional office where the Core Holder receives only matters considered worthy of direct attention, furnished for work rather than audience. The queue to reach it is filtered by advisors. Most petitions that arrive here have already failed somewhere else, which is how they earned the room. The chamber is old construction plainly restored, its wall fabric visible behind a desk, a few chairs and nothing resembling a throne. The light is steady and unremarkable and does not announce the hour the way the public levels do. Matters arrive already summarised, and the people who bring them are expected to say what they want rather than describe the problem at length. A single worn chair faces the desk, its arms rubbed pale by the hands of people waiting to be told no.

Darkstar's Residence.description: Private residential space inside the Citadel, restrained rather than luxurious, built into older structure that earlier holders furnished very differently. Staff access is limited and rotated. Nothing in it suggests permanence, which visitors read as either discipline or a statement about the office he holds. The rooms carry outlines of grander arrangements stripped back rather than restored, doorways blocked and alcoves left empty. Light reaches them through upper glass and moves with the city's routing, which nobody has attempted to correct. Household staff work to a short list and a strict rotation, and the roster is reviewed as a security matter rather than a domestic one. A plain chair sits by one window in a position that has clearly not changed in a long time.

Private Foresight Room.description: A controlled, isolated space where possible outcomes can be considered without public interruption or observation, shielded against ordinary recording. Its use is not announced. Advisors treat the closed door as a scheduling fact rather than a mystery, and have learned not to ask what came of it. The room is small, bare and deep in the structure, built into a shell of ancient star-metal that later governments reinforced for entirely different reasons. Its light is fixed and independent of city routing, so the hour is not readable from inside it. Nothing is stored here, nothing is filed here, and the staff who clean it work under the same restriction as everyone else with access. The only furniture is a seat and a low table, both older than the current arrangement of the building.

Vega's Diplomatic Office.description: A practical office for diplomacy and house relations, used when Vega works from Relstaris rather than travelling. It holds briefing files on every major house and several minor ones. The room is arranged for two-person conversations, because that is where most of its actual work happens. The office is newer fitting inside an old outer wall, with a Corsair-era balcony door that opens onto a narrow ledge and is kept shut during formal meetings. The files are paper as well as recorded, because a document that cannot be pulled from a system is sometimes the point. Visitors are received by appointment and one at a time, and a delegation arriving together is asked to choose who comes in. A tea service in the corner is used constantly and never quite matches.

Castro Protection Wing.description: Quarters and duty stations for House Castro personnel assigned specifically to the Core Holder and the Citadel, including briefing rooms and equipment stores. Rosters are kept tight and reviewed often. Its officers are aware their presence is politically read, and behave with conspicuous, exhausting correctness. The wing occupies old garrison fabric, bunk alcoves and store rooms cut into a structure that has housed somebody's guards under every government here. Equipment is signed out and signed back, and the store's ledger is audited by Citadel staff rather than by the house. Personnel are barred from the Republic levels except on escort duty, a limit their officers over-enforce. The duty board by the door has a column for who is owed rest and is perpetually behind.

Family Reception Room.description: A private but informal space for Castro family visits, with ordinary seating and none of the ceremonial staging of the public levels. Conversations here are family first and politics second. It is one of the few rooms in the Citadel where somebody is likely to be laughing. The room is a restored corner of older residential fabric, its heavy window frame original and its furniture plainly chosen for comfort rather than to match it. Light comes in from the upper glass and swings with the city's routing, which gives the room a noticeably different feel across a single visit. Staff bring food and then leave, and the door is closed by the family rather than held by anyone. A low table carries a ring mark that has been there long enough to be considered part of the furniture.

Secure Family Transit.description: A protected internal route connecting the Citadel to the Castro Compound and other approved destinations, screened along its length and logged at both ends. Use is restricted to an approved list. The log itself is sensitive, since who travelled when is often more informative than what was said. The route runs through older service fabric, a reused passage with newer screening stages fitted at intervals and ancient conduit housings still clamped alongside. Its lighting is on the route's own supply and holds level regardless of what the city grid is doing. Transit staff check names against the list and have refused people whose standing suggested otherwise. One screening stage has a door that catches, and the crews have learned to lift it rather than wait for the repair.

Private Reflection Terrace.description: A high terrace overlooking the city rather than a ceremonial balcony, unroofed and exposed to wind off the upper structure. The Core glow is visible below as a slow line through the avenues. Nobody is announced here, and nobody speaks from it to a crowd. The terrace is a Corsair-era addition, its balustrade and outward curve entirely unlike the defensive fabric it was fixed to, and the junction between the two is plainly visible from the doorway. From here the city's mixed colours are laid out at once, silver and white in the central streets, warmer and darker frontages further out, all crossed by the blue of the roadbeds. Access is through a single door with no waiting space behind it, so nobody arrives here by accident. A single bench faces outward and is bolted down against the wind.

Core Challenge Court.description: The formal declaration space where a Starian may publicly contest the Core Holder, with a registrar's bench, terms boards and recording that cannot be stopped once opened. Declarations are rare and immediately citywide news. The room is kept ready at all times, which residents find reassuring and unsettling in equal measure. The court is among the oldest intact spaces here, a Genesis-era challenge hall whose supports carry later reinforcement and current recording fittings. Light here is plain and unchanging, so nothing in the room favours either party. The registrar records terms in the claimant's own words and refuses declarations that do not meet the filed form. The terms boards are wiped and reset after every use, and the surface has gone cloudy from it.

Witness Gallery.description: Tiered observation where representatives, officials, historians and invited observers confirm challenge terms and outcomes on the record. Attendance is itself a political act. The gallery is where a disputed result becomes either settled history or the beginning of a much longer argument. The tiers are newer seating dropped into an ancient viewing shell, the old stone steps behind them unused and unremoved. Places are allocated by the registrar's office rather than claimed, and the allocation list is examined afterwards as closely as the outcome. Observers may record their own account but may not interrupt, and the one rule enforced physically is silence during the reading of terms. The rail along the front tier is worn in six places where six sets of staff always stand.

Protected Contest Floor.description: A reinforced contest space designed to keep a formal challenge away from Core machinery and public districts, its surfaces built to absorb what a Starian contest produces. Technical staff verify containment before any use. It is the most carefully engineered room in the Citadel and the least often occupied. The shell is ancient work reinforced under several governments, so the wall at the inspection hatch reads as three materials layered together. Its lighting runs on a dedicated supply that holds steady whatever the grid is doing, which is noticeable to anyone arriving from the public levels. Access is barred except for verification, maintenance and a declared contest. The floor is resurfaced after every use, and the newest patch is always obvious.

Core Descent.description: The restricted passage leading down toward the Core, a long shaft of layered security stages where the blue light grows steadily stronger and the air turns cooler. Authorisation is checked at each stage, not once. Few people who work in the Citadel have ever been past the second gate. The shaft is ancient, its walls carrying conduit channels cut long before the gates were fitted, several still live inside newer casing. The light does not come from fittings but from the system below, which means it moves with demand and routing rather than with any switch. Descent is escorted, logged and refused without a named authority, and the refusals are recorded as carefully as the passages. A maintenance ladder bolted beside the third gate is older than the gate itself.

Core Security Ring.description: The final protected perimeter around direct Core access, a closed ring of monitored stations staffed continuously by vetted personnel. Nothing passes without dual confirmation. The duty here is famously tedious until the one shift in a career when it is not. The ring is set into old structural fabric, its station alcoves cut into stone shaped for an entirely different security arrangement. The light is the Core's own, strong and slightly unsteady, and the staff read the city's load off it without needing a board. Personnel serve fixed rotations, are barred from carrying records out, and are rotated between stations so that no one person holds a whole picture of the ring. A station log records the same shift handover phrase thousands of times over.

Emergency Isolation Chamber.description: A sealed space used when a Core incident threatens the Citadel or the central grid, able to cut the upper structure off from the descent entirely. Drills run without warning. Its existence is public, its activation procedure is not, and the difference matters during an evacuation. The chamber is heavy ancient work with later isolation gear fitted into it, the seatings for whatever sealed the passage before still cut into the stone alongside. Its own lighting is independent of the grid, which is the point, and it stays at one flat level while everything above it shifts. Only named technical staff and protection officers may operate it, and a drill that finds anyone else inside is written up. A hand-cranked backup beside the main control is tested more often than it is explained.

Deep Citadel Archive.description: Restricted records concerning challenges, transitions, sabotage and emergency authority, held below the administrative levels under access controls stricter than the Republic's own. Retrieval requires named authority and leaves a trace. Several holdings are legally reclassified rather than released, and a few were never catalogued at all. The archive occupies old vault space whose shelving has been replaced inside walls that have not, the oldest racks left at the far end. The air is dry and the light low and steady, insulated from the routing shifts above. Archivists refuse requests without the named authority and will not say whether a record exists, applying both rules to representatives too. A reading desk near the door carries a lamp far newer than anything around it.

Sealed Former-Holder Quarters.description: Preserved or repurposed rooms from earlier governments, some elegant, some plainly defensive, a few still politically sensitive enough to remain closed. Custodians maintain them without restoring them. Walking the corridor is the clearest available argument that the Citadel is older than any house currently claiming it. The rooms run through different materials and colours, heavy defensive stone giving way to trade-era balconies and then to quieter later work, the joins left as they were made. Some are lit and some dark, the dark ones because their supply was cut rather than by choice. Access is granted for maintenance, historical research and formal inspection, and refused for everything else. One sealed door carries a newer plate over an older mark, and neither has been removed.

The Relstaris Core.name: The Relstaris Core
The Relstaris Core.basicInfo: The Relstaris Core is the vast ancient energy system housed beneath the Citadel that powers the capital. It is machinery, not a throne or a source of personal power, and most residents know it simply as the light beneath the city and the reason control of the Citadel matters. Only specialists understand its full architecture, and only a small number of authorised staff ever stand inside it. Its energy carries city lighting, vertical transit, civic infrastructure, water and utility distribution, emergency barriers, Citadel systems and the visible Corelight threaded through the streets above. The system is not a single build: ancient star-metal chambers hold control platforms from several past governments, old conduits still run live inside newer casing, and current Republic fittings are bolted to surfaces shaped for equipment nobody now uses. The light down here is the same light the city reads as a clock, and its rise and fall with demand, routing and maintenance is planned and watched from these floors rather than merely observed. Nothing about the Core is free to the districts it serves, since utilities carry local costs, and the routing choices made here decide which neighbourhoods feel a shortage first. Crews work in short rotations, carry their own logs, and treat every unlabelled branch as older than the record that should describe it.
The Relstaris Core.hiddenInfo: Access is the whole politics of this place. Entry is controlled through the Citadel's descent and verified again at the Coreward Threshold, so the engineers who keep the city lit answer to a security chain rather than to the Republic floor, and the Core Systems Coordination Office above them has influence over demand but no authority over the machine. Routing decisions made on the Core Control Platform determine which districts feel a shortage first, and those decisions have repeatedly been leaned on for political reasons that never appear in the routing log. The Historical Holder Stations and Deep Power Conduits predate every current house: sections of the old architecture still respond to inputs modern systems no longer document, and maintenance crews maintain informal knowledge the official schematics do not carry. The Transition Verification Chamber exists because a contest outcome above means nothing until functional control is confirmed down here, which makes this the actual point where a change of government becomes real.

Coreward Threshold.description: The final authorised staging area before direct Core systems: equipment checks, suit calibration, authority verification and a last chance to turn back. Crews assemble here in silence more often than not. The blue light bleeding through the inner door is already bright enough to read by. The staging bay is newer fitting inside an ancient antechamber, its lockers and calibration frames bolted into stone cut for something long since removed. Verification is done by two staff independently, and anyone whose authority does not resolve is turned back without argument or explanation. Crews log equipment out and back, and a tool that does not return closes the threshold until it is found. A bench along the wall carries the worn hollows of generations of people sitting to fasten their boots.

Primary Power Chamber.description: An immense chamber containing the visible Core structure and main energy output, its scale hard to judge because the far wall is lost in glare. Sound arrives as a low continuous pressure rather than noise. Standing on the entry platform, the Citadel above stops feeling like the important building. The chamber shell is ancient star-metal, and the walkways strung across it belong to three later periods, each bracketed onto fixings made for something else. The light flares and settles as the city draws on it, so the chamber brightens when the work period opens and eases through the maintenance window. Entry is limited to crews with a task, and nobody works the floor alone. Handrails along the entry platform have been replaced in a newer alloy that does not match the walkway it serves.

Core Control Platform.description: The operational deck used to route, regulate and monitor the city grid, a curved bank of controls facing the Core with district loads displayed in live columns. Two operators are required for any routing change. What happens here is felt in ordinary kitchens across Relstaris within the minute. The deck is current equipment set into an older platform frame, and the cable runs beneath it use conduit channels cut for a system long replaced. Operators hold to a posted priority order, refuse informal requests from district offices, and record every change with both names against it. Maintenance windows are declared from this deck, which is why the city's light thins on a schedule rather than at random. A printed priority list taped beside the main column has been amended by hand more than once.

Energy Routing Gallery.description: A long gallery tracking distribution toward the major city sections, its wall a schematic of Relstaris rendered in moving light. Technicians walk its length reading balance rather than numbers. A section dimming here means a district somewhere above is about to start filing complaints. The gallery is a narrow older corridor with the schematic wall built across one side, its far side still showing the original channel mouths where conduits once entered. Technicians pace the length on a fixed round and hand over by walking it together at shift change. Requests to favour one district over another arrive constantly and are referred upward rather than answered here. One section of the schematic has been rebuilt in a slightly different colour and nobody has matched it.

Stabilization Floor.description: The technical floor of systems that prevent dangerous fluctuation, crowded with damping assemblies that run warm and are inspected constantly. Alarms are set conservatively and treated seriously. Engineers here judge the Core's mood by vibration through the deck plating before any display confirms it. The assemblies stand in rows on an old floor that was levelled and relevelled around them, and the oldest units sit on mounts cut for a different frame entirely. The air is warm and dry and carries the faint smell of hot metal that never entirely clears. Crews work in short rotations for heat exposure and sign off each other's inspections rather than their own. A hand-written chart of which assembly runs hottest hangs where the shift supervisor can see it.

Core Maintenance Access.description: Specialist service platforms and protected machinery routes threading between the Core's outer assemblies, narrow, well lit and physically demanding to work. Crews rotate on short shifts for heat and exposure limits. Most of the system's real knowledge lives with the people who work this route daily. The platforms are later work bolted to ancient housings, and the newer grating stops short in places where the original structure will take no more fixings. Light comes off the assemblies themselves and shifts with load, so the route is brightest exactly when it is least comfortable to work. Access is refused to anyone without a current qualification, including senior staff who let theirs lapse. A chalked note at one junction warns about a step that is not where the plan says it is.

Emergency Shutdown Ring.description: A ring of hardened stations able to compartmentalise sections of the grid during catastrophic fault, each requiring physical action rather than remote command. The procedure is rehearsed and the consequences are understood. Using it saves the Core and darkens whole districts, and both facts are printed on the station covers. The stations are set into an ancient ring corridor, their modern mechanisms seated in the mountings of whatever served the same purpose before them. Their lighting runs independently of the grid they can cut, so the ring holds one steady level while everything else moves. Drills run unannounced, and a station found obstructed is reported the same shift. The covers are scratched around their edges from being opened and closed by gloved hands.

Historical Holder Stations.description: Earlier control platforms preserved from previous governments, their interfaces incompatible with modern practice but still physically connected to the system. Custodians maintain them as record and as fallback. Every so often one of them registers activity that the current control platform did not initiate. The stations stand in a row along an old gallery, each in the style of its era, so the line runs from heavy defensive casing through ornate trade-era panels to plainer later work. Custodians clean and test them without modernising them, and a repair that would change an interface is refused. Historians visit by arrangement and are not permitted to operate anything. One station carries a brass-cased switch that has been labelled and relabelled by three different hands.

Deep Power Conduits.description: Ancient channels carrying energy down into the city's foundations, older than any house record and built to tolerances nobody has since had to meet. The walls are warm and the light moves along them like current in water. Survey teams still find branches that are not on any schematic. The channels have been tapped repeatedly, later casings clamped over original openings and modern cabling threaded through cuts made for something else. Light here is unmediated and moves with the city's demand, brightening and thinning in slow waves along the wall. Survey work is scheduled, escorted and logged, and crews are forbidden to open an unrecorded branch on their own authority. A set of cut marks near one junction was clearly made by tools the current inventory does not contain.

Restricted Core Center.description: The most protected portion of the system, reachable only under exceptional authority and never by a single person alone. Entry is logged at the Citadel and at the threshold. Those who have been inside describe it less as a room than as standing in the middle of the reason the city exists. The enclosure is original fabric, almost untouched, with later reinforcement standing clear of it rather than fixed into it. The light inside comes from the system and is strong enough that crews work in shielded visors regardless of task. Authority is granted case by case, expires with the task, and is refused far more often than it is given. The floor immediately inside the seal is worn in a narrow arc where people stop before going further.

Holder Access Station.description: The recognised operational position used by the current Core Holder, symbolic because of the control it exercises rather than any change it works on the person standing there. It is plain, precisely positioned and continuously monitored. Its authority is procedural, which is exactly what makes it worth contesting. The station is a small newer platform seated on an ancient mounting older than every government that has used it. Its light comes off the Core directly and moves with the city's load, so the position is never evenly lit twice. Verification staff attend, record the sequence, and refuse operation to anyone not recognised as holder. A plain rail around the platform has been polished bright by a small number of hands over a long time.

Transition Verification Chamber.description: The chamber used to confirm that a new holder has secured functional control after a successful contest, with independent verification staff and recorded sequence testing. Nothing about a transition is final until this room signs it. Its records are among the most consequential documents the city produces. The chamber is old work refitted for the purpose, its recording equipment on brackets that carried earlier verification gear. The light is deliberately fixed and independent of the grid, so that nothing in the test can be read off the room itself. Verification staff hold no house affiliation on duty and will restart a sequence over one ambiguous reading. A cabinet of superseded verification protocols is kept here rather than archived, and it is not a short shelf.

Starian Republic Forum.name: Starian Republic Forum
Starian Republic Forum.basicInfo: The Republic Council meets inside the Citadel; the Starian Republic Forum is the larger public political complex where representatives explain, defend and negotiate those decisions in front of everyone. It is formal, loud, visible and genuinely pluralistic, crowded with delegates, press, minor-house observers, district representatives and protesters who all have legal standing to be there. Ordinary citizens can walk in, read the record and watch their representative have a bad afternoon. The complex is a run of halls of different ages joined into one building, so a visitor crosses from heavy old civic stone into a trade-era colonnade and then into plain Republic fitting without leaving the public route. Star-metal bracing shows through where later facing was cut back, old conduit channels carry the current lighting runs, and the colours change hall by hall because nothing here was built to one scheme. Corelight reaches the public galleries through upper glass and shifts with city routing, brightening as the work period opens and thinning through maintenance, which is how the staff know a long session has run past its hour. Entry to the public areas costs nothing, but standing, filing fees, advocates, travel and time away from paid work all cost a great deal, and the difference between the houses that can absorb that and the people who cannot is visible in every queue.
Starian Republic Forum.hiddenInfo: The Forum is where the Republic's failures surface first. Dravon's delegation runs a sustained legal campaign against Castro legitimacy from its public-facing office, arguing civic failures rather than making accusations it cannot document, and each genuine service collapse strengthens it. Minor houses use the Observer Gallery and Petition Season Pavilion to force procedural recognition that the major seats keep deferring, and the pressure is building rather than easing. The Representative Dining Court produces more binding agreements than the Speaking Floor, which is why press coordinators watch its entrances. In the Intercity Emergency Coordination Room an aid request from another city quickly reveals which houses will help and which expect concessions first, and those ledgers are remembered long after the emergency ends. Leaks are common here and rarely accidental: a decision made privately in the Citadel is often reframed on the Press Court floor before its authors have agreed how to describe it.

Public Assembly Hall.description: A large tiered hall for civic debate and nonbinding public sessions, open to any resident who registers at the door. Sessions run long and the floor microphones are fairly distributed. Nothing decided here is binding, which frees people to say what they actually think and occasionally changes votes elsewhere. The hall is old civic construction with newer tiers fitted inside it, the original gallery brackets still fixed above the current seating. Light comes through high glass and moves with the city's routing, so a session begun in bright conditions ends in a dimmer room. Registration is free but capped, latecomers are turned away, and the doorkeepers hold to the count regardless of who is asking. The register itself is a worn board by the door where people write their own names.

Representative Speaking Floor.description: The formal address floor for the major-house seats, a raised platform facing banked seating with speaking time tracked visibly. Representatives defend positions they may have opposed privately. The floor's recordings are the most quoted political material in the city and the most carefully rehearsed. The platform is newer work set into an older hall whose heavy ribbing runs unbroken above it, and the six seat positions are marked in the floor rather than built as furniture. Time is enforced by a clerk who will cut a speaker mid-sentence and has done so to every seat at least once. Public seating is unassigned and the front rows fill early, mostly with aides and students. The rail along the front of the platform carries a shallow dip where speakers grip it.

Republic Press Court.description: An open court for public questioning, announcements and political coverage, where correspondents from across Nexara hold assigned positions and shout anyway. Statements made here are immediately citywide. A representative who survives twenty minutes without a correction is considered to have done well. The court is a broad paved space roofed in later glass, the roof frame bolted onto an older colonnade that was never meant to carry one. Positions are allocated by accreditation, contested every cycle, and the allocation list is itself a minor political document. Staff refuse questions shouted from unaccredited positions and clear the approach lanes before a delegation arrives. The paving in front of the speaking step is scuffed pale in a rough semicircle where the front rank stands.

Civic Hearing Rooms.description: A suite of specialised rooms handling hearings on housing, markets, Academy policy, labour and public safety, each with its own clerk and rolling schedule. Witnesses wait in a shared corridor. Most of the Republic's real legislative work happens in these unglamorous rooms with eleven people in attendance. The rooms are uniform partitions dropped into one older hall, and the original ceiling runs above all of them, ignoring the walls entirely. Hearings are free to attend and free to address, but a witness pays their own travel and loses a day's wages to do it. Clerks refuse evidence filed late, refuse to hold a slot open, and are entirely consistent about both. A rack of numbered seat cards by the corridor door is always missing two or three.

Major-House Delegation Offices.description: Public-facing offices for each Republic seat, arranged along one frontage so that citizens can visit six houses in an afternoon. Staff receive petitions, complaints and lobbying without distinction. The contrast between the offices is itself a political exhibit that every delegation is fully aware of. The frontage is one older arcade with six separate fit-outs behind it, so the doors run through six different materials, colours and degrees of expense. Each office keeps its own hours and its own reception style, and the ones that close earliest are remarked on. Callers without an appointment are seen in order of arrival, which some offices honour more carefully than others. The arcade floor is worn in an uneven line that is deepest outside two of the six doors.

Minor-House Observer Gallery.description: Formal observation seating with limited speaking access for the smaller houses, positioned high enough to see the floor and low enough to be heard when a speaking slot is granted. Slots are rationed by rota. The gallery is the loudest part of the Forum whenever rationing is discussed. The gallery is a later insertion into an older upper level, its benches fixed to a frame that was cut into the original stonework and never disguised. Houses pay for their accreditation and for the staff who sit here, which quietly shapes who is present on any given day. Observers may not interrupt, and the one who does is removed for the session rather than the cycle. A tally of granted and refused slots is kept on a board at the back by the observers themselves.

District Delegate Chamber.description: Where representatives from Central, North, East, South, West, Low and High Relstaris present local concerns directly, with district data displayed alongside each speaker. Delegates are elected locally and owe the houses nothing. Their testimony is the closest the Forum gets to hearing the city describe itself. The chamber is plain and rectangular, fitted inside older fabric whose windows were narrowed and later partly reopened. Data walls carry service, transit and protection figures beside each speaker, and delegates are held to the figures rather than to their arguments. Sessions are public, unticketed and often thinly attended except by the districts concerned. A set of district markers stands along the back wall, one of them repaired with a different clip from the rest.

Public Records Hall.description: A searchable public hall of current decisions, budgets, appointments and regulatory changes, staffed by archivists who will help anyone who asks properly. Terminals are free to use and heavily used. Journalists, students and aggrieved shopkeepers work the same tables in silence for hours. The hall is a converted older chamber with terminal tables set out beneath a ceiling that still carries the fixings of whatever hung there under a previous government. Searching is free but certified copies are charged for, and the charge is the point at which many small claims quietly stop. Archivists refuse vague requests and will spend an hour on a precise one. The third table from the door has a wobble that regulars correct with a folded card kept in the drawer.

Protest Plaza.description: Legally protected demonstration ground directly outside the Forum's main frontage, where standing permits and sound limits are enforced and nothing else is. Several causes usually share it at once. Representatives entering the building are required to pass within hearing of it, which was the point of the design. The plaza is plain paving of mixed stone and composite laid over an older surface, with the patch lines of decades of repairs crossing it in every direction. Permits are issued by time and by pitch, and groups without one are moved rather than dispersed. Wardens hold the approach lane open, measure sound at the frontage, and ignore everything else said about them. A row of bollards along one edge has been reduced by one, and the gap is where the food carts park.

Representative Dining Court.description: An informal dining court where representatives, aides and lobbyists eat in full view of each other and of anyone else with a seat. Social pressure works harder here than procedure does. More compromises are settled over a shared table than are ever announced on the Speaking Floor. The court is a Corsair-era arcade with later glazing, its balconies still carrying the ornament of a period that valued them and its tables plainly modern. Food is bought and priced like anywhere else in the city, and the cheaper counters at the far end draw staff while the frontage tables draw the seat holders. Tables are not reserved, which forces encounters that nobody would have arranged. One long table by the pillars is understood to be neutral ground and is never claimed for a delegation.

Emergency Public Briefing Hall.description: A hall reserved for citywide crisis announcements, with independent broadcast capacity and standing seating for press and public. It sits empty most of the year. When the doors are unlocked outside a drill, the city notices before the first word is spoken. The hall is hardened older construction, and its broadcast equipment is mounted on brackets that carried an earlier generation of the same function. Its lighting runs on a separate supply and does not follow the routing shifts visible everywhere else in the complex. Access during an announcement is open to the public until the standing area fills, after which the doors are held. A folded stack of chairs against the back wall is inventoried annually and never used.

Petition Season Pavilion.description: Expanded temporary chambers raised during major minor-house petition periods, modular halls that double the Forum's hearing capacity for a few weeks. Brokers, advocates and families fill them from early morning. When the pavilion comes down, whatever was not heard waits a full cycle. The modules are set on a permanent hardstand whose anchor points are cut into much older paving, and the sockets stay visible all the rest of the year. Lighting is strung from temporary frames and runs off a routed civic supply, so it dims with the same maintenance windows as the streets outside. Brokers charge for their services, families travel and lodge at their own cost, and both facts shape who actually files. A queue marker painted on the hardstand has been repainted in a different colour each season.

External Relations Hall.description: Public-facing diplomacy: visiting delegations from other Nexaran cities, reception protocol and preparation for contact not yet made, without assigning space to anyone who has not arrived. Its galleries are deliberately unfinished in places. Staff describe the hall as an argument about the future held in architecture. The hall mixes restored older reception rooms with plain newer building, the unfinished galleries bare structure with their service runs visible. Light through the upper glass moves with city routing, which visiting delegations invariably ask about. Reception protocol follows city of origin rather than house, and staff refuse requests to be received under a different standing. A shelf of prepared reception folders is labelled by procedure, with several blanks left at the end.

Shared Declaration Chamber.description: Where houses negotiate language intended to speak for Nexara while preserving formal dissent, drafting surfaces tracking every amendment and its author. Sessions run past midnight over single clauses. Agreement on the action is common; agreement on the sentence describing it is the difficult part. The chamber is a restored older room with a long modern table and drafting walls fitted where earlier fixtures were stripped out, their mounting scars left in the stone. Its lighting is held at one level through a session, deliberately isolated from the shifts that mark the hour elsewhere. Dissent is recorded in the same document as the agreement rather than in a separate filing, which is why the drafting is so slow. A jug and a tray of plain cups are refilled by staff without being asked.

Forum Emergency Coordination Room.description: Public and administrative coordination when one city requests aid from the others, with open channels and a visible ledger of what has been asked and offered. The room is kept staffed continuously. Its record of who hesitated during which crisis is consulted for years afterward. The room is compact and heavily fitted, its channel stacks built into older wall recesses that once served an entirely different communication system. Aid is arranged by negotiation rather than obligation, and staff say so plainly to anyone who arrives expecting otherwise. Costs, transport capacity and receiving capability are settled before anything is committed, which is where most delay occurs. The ledger board is public, which means arguments about its wording happen in front of whoever is standing there.

Treaty and Contact Archive.description: Storage and reading rooms for current external agreements, historical contact procedures and future diplomatic frameworks, accessible to accredited researchers and representatives. Documents are preserved in original form alongside working copies. Old intercity agreements here regularly undercut positions taken confidently on the floor above. The archive is newer cases inside an older vault whose original shelving remains above, empty and left in place. The air is dry and the light low and steady, kept clear of the routing shifts that move through the public halls. Accreditation is checked, reading is supervised, and copying is charged at a rate researchers complain about openly. A reading table by the window carries a blotter replaced so rarely that its stains are a kind of record.

The Living Archive.name: The Living Archive
The Living Archive.basicInfo: The Living Archive preserves the political, administrative, architectural and custodial history of the capital, from recognised Core holders to the governments that left nothing but foundations. It does not duplicate the Ravello Archive House in Solvraxis, which protects cultural memory; this institution holds the record of how Relstaris was governed and by whom. Scholars, representatives, property claimants and ordinary families researching their own histories work its floors side by side. The building is its own best exhibit, a heavy older shell that has been extended, subdivided and restored so often that a single corridor can run from defensive stonework through a trade-era gallery into plain modern reading rooms. Star-metal ribs stand exposed where later facing was cut back for cabling, old conduit channels carry the current lighting, and the wings differ in colour because each was finished in its own period and never brought into line. Corelight reaches the public floors through upper glass and moves with city routing, so the reading rooms brighten as the work period opens and dim through the maintenance window, which is when the staff begin asking people to finish. Consultation is free, but certified copies, expedited retrieval and accredited access all carry fees, and those fees decide a great many claims long before any archivist reads the file.
The Living Archive.hiddenInfo: The Archive is a weapon that everyone pretends is a library. Dravon and Genesis researchers maintain contradictory, professionally argued accounts of the same transitions, and the Contested History Court hears those disputes on an open schedule that both houses treat as a political fixture. Work in the Sol Custodian Archive keeps producing evidence that the ancient Sol holder mattered more than public education suggests, which unsettles several later legitimacy claims. The Property Claim Vault is the quietly explosive holding: housefront and inheritance claims running across multiple governments regularly show that a currently occupied property was acquired through a disputed concession, and a single retrieval can unmake a minor house's standing or make one. Restricted Civic Records exist because Relstaris reclassifies rather than destroys, so material concerning sabotage, mass harm and unresolved challenge legitimacy is still here, held behind authority levels that are themselves contested in the Republic.

Core Holder Record Hall.description: The Archive's central hall, a public record of every recognised holder and every contested transition, presented with the disputes intact rather than smoothed away. Panels cite their own sources. Visitors often arrive expecting a list of names and leave with a much less comfortable understanding of succession. The hall is the oldest intact room here, its ancient ribbing bare above newer panel frames deliberately not fixed into the original fabric. Light is kept even across the panels and does not follow the routing shifts felt elsewhere in the building. Entry is free and unescorted, and staff correct visitors who treat an acknowledged gap as a concealment. One panel stands with its citation column half empty, and the emptiness is the exhibit.

Ancient Government Gallery.description: Surviving evidence of governments that predate reliable house records: fragments of law, structural drawings, tools and administrative objects whose function is inferred. Labels state clearly what is guesswork. It is the quietest gallery in the building and the one historians argue about most viciously. The gallery is a low vaulted space at the base of the older structure, where the walls themselves are older than most of what stands in the cases. Light is kept low for the material and comes from the cases rather than the room, so visitors move between pools of it. Handling is refused without accreditation, and accreditation is refused to anyone who will not name their research. A case in the corner holds three objects and four competing labels, all of them current.

Sol Custodian Archive.description: Documents, recorded oral histories, artefacts and open disputes surrounding the ancient Sol holder, held together in one wing so the contradictions stay visible. Researchers book time months ahead. The wing's own catalogue has been revised three times because new material kept undermining the previous arrangement. The wing is a later addition built against the old shell, its joints with the original wall left open and visible rather than faced over. Reading desks are limited and allocated by booking, and a missed booking is given away rather than held. Sol families donate material here and are entitled to see how it is catalogued, which they do. A shelf of superseded catalogues is kept on open display alongside the current one.

Genesis Era Vault.description: Defensive plans, challenge records and civic construction documents from Genesis-backed periods, including engineering that still underlies parts of the capital. Access is open to accredited researchers. Genesis delegates visit often, and are careful to be seen requesting the material through ordinary channels. The vault is heavy work with a star-metal frame matching the construction it documents, the fittings inside plainly newer and lighter by contrast. The light is fixed and low, on a supply separate from the reading floors above. Documents are consulted at supervised tables, copying is charged for, and engineers queue like everyone else. A drawer of drawings for works that were never built is among the most requested holdings here.

Dravon Administration Wing.description: Laws, security system designs, access restrictions and surviving public records from Dravon rule, retained complete because incomplete evidence would serve Dravon better. The reading room is monitored. Scholars working here are used to being asked, politely and repeatedly, what they are looking for. The wing is an original Dravon-era administrative block absorbed into the Archive, its corridor sightlines and single entry point preserved because they were cheaper to keep than to remove. The lighting is flat and bright, and the room offers nothing to sit on except at a supervised table. Requests are logged with a stated purpose, and refusing to state one ends the request. A wall panel of surviving access regulations is read by visitors far more closely than the documents in the cases.

Corsair Expansion Records.description: Trade agreements, route openings, market charters and urban expansion plans from the period when the capital opened outward, with maps showing districts that no longer exist under those names. Merchants consult them for precedent. Several current route rights rest on documents in this room. The room is a Corsair-era gallery kept largely as it was built, its balcony and ornamented frontage restored rather than replaced and its shelving fitted between the original columns. Light comes through wide glazing and moves with the city's routing, which makes the map colours read differently across a working day. Copies are charged for, and a merchant with a live dispute pays the same as a student. The largest map on the wall has three eras of street names written over one another.

Castro Transition Chamber.description: Records concerning Darkstar's rise and the formation of the Republic, displayed with the objections of the time preserved alongside the outcome. The chamber avoids triumphal framing on principle. Visitors from houses that opposed the transition come here to check whether their opposition is still on record; it is. The chamber is recent construction inside an older room, deliberately plain, with the original walls left visible above the display frames. Light is even and unshowy and holds through the day rather than moving with the grid. Material is added as it is released, and the additions are dated in the open so that nothing appears to have always been here. A case of objections filed at the time is longer than the case holding the founding documents.

Contested History Court.description: A formal court where scholars and representatives dispute the interpretation of major events on the record, with citation requirements and a presiding archivist. Sessions are public and well attended. Findings do not change the past but do change which account gets taught in civic schools. The court is a restored older hall with modern recording fittings set on brackets that once held something ceremonial, the brackets kept and the ceremony gone. Sessions are free to attend and free to address if a citation is filed in advance, which is the obstacle that quietly limits who speaks. The presiding archivist cuts off argument without a source and is not appealed to for tact. The citation ledger by the door is the thickest book in the room.

Public Research Floor.description: Open floor for historical research and civic genealogy, rows of terminals and document tables used by students, journalists and families tracing a house branch. Staff assistance is free and unhurried. It is normal to see someone discover something about their own family and sit very still for a while. The floor is one long hall of newer tables under an old ribbed ceiling, with the terminal cabling run through channels that were cut for an earlier system entirely. Light falls from the upper glass and moves with the city's routing, which is how regulars know how much of the day they have left. Terminals are free, certified copies are not, and the difference stops many searches at exactly the point they become useful. A tray of pencils by the door is refilled daily and empty by the evening.

Oral History Court.description: A recording court collecting testimony from elderly residents, workers, families and communities that formal records excluded, with interviewers trained to ask rather than steer. Recordings are indexed by neighbourhood and trade. The court has become the single best source on what earlier transitions actually cost ordinary people. The court is a set of small quiet rooms built inside an older hall, acoustically lined and fitted with equipment that is replaced far more often than the rooms around it. Recording is free, travel is not, and the court sends interviewers out to people who cannot afford to come in. Testimony is kept as given, with corrections attached rather than merged into the original. A wall of index cards outside the rooms is written in dozens of different hands.

Property Claim Vault.description: Secured storage for housefront, district and inheritance claims extending across several governments, retrieved on request with a logged justification. Claim archivists are meticulous and unexcitable. A single folder from this vault can end a property dispute or start one that runs for a generation. The vault is old strongroom fabric with newer cases inside it, and the original iron-bound racks still stand along the back wall holding nothing. The air is dry, the light low and steady, and the room is entirely insulated from the shifts that mark the hour upstairs. Retrieval carries a fee and a wait, both of which fall hardest on the small houses whose claims are most often contested. A counter ledger records every retrieval by hand as well as by system, because it always has.

Restricted Civic Records.description: Sensitive holdings involving sabotage, mass harm, covert agreements and unresolved challenge legitimacy, kept under authority controls and reclassified rather than destroyed. Requests are recorded and reviewed. The reading room seats four, has no external connection, and is booked more often than the Republic admits. The holding is deep in the oldest structure, behind a door frame predating the classification system by several governments. Its lighting is independent of the civic grid and never changes, which staff describe as convenient rather than symbolic. Archivists will not confirm whether a record exists, apply that rule to representatives as readily as to students, and log the asking. The reading room table carries a single fixed lamp and no drawer of any kind.

Civic Commons.name: Civic Commons
Civic Commons.basicInfo: The Civic Commons is the district that keeps Central Relstaris from belonging only to officials: gardens lit by the city grid, festival plazas, family services, school courts and affordable food terraces under the shadow of government towers. Residents eat lunch here, children visit public institutions, and mixed-house families gather without anyone checking whose house they belong to. It is open and lively, and considerably less formal than anything uphill. The district was built and rebuilt in pieces, so its halls and terraces sit on older foundations that once served other purposes, with star-metal bracing showing through at the stair heads and old conduit runs reused to carry the garden lighting. Nothing here holds to one palette: the food terraces are warm stone, the service halls plain pale composite, the gardens dark planting over glowing paving, and the change from one to the next is abrupt. Corelight is the district's clock as much as its light, brightening as the work period opens, holding through the evening crowds and dropping back through the maintenance window, which is when the terraces begin to pack up. Everything here costs something, from a meal to a childcare place to a festival pitch, and the district's reputation rests on being the part of Central Relstaris where those costs are still manageable for an ordinary household.
Civic Commons.hiddenInfo: The Commons absorbs the human cost of the politics practised above it. The Petitioners' Rest Hall exists because ordinary people spend days navigating government, and its staff see who has been ground down by a process long before the Republic hears about it. Community Mediation Rooms handle mixed-house disputes that would become house incidents if they reached the Concourse, and mediators work hard to keep them local. Family Services caseworkers track patterns in household records that map neatly onto whichever district has recently lost services, which makes their aggregate reports politically awkward. Festival scheduling in the Shared Festival Plaza is negotiated between cultural groups under pressure from house sponsors who would prefer prominence, and the coordinator's rota is defended fiercely. The Open Debate Steps are watched informally by Forum staff, because an argument that catches on here reliably reaches the Speaking Floor within the month.
