Shared Festival Plaza.description: An open plaza built for citywide celebration and rotating cultural festivals, with fitted service points for stages, kitchens and light arrays. Between festivals it is simply a very large bright square. During one, it is the only place in Relstaris where eight cities' music plays within fifty metres of each other. The paving is laid over much older civic surface, the service points sunk into sockets cut through both layers and worn smooth by traffic. Pitches are allocated by permit and charged by position, and traders contest the corners that take the most custom. Light arrays run off the civic grid and dim with the maintenance window, which organisers plan around rather than argue with. A ring of scorch-marked plates near the kitchen points is replaced more often than anything else here.

Corelight Gardens.description: Public gardens illuminated from below by the visible city grid, planted with species that tolerate constant soft light and arranged for sitting rather than display. Office workers claim the benches at midday. The blue underglow makes the foliage read slightly unreal, which residents stopped noticing years ago. The glowing paths run along reused conduit channels, and the beds are built over an older surface that shows at the margins. The underglow rises and falls with city routing, so the gardens are brightest at the turn of the work period and noticeably dimmer during maintenance. Caretakers replant constantly and post notices asking people not to sit on the light strips. One bench has been repaired in a wood that does not match the others and is the most used in the garden.

Open Debate Steps.description: Shallow public steps where anyone may speak, argue or heckle without a permit, facing a paved area that fills and empties through the day. Regulars hold their usual positions. Forum staff pass through often enough that a good argument here has a genuine chance of reaching a hearing. The steps are old stone patched in newer composite where the traffic has worn them through, and the patches have themselves been patched. Light comes up through the paving in front of them and strengthens through the evening, which is when the crowd is largest. Nobody schedules or moderates, and the only enforcement is a warden who arrives when the paving stops being passable. A worn flat stone near the centre is understood to be where a speaker stands, and people step around it when nobody is using it.

Family Services Hall.description: Childcare assistance, household records, mediation intake and public support, handled at open desks with private rooms available on request. Caseworkers carry heavy loads and know their neighbourhoods. The hall is designed to be walked into by someone who has not yet decided to ask for help. The building is plain newer construction around an older civic core, the original stair and its heavy balustrade left standing in an otherwise modern room. Light is warm and steady and does not dim with the city's routing, because the hall keeps longer hours than the offices uphill. Caseworkers are direct about what is subsidised and what must be paid, since childcare, housing and records all carry costs. A basket of spare hair ties and clips by the desks exists because parents keep needing them.

Civic School Court.description: A court built for field trips, public history lessons and youth events, with demonstration spaces and seating scaled for children. Classes from every district cycle through weekly. Teachers use the Citadel visible above as a teaching aid and spend a lot of time correcting what the children already believe about it. The court is set into a gap between two older buildings, its walls carrying the cut lines of a structure that was removed to make room for it. Its paving is soft composite over older stone in blocks of different colours, replaced in sections rather than all at once. Visits are booked by school and free, though travel costs fall on the schools furthest away. A painted line marking where classes assemble has been repainted slightly off the original at least twice.

Public Performance Walk.description: A pedestrian walk given over to street performers, student groups and cultural demonstrations, with marked pitches allocated by a public rota. Standards vary wildly and the crowd is honest about it. On good evenings, three traditions from three cities are being performed within earshot of each other. The walk runs beneath an older arcade whose columns carry newer lighting brackets bolted into fixings cut for something else. The light strengthens as the evening crowd builds and thins again through the maintenance window, which performers treat as closing time. Pitches are free but rationed, the rota is posted and policed by the performers themselves, and a pitch held beyond its slot is a genuine argument. A chalked score of pitch numbers on one column is redrawn every few days.

Youth Flight Park.description: A controlled movement and flight play space with soft field boundaries, graded height limits and supervisors who intervene rarely but decisively. Children learn to fly properly here rather than off a residential roof. The park is loud, chaotic and the most genuinely equal space in Central Relstaris. The field emitters sit on a frame built over an older open court, the original paving still visible beneath the soft surfacing at the edges. Boundary lights hold their level through the day because the park runs on a protected supply, unlike the terraces around it. Use is free, equipment loan is not, and supervisors ground a child for the session without consulting the parent first. A dented panel on the lowest boundary frame has been repaired until its colour matches nothing around it.

Community Mediation Rooms.description: Small neutral rooms for neighbourhood and mixed-house dispute resolution, booked freely and staffed by mediators with no house affiliation on duty. Sessions are confidential and unrecorded. Most disputes settled here would have become formal house matters if they had travelled another kilometre uphill. The rooms are partitions inside a single older hall, and the original ceiling runs above them unbroken, carrying conduit that serves the whole block. Their lighting is flat, warm and identical in every room, chosen so that no room reads as the better one to be given. Booking is free and open to anyone resident in the city, and mediators refuse sessions where one party has been brought under pressure. A jug of water and two plain cups sit in every room, and the cups never match.

Public Food Terraces.description: Stepped terraces of affordable food stalls drawing on traditions from across the city, with shared seating and no reserved tables. Prices are posted and modest. Protesters, clerks and off-duty protectors regularly end up at the same table because there is nowhere else to sit. The terraces are cut into an older slope, the stall bays fitted into arches that served some other purpose before the kitchens arrived. Stallholders pay for their pitches and for their power draw, which is why the boards list what is cheap today rather than a fixed menu. Light here is warm and local rather than the blue of the roadbeds, and it comes on early because the terraces open before the offices do. The long shared tables carry initials cut into them going back further than any current stallholder.

Central Recreation Court.description: Open court space for public games, exercise and noncompetitive training, marked for several sports and used for all of them at once. Equipment is available on loan. Academy students occasionally come down to train here and are reliably beaten by local pensioners at something. The court is laid over an older civic surface, and the markings of at least three games overlap in different colours, none of them removed when the next was added. Light comes from posts around the perimeter and dims with the city's maintenance window, which ends play more reliably than any rule. Loan equipment is free against a deposit, and the deposit is why the better gear is always out. A goal frame at one end has been straightened so often that it no longer quite matches its partner.

Petitioners' Rest Hall.description: Practical shelter for citizens spending days navigating government: seating, charging points, water, lockers and advice on which office actually handles what. Staff keep it calm and warm. The hall's informal knowledge of the bureaucracy is better than the bureaucracy's own, and it is offered free. The hall is an older civic room refitted plainly, heavy original beams above and cheap comfortable seating below. Its light is warm and constant rather than following the routing shifts outside, because people sleep here between hearings. Lockers are free for the day, water is free, and the food counter charges the lowest prices in the district. A wall board of handwritten office directions has been corrected by so many hands that the original is barely visible.

Night Garden Walk.description: A quiet path through planted terraces used after dark for dates, recovery and the conversations that follow difficult political sessions. Lighting is kept low enough to see the sky. It is the one route in Central Relstaris where people slow down without being asked to. The path runs along an older retaining structure, its stonework left rough where later work was removed rather than faced over. The low lighting is on a separate supply and holds its level rather than moving with the grid, which the people who use it appreciate. Caretakers work the path before it opens and after it empties, and vendors are not permitted along it at all. A bench set slightly off the path in a gap between plantings is the most sought-after seat in the district and is never advertised.

Grand House Concourse.name: Grand House Concourse
Grand House Concourse.basicInfo: The Grand House Concourse is the shared ground linking the six major-house compounds and connecting them to the wider Hundred Houses Quarter. No house may permanently close it or move unrestricted forces across it, a rule maintained by the Republic and enforced at clearly marked boundaries. It is impressive, competitive and culturally diverse, and every ceremony held on it is also an argument about precedence. The Concourse itself is older than most of the frontages on it, laid on ancient star-metal foundations with reused energy conduits running beneath the processional and surfacing at inspection covers set into the paving. The compounds facing it were each finished to their own house's taste, so the street runs through six incompatible palettes and six kinds of stonework within a short walk, and the shared paving between them is deliberately plain so that nothing in it can be claimed. Corelight reaches the Concourse through the paving and the boundary markings and shifts with city routing, brightening as the work period opens and dropping through the maintenance window, which is why ceremonies are scheduled around it. Everything on the shared ground costs somebody something: pitches, bookings, guest accommodation and ceremonial allocations are all charged and all contested, and the review office that settles those arguments is busier than any ceremonial hall here.
Grand House Concourse.hiddenInfo: Neutrality here is maintained by constant administrative effort. The Shared Ground Review Office currently handles a steady flow of attempts to claim, restrict or quietly alter civic property: a boundary marker moved by two metres, a residence walk annexed by a security cordon, a rotunda booking that excludes a rival by scheduling. Historical Claim Markers are the most sensitive objects on the Concourse because several record compound boundaries that have since changed, and more than one house would prefer those markers reinterpreted. Delegation arrivals at the Representative Arrival Court are choreographed so that rival houses do not meet, and the ceremony coordinator's timetable is treated as confidential for good reason. Minor houses use the Minor-House Passage precisely because it requires no major-house permission, and pressure to narrow, reroute or close it during major events is a recurring dispute that the Republic keeps refusing. Neutral security staff answer to the Concourse, not to any compound, and are constantly courted.

Major-House Processional.description: The formal route used for delegations and public ceremonies, a broad paved way running between the compound frontages with sightlines to each. Ceremonial order along it is negotiated in advance and remembered afterward. On ordinary days it is simply the fastest way to walk across the district. The paving is old work relaid in sections, the seams running across the route rather than along it so the surface changes colour underfoot. Light rises through the seams with the strength of the city routing, brightest at the turn of the work period. Concourse wardens keep the route clear of stalls and move compound staff back behind their own boundaries when a ceremony forms. A set of fixing sockets down the centre is used for ceremonial staging and is capped the rest of the time.

Neutral Reception Court.description: A shared arrival and meeting space with no house symbols permitted, furnished plainly and maintained by the Republic. Parties who will not enter each other's compounds meet here instead. The court's studied blandness is the most expensive kind of design decision in the district. The court is newer construction on an older platform whose original edge mouldings were left in place, since removing them would have meant choosing a replacement style. Its lighting is even, colourless and held at one level regardless of what the grid is doing elsewhere. Bookings are made through the Republic, refused to anyone wanting exclusive use for a day, and logged publicly. The seating is identical on every side of the room, down to the wear on the arms, which the staff maintain on purpose.

Public House Gallery.description: Rotating exhibitions in which each house explains its culture, history and current work to the public, curated to a shared standard that nobody is fully happy with. Attendance is free and steady. Residents treat the gallery as entertainment and delegates treat it as a scoreboard. The gallery is a long older hall with six equal bays fitted into it, and the bays are identical in size and lighting because any difference would be read as a ranking. Each house dresses its bay in its own materials and colours, so the hall runs through six schemes that clash comfortably. Curators hold houses to the shared standard, refuse late changes, and rotate the bay order on a published cycle. A visitors' comment board beside the exit is emptied daily and is never less than full.

Formal Petition Steps.description: Steps where citizens may publicly address house representatives, with a registrar recording who spoke and to whom. Delegations are expected to receive petitions even when they intend to do nothing. Being refused here in public is often more useful to a petitioner than being politely heard inside. The steps are old stone with newer treads let into the worn centre, and the join between them is the line most petitioners stand on. Light rises from the paving at their foot and strengthens through the day, which is why the busiest addresses happen late. The registrar takes names, refuses anonymous addresses and will not record a petition made on another person's behalf without their filing. An old iron rail along one side is polished bright where people grip it while waiting to be called.

Shared Negotiation Rooms.description: Neutral meeting chambers maintained by the Republic, swept for recording devices and booked through a shared registry. Houses use them when a venue would otherwise be a concession. The rooms are comfortable, identical and deliberately devoid of anything that could be read as an advantage. The block is newer building inside an older shell, and the shell's heavy window frames were kept while everything behind them was replaced. Lighting inside is fixed and identical room to room, insulated from the shifts that mark the hour outside so that no session can be hurried by the light. Booking is charged at a flat rate to every house, and the registry refuses a booking held in another party's name. Each room holds the same plain table, the same six chairs and the same jug, replaced as a set.

House Security Boundaries.description: Clearly marked limits between private compounds and shared ground, set into the paving as lit lines with sensor posts at intervals. Compound security stops at the line; Concourse security patrols beyond it. Most boundary disputes in Relstaris are arguments about a few metres of this marking. The lines are cut into paving of several ages, and in places they cross older inlays that marked something else and were never lifted. The marking light comes off the civic grid and dims during maintenance windows, which is when disputes about exact position tend to be raised. Review officers inspect the posts on a schedule, refuse compound requests to move a post for convenience, and log every refusal. One post carries a repair plate fitted by a house and later replaced by the Republic.

Delegation Residence Walk.description: A quiet residential row of guest houses and visiting-staff accommodation, tenanted by delegations from every house and several cities. Neighbours are rivals and behave accordingly. The walk is where junior aides make friendships their superiors would find inconvenient. The houses along it were built at different times and let separately, so the row runs through mismatched frontages, some restored and some plainly patched, on a shared older foundation. The street lighting is ordinary civic work and follows the city's routing, which means the walk goes quiet and dim at the same hour every day. Accommodation is let at rates that strain a small delegation's budget and are barely noticed by a large one. A shared side yard holds a drying line that nobody will admit to using.

Historical Claim Markers.description: Visible stone and light markers recording former compound boundaries and contested expansions, maintained as record rather than as current law. Several contradict the lines now in use. Houses that benefited from the changes prefer visitors to read the markers quickly and move on. The markers are of every material the district has used, ancient cut stone beside later metal plates and current lit inlays, and none has been brought into a common style. Their light is low and steady, on a separate supply from the boundary marking so the two cannot be confused. Custodians maintain them without correcting them, and refuse requests to remove a marker that a current occupant finds inconvenient. One marker stands inside a planted bed that has grown around it without being cut back.

Public Cultural Rotunda.description: A domed open venue for performances, ceremonies and public house events, allocated by rota with capacity limits enforced. Its acoustics flatter singers and expose speakers. Booking disputes over the rotunda occupy more of the review office's time than any structural matter. The dome is a trade-era expansion set on much older footings, its ornamented ribs restored while the platform beneath them was replaced entirely. Light enters through the dome glazing and moves with the city routing, which performers work around by scheduling to the brighter part of the evening. Slots are charged for, capacity is counted at the doors, and an event that overruns is closed rather than extended. A repaired section of the floor rings differently underfoot and singers know exactly where it is.

Representative Arrival Court.description: A controlled arrival space for high-level house figures, with screened approach lanes and staged waiting bays that keep rival delegations from meeting. Coordinators run it to the minute. A delay of five minutes here has more than once been read across the district as a deliberate insult. The court is later construction on an old landing platform, and the original setdown markings are still visible under the current lane paint in low light. The bays are lit separately so that no delegation can judge another's arrival by the light, a refinement added after complaints. Coordinators refuse unscheduled arrivals, hold lanes for emergency use, and will not disclose another delegation's timing to anyone who asks. A bay screen that sticks halfway has been on the repair list all cycle.

Minor-House Passage.description: A route connecting smaller housefronts to the Concourse without requiring any major-house permission, narrow but properly built and lit to the same civic standard. Minor-house staff use it constantly. Attempts to close it during major ceremonies are refused on record every time they are made. The passage runs between two compound walls of different ages, its paving laid later than either and its lighting brackets fixed into both. Its light follows the same routing as the main Concourse, which was itself argued over when the passage was fitted out. Wardens patrol it on the same round as the shared ground and move on anyone attempting to gate it. A hand-lettered notice at the Concourse end states the passage's standing and is replaced whenever it is defaced.

Shared Ground Review Office.description: The administrative office handling disputes over attempts to claim, restrict or alter neutral civic property, staffed by shared-ground specialists with authority to order a boundary restored. Its filings are public. Officers here are polite, unimpressed by titles, and quietly among the most powerful people in the district. The office is plain newer fitting inside an older gatehouse, the original heavy door frame kept with a modern counter across it. Complaints are taken in writing, scheduled by filing order rather than by house, and answered on public record. Officers refuse to discuss an open matter with anyone but the parties, delegates included. A wall map of the shared ground carries so many corrections that a fresh copy is printed each cycle and immediately marked up again.

Castro Compound.name: Castro Compound
Castro Compound.basicInfo:
The Castro Compound is House Castro's permanent presence in the capital, entirely separate from the Citadel: Darkstar lives in the Citadel because he holds the Core, while the house maintains this compound because it has its own family, staff, representatives and obligations. Restrained and elegant in Solvraxis style, it is socially open and carefully managed, with public lectures, a legal office and an aid desk facing the Concourse. If Castro ever lost the Core, the Citadel would pass on and this compound would remain Castro property. The compound is not new ground: its footings and outer wall are far older than the house, ancient star-metal bracing still carrying the pale stone and glass of the current restoration, with old conduit channels reused for the modern lighting. The restraint is a choice rather than a lack of means, and the pale, quiet palette reads deliberately against the louder frontages further along the shared ground. Corelight reaches the courts through the paving and the water channels and moves with the city's routing, brightening as the work period opens and easing through the maintenance window, which is when the public rooms begin closing. The aid desk charges nothing, while the compound's upkeep, guest accommodation and staff are paid for by the house and audited as house expenditure rather than civic cost.

Work on offer here: House Castro — The Offer That Can Be Refused (ask Lucan Castro).
Castro Compound.hiddenInfo: The compound's difficulty is that house interest and the Core Holder's duty are not the same thing, and everyone here knows it. Staff who move between the compound and the Citadel through the Secure Citadel Transit are routinely accused of receiving privileged access, and the accusations are not always wrong; the transit log is a genuinely sensitive document. Nina's Unofficial Entrance is described in compound records as a service passage and used far too often for that description to survive scrutiny, which suits several people. The Public Aid Office quietly supports citizens harmed by major-house conflict, including people injured by Castro's own political choices, and its caseload is a more honest record of the city's damage than anything published. Solvraxis visitors arriving through the Guest Residence Garden regularly collide with Relstaris political culture, and the cultural gallery exists partly to soften a philosophy the capital has never fully accepted.

Castro Housefront Court.description: The public-facing entrance and formal reception, a restrained court of pale stone and water channels with the house mark set discreetly into the floor. Visitors are greeted rather than processed. The absence of display is itself the statement, and Solvraxis guests recognise it immediately. The court stands on much older footings, the base course of the outer wall ancient work left exposed where the pale facing stops short. The water channels carry light from the paving beneath them, so the court brightens and dims with the city's routing rather than by any switch here. Reception staff take names, decline gifts, and direct petitioners to the aid office rather than turning them away. A worn step at the inner door has been replaced in matching stone that has not yet worn to the same colour.

House Delegation Hall.description: Offices for Castro's Republic representative and staff, working rooms rather than ceremonial ones, with direct filing links to the Forum. Aides here draft positions the Core Holder may publicly decline to support. The distinction between house policy and city policy is maintained deliberately and with visible strain. The hall is plain newer fitting inside an older wing, its heavy original doorframes kept and everything between them replaced with light partitions. Light comes from upper glass and moves with the routing, and the hall keeps working well past the point where it dims. Staff refuse to take Citadel business here, refer it uphill in writing, and log the referral. Filing tokens by the door are colour-sorted so house and civic papers cannot be picked up together.

Solvraxis Cultural Gallery.description: A gallery presenting Castro philosophy and Solvraxis practice without proposing that Relstaris reorganise itself around either, arranged for quiet reading rather than spectacle. School groups visit. Relstaris-born visitors often leave more sympathetic to the ideas and no more inclined to adopt them. The gallery is a restored older room with newer cases standing free of the walls, so the original stonework and its repairs remain visible behind them. The lighting is low, warm and steady, deliberately unlike the blue that runs through the streets outside. Entry is free, school visits are booked, and staff answer challenges from visitors rather than moving them along. A reading bench at the end holds a small stack of well-handled texts that are replaced when they fall apart.

Family Residence Wing.description: Temporary and permanent housing for the Castro family, comfortable and unostentatious, with shared rooms that see real family life rather than staged hospitality. Staff access is limited. It is the part of the compound that most contradicts how the house is imagined from outside. The wing is built into the oldest surviving structure here, its ancient inner wall left bare in the stairwell where later plasterwork was stripped. Light through the upper glazing follows the city's routing, and nobody has fitted the compensating fixtures a grander household would. Household staff work to a short rota, and the wing is closed to compound visitors without a family invitation. A scuffed patch of floor by one doorway marks where something heavy is habitually dropped.

Protective Training Court.description: A training court for restraint, precision and controlled movement, floored for falls and open to the sky. Instructors emphasise stopping over striking. Visitors expecting a martial display are usually surprised by how slow and exacting most of the work looks. The court sits inside old walls that carried very different training under an earlier owner, the anchor points of those fittings still bolted into the stone above. The surfacing is replaced in panels rather than whole, so the floor is a patchwork of slightly different shades. Instructors admit visitors to watch from the edge, refuse anyone who wants to join without an assessment, and stop a session when form slips. A rack of practice staves at the side is worn smooth in the same two places on every one.

Public Choice Forum.description: A lecture and discussion space for civic conversation about personal sovereignty and protection, open to the public and frequently contentious. Speakers are not vetted for agreement. The forum regularly hosts people arguing that Castro philosophy is comfortable nonsense, which the house considers the point. The room is a plain modern insertion into an older hall, with tiered seating built clear of the original walls so the stonework behind remains visible. Its lighting holds one level through a session rather than following the grid, which speakers appreciate and the house pays for. Attendance is free, seats are unreserved, and the house neither records the room nor asks who has come. A lectern at the front has been repaired with a bracket that does not match, and nobody has replaced it.

Castro Legal Office.description: Handling house matters, family disputes and representation, staffed by advocates who also take a portion of civic work without charge. Files are kept separately from anything Citadel-related, a separation that is audited. Its lawyers are very careful about which building a document was drafted in. The office is newer fitting inside an old corner tower, its curved outer wall original and its floors later additions. Paid house work funds the unpaid civic work, and the advocates say so plainly to citizens who ask why the help is free. Intake is by appointment, and matters involving the Core Holder's office are referred rather than taken on. A sealed cabinet for civic files stands on the opposite side of the room from the house cabinets, with the floor between them left clear.

Guest Residence Garden.description: Quiet housing for Solvraxis visitors set around an enclosed garden planted with species from home, maintained at some expense. Guests arrive expecting a familiar pace and find the capital does not offer one. The garden is where most of them recover from their first week. The residence buildings are later work on old foundations, and the garden wall is ancient, patched in three obviously different stones along its length. The garden lighting is kept low and on its own supply, so the space does not brighten and dim with the city the way the courts outside do. Rooms are allocated by the house rather than let commercially, and the waiting list is longer than the house likes to discuss. A bench under the oldest planting has a leg packed with a folded shim that has been there for years.

Secure Citadel Transit.description: The protected route used by Darkstar, Vega and approved staff between the compound and the Citadel, screened along its length and logged at both ends. Its user list is short and politically explosive. Guards on this door are chosen as much for discretion as for capability. The route leaves the compound through an old service passage that was widened and rescreened, and the original doorway arch is still in place above the current frame. Its lighting runs on the route's own supply and stays level whatever the city grid is doing. Staff check names against the list without exception, refuse to hold the door for an unlisted companion, and record the refusal like any other passage. A boot scraper set into the floor by the inner door is worn down to a stub.

Nina's Unofficial Entrance.description: A side route officially recorded as a service passage and used so often, by one person in particular, that the description has stopped convincing anyone. Compound security have quietly stopped logging it properly. Staff maintain the fiction because correcting it would require a conversation nobody wants. The passage is genuinely old service fabric, narrow and plain, running between ancient wall and a much later storeroom addition. Its light is one civic-standard strip that dims with the maintenance window, which makes the late crossings notably dark. Deliveries do genuinely pass this way, which is what keeps the official description technically true. A catch on the outer door has been filed down so far that it no longer holds unless it is lifted.

House Archive Room.description: Castro records concerning Relstaris held entirely separately from the Citadel archive, in a modest room with strict retrieval procedure. The separation is legal, deliberate and frequently tested. What is filed here rather than uphill can matter enormously in a dispute years later. The room is small and dry, built into thick older wall fabric that needed no reinforcement for the purpose it now serves. Its lighting is independent of the civic grid, low and unchanging, and the room has no window of any kind. Retrieval requires a named authority within the house, is logged in writing, and is refused to civic officials without a formal request through the legal office. A ledger on the desk records every consultation, including the ones that found nothing.

Public Aid Office.description: Castro-supported assistance for citizens harmed by major-house conflict, offered without requiring a claim against anyone. Applicants are seen without appointment. The office's records amount to a running ledger of what house politics costs people who have no house at all. The office occupies the outermost rooms of the compound, plain work fitted into an older gate range so that nobody has to pass an inner boundary to reach it. Its light is warm and constant and the door stays open well after the surrounding rooms dim, which is deliberate. Staff explain what the house can cover and what it cannot, and are honest that rent, tuition and medical costs run past what the office is funded to meet. A row of mismatched chairs along the wall was assembled from whatever the compound had spare.

Dravon Compound.name: Dravon Compound
Dravon Compound.basicInfo: The Dravon Compound is legal, active and deeply controversial: House Dravon retains a Republic seat because Dravon citizens, students, businesses and interests exist inside Relstaris, and removing that representation would push all of it out of sight. Controlled, severe and constantly watched, the compound operates under strict capitol agreements governing weapons, personnel movement, cargo and access to shared systems. It is not a prison, and its staff take care to make that point in public. The buildings are older than the current arrangement, and the house has adapted rather than rebuilt: ancient star-metal footings carry corridors laid out for control rather than comfort, old conduit runs feed the modern monitoring fittings, and civic inspection gear is bolted to walls that were never designed to be watched from outside. Its palette is deliberately unlike its neighbours, dark stone and narrow glazing in a district of bright frontages, and the contrast is understood on both sides to be a statement. Corelight reaches the compound through the boundary markings and the cargo lane and shifts with city routing, which the inspection rota is timed against. The compound pays civic fees for its inspections, its cargo clearance and its accord filings, and the legal specialists who contest those costs are among its busiest staff.
Dravon Compound.hiddenInfo: Kaldor's campaign against Castro legitimacy is run from here as law and public argument rather than open threat, and every genuine civic failure becomes evidence in the next filing from the Formal Petition Chamber. The Capitol Accord Office works continuously to contest the restrictions placed on the compound, treating each concession as precedent. Legal cargo arriving through the Watched Cargo Entrance passes inspection and still serves an influence operation, because what moves is usually information, money and obligation rather than contraband. Internal Strategy Hall coordination stays carefully inside the accords, which is exactly what makes it effective. The Quiet Defection Room is the compound's most delicate space: Dravon citizens seek help there without publicly renouncing their families, and both loyalists and hostile outsiders would act on that list if it ever escaped. Ordinary Dravon students and workers in the capital carry collective suspicion they did not earn, and the Cultural Court exists because of it.

Dravon Delegation Hall.description: Offices for the Republic representative and staff, austere and precisely organised, with filing discipline that other delegations privately envy. Every document leaving here has been checked against the capitol accords. The hall is quiet in a way that visitors find deliberate rather than calm. The building is an old administrative block adapted rather than refitted, its corridor sightlines and single controlled entrance kept because they suited the house exactly as they were. Lighting is flat, cool and even, held at one level regardless of what the civic grid is doing outside. Callers are received by appointment, given a written answer rather than a conversation, and escorted both ways. A row of identical filing cabinets along the wall carries handwritten accord references on every drawer.

Formal Petition Chamber.description: Where legal challenges to Republic policy and Core-holder decisions are prepared and formally lodged, walls lined with precedent going back through several governments. Specialists work in teams on single clauses. The chamber's output is the most consistently effective political weapon House Dravon possesses. The room is high and narrow, fitted into older fabric whose window openings were reduced at some point and never reopened. The precedent shelving covers walls that still carry the mounting scars of whatever hung there before. Filings are paid for at civic rates like anyone else's, and the compound's specialists argue those rates as readily as the substance. A long table down the centre is scored with the marks of decades of documents being squared against its edge.

Historical Claim Gallery.description: Dravon's account of its past Core legitimacy, presented as documented history with citations and open access. It is scrupulously sourced and entirely one-sided. Visitors from the Living Archive come specifically to note which documents the gallery declines to display. The gallery is a restored older hall, its heavy ribbing cleaned and left visible above cases of severe dark metal that match nothing else on the shared ground. Its lighting is fixed, low and independent of the civic grid, so the room is unchanged at any hour. Entry is free and unescorted, staff answer questions precisely and briefly, and requests to see an uncited document are declined without explanation. A wall of citation references beside the door is longer than the exhibition it supports.

Restricted Security Court.description: The approved training and internal protection area, bounded by accord limits on equipment and numbers that are inspected without notice. Drill here is drilled correctly, and observed. Compound security understand that a single violation would cost more than any advantage it could buy. The court is enclosed by old defensive walling with newer inspection fittings bolted through it, the civic sensors mounted where the house cannot service them. Its lighting is on the compound supply and stays level, while the boundary markings outside dim with the civic maintenance window. Inspectors arrive unannounced, count equipment against the filed list, and are admitted without argument every time. A store door carries two locks, one of them civic, and both are logged whenever it opens.

Diplomatic Residence.description: Housing for senior Dravon visitors, comfortable, shuttered and set well back from the compound frontage. Arrivals are logged under the accords. Residents rarely appear in public spaces of the capital, which does nothing to reduce speculation about why they came. The residence is later work built against an older inner wall, its windows narrow and its approach overlooked from three sides by the compound's own structure. Interior lighting is warm and domestic and entirely separate from the cold fittings of the working buildings. Accord logging records arrival and departure but not movements inside the compound, a boundary the house defends and the inspectors accept. A service stair at the rear is used far more than the formal entrance and is kept just as clean.

Loyalist Reception Rooms.description: Reception space for political supporters, cultural groups and carefully screened guests, warm in presentation and cold in admissions policy. Invitations are issued selectively and withdrawn quietly. Attendance here is noted by people outside the compound as well as inside it. The rooms are the most decorated in the compound, older panelling restored in deep colours that sit strangely against the severity of every corridor leading to them. Their lighting is warm and held steady, which makes the transition from the cold working wings abrupt and intentional. Guests are received by name, admitted from a list, and are not shown any other part of the compound. A visitors' book at the inner door is kept in the house's own hand and has never been shown to an inspector.

Internal Strategy Hall.description: Private planning and opposition coordination, conducted around a long table with shielded surfaces and no external links. Sessions stay technically within the accords. The hall's discipline is the reason Dravon's political attacks arrive fully formed rather than as outbursts. The hall sits in the oldest part of the block, thick walls of ancient work that required no shielding of their own, with the modern screening fitted inside them. Its lighting is fixed and separate from the civic supply, so nothing about the hour is readable from inside the room. Attendance is by summons, notes are collected at the end of a session, and staff without standing are not told a session is happening. The table surface is dulled in six places where the same seats are always used.

Watched Cargo Entrance.description: The inspected route for legal deliveries, with weighing plates, scanning arches and civic inspectors permanently stationed under the accords. Inspections are thorough and mutually resented. Everything that passes is legal, which is a statement about what is worth moving rather than about intent. The entrance is an old cargo gate with civic arches built across it, the original housing left around fittings the house does not own. The lane lighting is civic and dims through the maintenance window, which slows inspection and is the subject of a standing complaint. Inspectors hold consignments that do not match their filing, charge the compound for storage, and are not persuaded otherwise. A queue line painted on the approach has been extended twice in a slightly different colour.

Dravon Cultural Court.description: A public court hosting events intended to separate Dravon identity from automatic criminal suspicion: music, food, family traditions and open days. Attendance from outside the house is cautious but real. For Dravon-descended residents of Relstaris, it is often the only place that feels uncomplicated. The court is an old yard resurfaced and opened outward, a section of the original perimeter wall taken down and its cut ends left visible. Its lighting is warmer than anything else here and comes up early on event days, drawn from the civic supply. Entry is free, events are advertised publicly, and staff do not record who attends, a policy the house repeats often. A serving counter along one side is the only part of the compound with a queue that anyone joins willingly.

Public Statement Balcony.description: An elevated balcony over the Concourse frontage used for speeches, accusations and carefully staged responses to Republic decisions. Timing is chosen for maximum press attendance. What is said here is intended for the record, and the record is exactly where it will be used. The balcony is a later addition bolted to an older frontage, its brackets driven into ancient facing and its lines matching nothing above or below it. It is lit from the compound's own supply so that a statement is never made in a dimming street, which was the point of installing its fittings. Press positions below are civic ground, allocated by accreditation, and the house has no say in who stands there. The balcony rail is worn at one end and untouched at the other.

Capitol Accord Office.description: Where Dravon legal specialists contest the restrictions placed on the compound, clause by clause, year after year. Small victories are documented and cited in the next round. The office treats the accords as a negotiation that has not ended rather than a settlement. The office is a plain working room in an older wing, its walls lined floor to ceiling with filing that has outgrown every cabinet installed for it. Lighting is bright, flat and constant, on the compound's supply, because the work continues regardless of the civic hour. Specialists file at civic rates, appeal refusals, and contest the fees themselves as a matter of routine. A running tally of contested clauses is kept on a board by the door, with the resolved ones struck through rather than erased.

Quiet Defection Room.description: An unofficial room used by Dravon citizens seeking help without publicly renouncing their families, reached by a side corridor and staffed by people who do not take names. Nothing about it appears in compound records. Both loyalists and hostile outsiders would very much like to know who uses it. The room is old service space, small and plainly finished, with a second door onto a passage that leads out without crossing any controlled point. Its light is a single fitting on the civic supply, which means it dims with the streets and is often left off entirely. Nobody who works here is rostered to it, nothing is written down, and whatever is arranged is arranged through people rather than filings. A pot of tea on a warmer in the corner is kept full by whoever is present.

Contair Compound.name: Contair Compound
Contair Compound.basicInfo: The Contair Compound exists because Relstaris cannot responsibly run its most important technical systems without Contair expertise, and everyone involved finds the arrangement slightly annoying. It is functional and precise, with fewer ceremonial spaces than any other major-house presence: consultation desks, audit halls, a drone bay and a direct connection to gate coordination. Contair participates without accepting that house politics is thereby legitimate, and says so freely. The compound is the plainest frontage on the shared ground, working metal and unpolished composite where its neighbours built in stone and glass, and the only decoration anywhere on it is the labelling. It stands on old ground like everything here, ancient star-metal footings carrying newer structure, and the house has left the reused energy conduits and superseded fittings openly visible on the assumption that hiding a system is how a system gets forgotten. Corelight reaches the yards through the civic markings and shifts with routing, and the compound treats those shifts as data rather than atmosphere, logging them against the load figures it watches. Contair charges for consultation, audit and technical work at posted rates, refuses to discount them for political reasons, and spends a considerable part of its time explaining that its expertise is a service purchased rather than an allegiance owed.
Contair Compound.hiddenInfo: The compound's technical authority is a standing political problem. The Systems Audit Hall can order unsafe infrastructure shut down, and Republic offices have repeatedly postponed repairs for political reasons, producing a growing file in the Independent Failure Archive recording every ignored warning and its eventual cost. The Core Infrastructure Observation Room monitors interfaces between city systems and the Core grid without granting Contair any ownership of the Core, a boundary that is restated constantly because it keeps being tested from above. Dravon continues attempting to obtain indirect technical access through third parties and contractors, which is why the Dravon Exclusion Barrier is enforced as an absolute rather than a preference. The Restricted Maintenance Shaft reaches critical systems beneath North and Central Relstaris, making it one of the most security-sensitive doors in the district. Rezulith's office is used only when an error has been large enough to demand her personal attention, and its occupancy is treated as an alarm signal.

Independent Technical Office.description: The public-facing front of the compound: consultation intake, dispute filing and blunt technical advice offered to anyone who asks properly. Staff explain things once, clearly, without flattery. Officials who arrive expecting deference leave with a written assessment and a poor opinion of themselves. The office is a plain counter room, its walls carrying the bracket lines of equipment replaced twice and never made good. Its lighting is bright, flat and on the compound's own supply, so nothing about the room changes as the city's glow moves. Rates are posted, intake is taken in order of arrival, and a matter outside the compound's competence is refused and named as such. A shelf of superseded standards sits behind the desk for the arguments where someone insists an old one still applies.

Systems Audit Hall.description: Independent review of infrastructure modifications, conducted across long benches of test rigs and comparative data drawn from city systems. Findings are issued regardless of who commissioned the work. An audit finding from this hall can halt a project that a Republic office has already announced. The hall is a wide workspace inside older structure, the original roof trusses exposed and the rigs bolted to a floor cut and patched for cabling many times over. Its light is even and unchanging, on the compound's supply, because comparative work cannot tolerate a shifting room. Audits are paid for by whoever commissions them and published regardless of who that is. A rack of rejected modification samples along one wall is labelled with the system each would have failed.

Gate Coordination Office.description: The technical connection to the Grand Lunar Gate Hub, tracking alignment windows, load cycles and fault reports in continuous shifts. The work is exacting and unglamorous. A misjudgement here would be felt across the city's entire arrival and cargo schedule within hours. The office is a compact room of consoles fitted into an older wing, its cable runs threaded through conduit channels cut long before the current systems existed. Its displays are the brightest thing in the room and its fixed lighting is kept low so they stay readable at any hour. Staff hold to the technical schedule, refuse requests to advance a window for a delegation's convenience, and record each refusal with the name attached. A handover sheet at the end of the console row is filled in by hand as well as logged.

Core Infrastructure Observation Room.description: A monitoring room watching the interfaces between city systems and the Core grid, deliberately configured so that it can observe without controlling anything. The distinction is posted on the wall in plain language. Contair repeats it because the Republic keeps hoping it will quietly erode. The room is fitted into old machinery space, the ancient housings behind the console bank still carrying live conduit inside newer casing. The interface readings rise and fall with demand and maintenance routing, so the boards move through the day as the streets do. Observers log anomalies, report them in writing, and refuse to act on them, which is a standing source of friction with civic offices. A blanked-off control panel beside the boards has had its connections physically removed and left in view.

Restricted Maintenance Shaft.description: Direct access to critical systems beneath North and Central Relstaris, a secured vertical route with staged authorisation and equipment stores at each level. Only certified crews descend. The shaft is one of the few doors in the district that compound security and city protection guard jointly. The shaft is ancient, cut long before the compound stood over it, its staged gates modern fittings seated in mountings made for something else. Light comes partly from the fittings and partly from the systems below, so the deeper stages brighten and dim with the city's routing. Descent requires current certification, is refused for a lapsed qualification regardless of seniority, and is logged at every stage. A store cage at the second level holds tools checked against a list after every descent.

Technical Dispute Chamber.description: Where engineers argue with administrators who approved something they did not understand, across a table with live system data projected between them. Sessions are recorded for later citation. The chamber is famous for producing correct outcomes and permanently damaged working relationships. The room is plain and hard-surfaced, built into older fabric with the acoustic treatment added late and imperfectly, so voices carry more than anyone intends. Its lighting is flat and constant and the data projection is the only thing in the room that moves. Sessions are scheduled by filing order, run to a posted time, and are closed by the chair rather than by agreement. A jug of water sits at the centre of the table and is almost never touched by either side.

Vexorath Communications Point.description: A secure contact station linking the compound to Contair facilities in Vexorath, hardened against interception and physically isolated from city networks. Traffic is technical and heavily compressed. Access is limited to a short list, and that list is not shared with the Republic. The station is a small hardened room in the oldest part of the compound, its shielding built into wall fabric that needed little help. Its power and lighting are independent of the civic grid, and the hour cannot be read off the light here at all. Entry requires two named staff, sessions are timed, and messages are logged by reference rather than content. A physical isolation switch beside the door is thrown at the end of every session and checked by the second person present.

Drone Service Bay.description: Maintenance and storage for authorised technical drones, a bright open bay of racks, diagnostic cradles and calibration frames. Units cycle out to inspection tasks across the capital constantly. The bay smells of hot polymer and coolant, and its technicians talk to the drones without noticing. The bay is a later hall on the compound's older core, its roof frame bolted into ancient wall that carries more than it was built for. Its lighting is strong, white and constant, unlike the shifting glow outside, because calibration tolerates no change in the room. Flight clearance is requested through civic lane control, refusals are accepted, and unauthorised launches are grounded before anyone complains. A cradle at the end of the row is labelled for a unit that has not come back.

Unauthorized Modification Desk.description: The intake point for dangerous alterations and for the people insisting they improved them, with a display case of confiscated work that is genuinely educational. Staff are patient exactly twice. Most of the city's near-disasters begin as something proudly described at this desk. The desk sits in a corner of the public range, plain fittings against an older wall, with the display case built into a recess that clearly held something else. The lighting is bright and unsympathetic and does not soften at any hour. Staff refuse to return a confiscated modification, charge for the inspection that condemned it, and explain the charge in the same flat tone as the fault. A handwritten notice taped to the case lists the three modifications the desk sees most often and asks people to stop.

Rezulith's Unused Meeting Office.description: A formal office maintained for protocol and opened only when a problem has become severe enough to require her presence in person. Staff keep it ready and hope not to use it. Its lights coming on has become an informal citywide indicator that something serious has gone wrong. The room is the only finished space in the compound, a restored older chamber with proper seating, sitting awkwardly among working rooms that were never given the same treatment. Its lighting is on the compound supply and is normally left off entirely, which is what makes its use so visible from the Concourse. Staff clean it, keep its files current, and refuse to book it for anything else however short the compound is of meeting space. A single chair behind the desk shows no wear at all.

Independent Failure Archive.description: A record of every warning Contair issued and every consequence of ignoring it, indexed by system, date and the office responsible. Entries are never removed. The archive is consulted during disputes and is the single most effective argument the compound owns. The archive is a long narrow room of plain racking inside older fabric, expanded twice by taking down partitions whose scars run across the ceiling. Its lighting is low and steady and independent of the civic supply, because the room is worked in at every hour a dispute demands. Consultation is charged for, open to any party in a dispute, and refused to nobody, including the offices named in the entries. A board at the entrance lists the systems most frequently represented, and it has not changed in a long time.

Dravon Exclusion Barrier.description: A hard technical access boundary enforcing Contair's permanent refusal to support Dravon systems, implemented in hardware rather than policy so it cannot be quietly waived. Attempts to route around it are logged and reported. The barrier is the most political object in an aggressively apolitical compound. The installation is physically obvious, a bank of disconnected couplings in an older service bay, the severed runs capped and labelled rather than removed. Nothing about it draws civic power, so it is unaffected by routing and unaffected by anything the city does. Requests to restore a connection are refused in writing without reasons, and the refusals are filed with the same reference every time. A cut cable end mounted above the bank has been there long enough to have collected dust.

Corsair Compound.name: Corsair Compound
Corsair Compound.basicInfo: The Corsair Compound is one of the busiest houses on the Concourse, because almost every major Relstaris institution depends on movement, cargo, visitors or commercial negotiation. It is welcoming, expensive and socially connected: route negotiation floors, a hospitality court, merchant lodgings and a kitchen that never closes for arriving couriers. The warmth is genuine and should never disguise how much information passes through the building. The compound is the most extended structure on the shared ground, an old core wrapped in generations of balconies, galleries and additions in the manner Corsair brought to the whole city, with ancient footings beneath and reused conduits carrying the light into every later storey. Its colours are its own and quite unlike its neighbours, warm stone and deep glazing with the balcony fronts picked out brightly, on the working theory that a house in trade should be easy to find. Corelight reaches the courts and the roof through the civic markings and moves with routing, brightening as the work period opens and thinning through the maintenance window, which is when the courier traffic is heaviest and the kitchen busiest. Everything here is priced, from lodging to contract facilitation to the drinks in the lounges, and the compound is entirely open about the fact that hospitality is an investment rather than a gift.
Corsair Compound.hiddenInfo: Hospitality is the compound's intelligence apparatus. The Commercial Intelligence Office does entirely legal market analysis, route risk assessment and political trade forecasting, and what it assembles from lounge conversation, cargo patterns and courier timings is frequently ahead of the Republic's own briefings. Route contracts signed on the Negotiation Floor regularly matter more to the city's actual behaviour than official votes, which produces recurring friction between Corsair profit and Republic policy. The Cargo Dispute Chamber is where shipments turn out to carry political consequences: a delayed or misrouted consignment has more than once exposed an arrangement nobody intended to publish. The Xyren Sign Gallery is a working provocation, a professionally curated collection of anti-Xyren signage from across Nexara that turns trade hostility into public embarrassment, and Xyren responds in kind through influence rather than complaint. The Inheritance Archive holds records of old Corsair Core influence and route agreements that still shape who may move what through the capital.

Corsair Delegation Hall.description: Republic representation and commercial policy offices, run at the pace of a trading floor rather than a government building. Aides handle politics and freight in the same breath. The hall's noise level is a reliable indicator of how well the city's routes are running that week. The hall is an older room opened up and galleried, a balcony running around three sides added long after the floor below. Light falls from the upper glazing and moves with the city routing, and the hall simply gets louder rather than quieter as it dims. Callers are seen without appointment if they are brief, commercial enquiries are charged for and political ones are not. A board of route conditions along one wall is updated by hand between system refreshes because the hand is faster.

Route Negotiation Floor.description: Open floor where agreements on cargo, travel, emergency supply and house access are hammered out, with route maps and capacity boards updating live along one wall. Parties negotiate standing up. Deals struck here reshape what reaches the capital long before any policy acknowledges it. The floor is a broad hall on old footings, its map wall built across an older opening whose frame is still visible at the edges. Board light dominates the room while the fixed lighting is kept warm and low, which is deliberate and reliably makes visitors talk longer. Facilitation is charged as a fee on the agreement, refused where the compound holds an interest it has not declared, and declared loudly where it does. A rail along the map wall is worn where people lean to trace a route with a finger.

Visiting Merchant Residence.description: Temporary lodging for Corsair families and major clients, comfortable, well-serviced and pitched at people accustomed to being looked after. Guests from six cities cross paths at breakfast. The residence staff remember preferences with an accuracy that is flattering and slightly unnerving. The residence is balconied storeys added to an older block over generations, so the frontage runs through three periods of ornament, none brought into line. Interior lighting is warm and steady rather than following the civic routing, which guests notice by sleeping later than they meant to. Rooms are let at rates that are quietly among the highest in the district, and the tariff is not posted anywhere a guest can see it. A guest book in the entrance hall is signed by almost nobody and kept anyway.

Premium Contract Lounge.description: Where high-value negotiations are conducted through hospitality: soft seating, excellent service, and no visible paperwork until agreement is near. Staff work discreetly and constantly. The lounge's expense is a business decision, and it earns its cost several times a season. The lounge occupies a Corsair-era balcony range, its ornamented frontage restored and its interior entirely modern behind it. Its light is warm, low and held steady, insulated from the shifts outside so that a long negotiation never feels long. Access is by invitation, the service is billed to the agreement, and staff decline to seat two parties who have asked not to meet. A tray of small glasses is refreshed so quietly that guests consistently underestimate how long they have been sitting there.

Commercial Intelligence Office.description: Legal market analysis, route risk assessment and political trade forecasting, assembled from public data, shipping patterns and a great deal of attentive listening. Analysts brief the delegation daily. Their picture of the city's near future is often sharper than anything the Republic circulates. The office is plain working space behind the public frontage, in older rooms whose windows were narrowed when the balcony range went up outside. Its lighting is bright and constant, unlike the hospitality rooms, because the work runs through every part of the day. Analysis is sold to clients as well as used in-house, kept in separate files, and staff refuse to discuss who asked for what. A wall of route maps carries pins in colours whose meaning is not written down anywhere.

Hospitality Court.description: A bright public court for events, visiting delegations and neutral receptions, where the compound's reputation for generosity is manufactured in plain sight. Invitations are widely issued. Rivals attend because refusing would be read as weakness, which is precisely the intended dynamic. The court is an old open yard roofed in later glazing, the roof frame carried on brackets driven into ancient wall that shows plainly beneath it. Its lighting is warm and generous and runs on the compound's supply, so the court stays bright while the street outside dims. Events are free to invited guests and the costs are carried by the house, which mentions the fact often enough that nobody forgets it. A serving counter along one side has a worn step in front of it that has been replaced twice.

Courier Roof.description: The launch and landing point for high-speed message and priority delivery flights, marked with lane guides and staffed around the clock. Couriers turn around in minutes. From the parapet the capital's actual information network can be watched operating in real time. The roof is later decking laid over an older structure, its lane guides set into panels that are lifted and replaced regularly enough that the fixings are all newer than the deck. Guide lighting is civic and dims through the maintenance window, which the dispatchers plan the heaviest runs around. Couriers are paid by the run, priority carries a premium, and dispatch refuses a run that lane control has not cleared. A rack of spare harness clips by the stair head is picked over constantly and restocked by whoever notices.

Cargo Dispute Chamber.description: Where lost, damaged, delayed, misrouted and suspicious shipments are argued over, with manifests and tracking records displayed for both sides. Settlements are fast by capital standards. Occasionally a routine dispute reveals a shipment that somebody powerful did not want traced. The chamber is a plain room in the older core, its display wall fitted across a former doorway whose arch is still legible. Its lighting is even and functional, with nothing of the hospitality rooms' warmth, because the compound wants these sessions short. Filing carries a fee, settlements are charged as a share, and the chamber refuses to hear a dispute where the manifest has not been lodged. A box of damaged sample goods by the door is kept as evidence and is emptied far less often than it is filled.

Xyren Sign Gallery.description: A formal, immaculately curated collection of anti-Xyren signage gathered from across Nexara, each piece labelled with provenance and context in devastatingly professional language. Guests laugh, then read the labels and stop. The gallery is a commercial position expressed as an exhibition. The room is a restored older gallery with cases as good as anything in a civic museum, which is precisely the point. Its lighting is gallery-standard, even and constant, and the labels are printed to a house standard that does not vary. Entry is free to guests of the compound and by request to anyone else, and the curator declines offers to buy pieces out of the collection. A blank mount at the end of the last case is labelled only with a date and is never explained to visitors.

Neutral Contract Bar.description: A bar built for negotiations between people unwilling to enter one another's compounds, with sightlines arranged so no table overhears another. Drinks are good and the service is deliberately unhurried. Several standing intercity arrangements were agreed at these tables rather than in any chamber. The room is an older vaulted space subdivided by screens and planting, the original heavy arches left visible above the new arrangement. Its lighting is low and pooled at the tables, steady rather than shifting, so the room reads the same at any hour. Tables are booked and charged for whether or not anything is bought, and the staff will refuse a booking that would place two parties within sight. A brass rail along the bar front has been polished down to a different colour at three points.

Inheritance Archive.description: Records of old Corsair Core influence and the route agreements that came from it, maintained as commercial asset rather than sentiment. Researchers require an appointment and a reason. Documents here show how the capital first opened itself to movement, and on whose terms. The archive is a dry, quiet room in the oldest part of the compound, its cases modern and its walls original, earlier shelving scars still showing between them. Its lighting is low, fixed and independent of the civic grid, and nothing about the city's hour reaches inside. Consultation is charged at a commercial rate, refused where the compound has a live interest in the same route, and always declared when it is. A folder of expired agreements sits on open shelf because the house finds their wording useful.

Late Arrival Kitchen.description: An always-open kitchen serving couriers, staff and travellers whenever they land, with a counter, long tables and no interest in the hour. Conversation runs frankly at four in the morning. More of the compound's useful information arrives at this counter than in any briefing. The kitchen is built into an old service range beneath the courier stair, its arched ceiling original and everything under it replaced several times. Its lighting is warm and never turned down, which makes it the one window on the frontage still bright when the street has dimmed. Food is charged at cost to staff and couriers and at a fair price to everyone else, and nobody is turned away for arriving at an awkward hour. The counter's edge is worn through its finish in the two places where people habitually lean.

Volen Compound.name: Volen Compound
Volen Compound.basicInfo: The Volen Compound represents Ignivex in the capital as something far broader than fire combat: thermal materials expertise, food and feast traditions, memorial practice, energy knowledge and a direct emotional style that many Relstaris officials find difficult to handle. It is warm in every sense, opening its hearth hall and feast chamber to the public and keeping an emergency heat response team on standby for the city. Politically it is impatient, and does not disguise it. The compound stands on the same inherited ground as its neighbours, ancient star-metal footings and old reused conduits beneath, but the house has rebuilt above them in its own materials, so dark heat-worked metal and deep fired surfaces run where the rest of the shared ground shows pale stone and glass. Nothing here matches the frontages on either side and nobody has ever suggested that it should. Corelight reaches the outer courts through the civic markings and moves with routing, but inside the compound the light is mostly its own, hearth and forge and ember, which is why the buildings look occupied at hours when their neighbours look closed. Materials, contract work and trade support are sold at posted terms, the public meals are given without charge and paid for by the house, and the distinction between the two is something the delegation explains far more often than it should have to.
Volen Compound.hiddenInfo: Volen's usefulness is also its leverage. The Emergency Heat Response Bay is a genuine civic asset that the city relies on during fire, geothermal and high-temperature incidents, and each deployment strengthens an argument the house is already making about being taken seriously between crises. The Direct Complaint Desk was created after Volen representatives refused to keep routing concerns through five layers of polite administration, and it now receives complaints from residents with no connection to the house at all, which quietly embarrasses several Republic offices. Memorial practice on the Ember Terrace regularly collides with Dravon, since Volen's remembrance of war losses names causes the Dravon delegation disputes in public. Ignivex materials become critical during city failures, giving the Trade Office influence out of proportion to its size. And more honest negotiation happens over a meal in the Feast Chamber than in any formal session, a fact Volen exploits deliberately.

Volen Hearth Hall.description: The main public reception and cultural center, built around a controlled open hearth whose heat carries through the whole hall. Guests are fed before they are asked their business. The warmth is not metaphor: the room runs several degrees above capital standard and unapologetically so. The hall is older structure stripped back and refitted in the house's own materials, its ancient wall base left exposed beneath dark heat-worked facing. Its light is hearth light rather than civic, steady and warm, so the room does not dim when the streets do. Anyone may enter during open hours, nobody is asked their standing at the door, and the house declines offers to pay for the food. A bench nearest the hearth is worn smooth and is understood to belong to whoever is coldest.

Ignivex Delegation Office.description: Republic and civic representation, run from working offices with an open door policy that other compounds consider reckless. Staff answer questions directly, including uncomfortable ones. The delegation's reputation for bluntness starts here and is entirely deserved. The offices are plain fitting inside an older wing, heavy original beams left visible with everything below replaced in the compound's darker materials. Light comes from upper glazing and moves with the city's routing, and the staff read the maintenance window as the point where the arguing starts. Callers are seen without appointment, given an answer rather than a procedure, and told plainly when the answer is no. A stack of Republic forms on the counter is annotated in the margins by whoever last found them confusing.

Thermal Materials Gallery.description: A gallery of forge work, heat-resistant construction and materials expertise, with samples visitors are encouraged to handle and test rigs running demonstrations. Engineers from across the city come for consultation. What looks like a cultural display is also a working technical showroom. The gallery is newer construction built against an older wall, its rig mounts bolted into ancient fabric that carries the load without complaint. The lighting is strong and constant, on the compound's own supply, because the demonstrations need to read the same whatever the grid is doing. Consultation is charged at posted rates, and staff refuse to certify a material for a use it will not survive. A sample block at the end of the bench has been handled so often that its edges have gone round.

Controlled Flame Court.description: An open court for training, ceremony, cooking demonstration and technical practice, with containment systems built into its walls and floor. Flame here is precise and purposeful. The court is one of the few places in Relstaris where fire is treated as a tool rather than an emergency. The court sits inside old walling refaced in heat-worked plate, the original stone visible at the corners where the facing could not be turned. Its own light overwhelms the civic glow entirely, and the court is brightest exactly when the streets outside are dimmest. Use is scheduled, containment is checked before and after every session, and civic inspectors attend unannounced and are admitted without argument. A scorched ring near the centre is resurfaced on a cycle and never quite disappears.

Public Feast Chamber.description: A long shared hall for public meals and direct political conversation, tables set for anyone who arrives and seating that mixes visitors with residents. Food is Ignivex in style and generous in quantity. More genuine negotiation happens here in an evening than in a week of sessions. The chamber is an old hall reroofed and refitted, its ancient columns left bare between tables and serving ranges of much newer work. Its light is warm and low and holds steady through the evening, indifferent to the routing shifts outside. Seating is not allocated, guests are not asked who they represent, and the house pays for the meals rather than recovering the cost from anyone. The long tables carry burn marks where dishes have been set down straight from the fire, and nobody sands them out.

Memorial Ember Terrace.description: An open terrace of small maintained embers remembering war dead, lost family and public sacrifice, each tended by the people it belongs to. Visitors are asked only to be quiet. The practice names causes as well as losses, which has made the terrace politically contentious more than once. The terrace is built on an older platform whose edge mouldings remain, the ember stations set in a plain grid of newer stone. The embers are the only light here, and they do not answer to the grid at all, so the terrace looks the same at every hour. Tending is done by families rather than by staff, the house maintains the stations and nothing else, and requests to remove a named cause are refused. A station at the far end has been tended by different hands for so long that its stone is worn unevenly.

Volen Residential Wing.description: Housing for representatives, workers and visiting family, communal in layout with shared kitchens that stay in use most of the day. Privacy is available but not assumed. New arrivals from Ignivex find it the only part of the capital that feels immediately survivable. The wing is older structure adapted, rooms opened into one another and kitchens fitted where a previous arrangement had none, its blocked doorways still visible. The interior is kept warm and lit from its own supply, which is why the wing does not go quiet when the district dims. Rooms are allocated by the house at cost, longer stays are charged against a delegation, and nobody is moved out for a more senior arrival. A kitchen table in the main range has been repaired with a plate of the house's own metalwork.
