The gallery is a restored arcade of polished stone and dark star-metal, lit low and evenly, with rooms rather than shopfronts and staff who open a door rather than call from it. Appointments are made in advance and casual visitors are received politely and briefly. Provenance is documented for every significant piece and the documentation travels with it. The visitors' book at the arcade entrance is signed by everyone who enters, which is the gallery's oldest security arrangement and its most effective one.

Independent Artisan Rows.description: Makers, designers, repair specialists and outright experimenters working from open-fronted units where the workshop is the shop. Customers watch things being finished. Many of these artisans keep a second bench over in Maker's Reach and sell the results here. The rows are lit from above through old star-glass panels, floors littered with offcuts, benches pushed close enough to the front that a customer can be handed a piece while it is still warm. Units are leased by the season and the good ones pass by recommendation rather than by advertisement. Commissions are taken with a deposit and a date that is usually optimistic. The chalked board at the end of the row lists which makers are taking work this season and which are not, and it is updated by the makers themselves.

Regional Food Exchange.description: Ingredients and prepared food from every major city, traded in a hall of cold rooms, heat cabinets and arguments about freshness. Chefs from across Relstaris buy here at dawn. The Culinary Institute sends students to learn what an honest supplier looks like. The hall is high and hard-surfaced, its cold rooms running off reused conduit that the Market has maintained rather than replaced, the whole of it smelling of everything at once and rinsed down at the close of each day. Trade is done in bulk before the Corelight reaches full daytime intensity and in small quantities afterward. Stock depends entirely on what the routes delivered. The board at the entrance lists which cities' goods arrived this cycle, and a blank line on it moves prices across the hall before anyone announces anything.

Training Goods Hall.description: Legal training equipment, clothing, protection systems and instruction materials sold under posted safety ratings, with testing rigs on the floor for buyers who insist. Open Circuit instructors kit out entire halls here. The counterfeit problem is worst in this room and everybody knows it. The hall is a broad space of racked stock under hard light, the rigs set in a cleared centre where a demonstration draws a crowd within moments. Sellers are required to display ratings and to permit a test on request. Equipment may be carried lawfully from here to approved schools and secured events, and the route restrictions are posted beside the door. The wall of withdrawn items behind the inspection bench is kept on display, each piece labelled with what it was sold as and what it actually was.

Dustfall Salvage Court.description: Recovered, repaired, repurposed and occasionally disputed goods from the independent mixed-house frontier, sold from open crates by traders of no single house identity. Everything here has had a previous life. Buyers hunt for parts nobody manufactures any more, and sometimes find more than that. The court is open to the air on three sides, floored in worn stone, its crates stacked on pallets and its lighting strung between poles because nothing here is permanent enough to justify fixed fittings. Ownership is asserted rather than documented, and a buyer who wants a chain of title is directed to the mediation court. The tarpaulins over the crates are patched in a dozen colours, and the patches are the most Dustfall thing in the Market.

Ignivex Materials Lane.description: Thermal materials, forge work, cooking systems and heat-resistant products, sold down a lane that stays several degrees warmer than the rest of the Market. Demonstrations involve real flame under real supervision. Ignivex sellers bargain loudly and consider silence rude. The lane is narrow, vented overhead and floored in plate rather than stone, its frontages dark with use and its stock stacked heavily enough that the Market inspects the loading annually. Demonstration bays are licensed and separated from the stock by a clear standing space. Prices are argued at volume and settled with a handshake that is expected to hold. The soot mark above each demonstration bay is cleaned on a schedule and back within days, and the sellers treat it as advertising.

Korrvane Competition Market.description: Tournament goods, training brands, fighter merchandise and match-analysis tools, arranged around display screens running recent bouts. Academy students and Open Circuit trainees shop side by side. Fan culture and equipment retail are entirely indistinguishable here. The stalls are bright and loud, hung with house and fighter colours in combinations nobody would choose for a building, and the screens are angled so that a crowd forms in the aisle and has to be moved on. Stock follows the Korrvane calendar and is discounted brutally when a favourite loses. The rack of last season's merchandise at the back of the market is the cheapest clothing in the district and is bought steadily by people with no interest in the sport at all.

Solvraxis Cultural Exhibition.description: Refined clothing, art, educational goods and protected-city products presented with more restraint than anything around them. Stock is limited by what Solvraxis permits to leave. Buyers are given the cultural context whether or not they asked for it. The gallery is a quiet run of pale rooms with wide spacing between pieces, lit softly and deliberately unlike the lanes on either side of it, its frontage the only one in the arcade without a sign in more than one colour. Stock arrives in small consignments and sells slowly. Staff explain provenance and intended use at length, and a purchase takes longer here than anywhere else in the Market. The bench opposite the entrance is used by people waiting for companions who have been inside considerably longer than they expected.

Quilrath Equipment Row.description: Dravon-region manufactured goods, widely regarded as inferior to Contair standards and still bought steadily for price, availability, compatibility or political loyalty. Sellers make the case plainly. Customers who argue the quality point get a shrug and the number on the tag. The row is plain and practical, stock stacked in crates with the prices chalked on the side, its lighting adequate and its frontages undecorated beyond a painted name. Nothing here is sold as something it is not, which the sellers regard as their only real advantage. The verification desk is a short walk away and the row's sellers point customers toward it without being asked, because the alternative is worse for everyone.

Vexorath Verification Desk.description: Confirms legitimate Contair standards and rejects counterfeit claims, testing items brought in by sellers, buyers and inspectors alike. A rejection slip is public. The queue lengthens noticeably whenever a fake consignment reaches the Market, which is how the Market learns one has. The desk is a counter and a testing bay in a plain bay off the main arcade, finished to technical standard and kept deliberately unwelcoming to conversation. Tests are charged and run in order, with no allowance for who is waiting. Results are issued in writing and posted by item rather than by seller. The board of current rejections beside the counter is read by every buyer in the Training Goods Hall before a major purchase, and by every seller in it the moment a new slip goes up.

Helvyra Trade Arcade.description: Corsair goods, travel supplies, alcohol, route-dependent stock, legal magical tools and specialized sword equipment under one long arcade. What is available depends entirely on which routes are running. Traders here have the best current information on route conditions in the district. The arcade is long and roofed in star-glass, its frontages hung with goods rather than signs, and the whole of it smells of oil, packing straw and whatever came in this cycle. Stock turns over fast and prices move with the routes rather than with the season. Magical tools are sold legally and openly and draw as many sightseers as buyers. The route board at the arcade's centre is copied from the Waypoint's own gallery and is annotated by traders who disagree with it.

Public Contract Hall.description: Vendor agreements, market leases and event contracts are registered and witnessed here, with standard terms posted on the wall for anyone negotiating alone. New sellers sign their first lease at these tables. So do the people about to lose one. The hall is a plain civic room of long tables and a registration counter, lit evenly, its walls carrying the standard terms in large plain lettering that has been repainted rather than reworded. Registration carries a fee and a witness is provided without charge. Clerks will read a document aloud on request, which is a service used more often than the Market admits. The bench along the back wall is where people sit to read what they are about to sign, and the hall keeps it deliberately far from the tables.

Market Mediation Court.description: Customer, landlord, counterfeit and commercial disputes are heard by mediators with authority to suspend a trading licence on the spot. Hearings are fast and public. A seller who loses twice in a season generally finds their lease is not renewed. The court sits in an open-fronted chamber where anyone passing can stop and listen, which is a deliberate arrangement and does more work than the penalties do. Filings are cheap and heard within days. Mediators rotate and are drawn from outside the trade in question. The bell above the chamber entrance is rung at the start of each hearing, and sellers in the surrounding lanes can tell from the number of rings what kind of dispute is being heard.

Failure Auction Floor.description: Legal sale of inventory, equipment and leases from closed businesses, conducted in the open so that nothing disappears quietly into a rival's hands. Bidders include vultures and old friends. The former owner is entitled to attend, and some of them do. The floor is a plain hall with a raised block, banked standing room and a side table where lots are laid out for inspection before the sale. Lots are catalogued publicly in advance and the catalogue names the business. Payment is immediate and collection is the buyer's problem. The chairs set aside at the front for the former owner are kept there whether or not anyone uses them, a practice the auction officers have maintained for longer than any of them can account for.

Rising Name Promenade.description: Premium frontage awarded temporarily to small businesses gaining public attention, allocated by a committee whose decisions are argued over across the whole Market. A season here can make a maker's career. Losing the slot at the end of it has ended a few as well. The promenade is a wide paved run with star-glass frontages and the best light in the Market, its units fitted out to a standard the Market maintains rather than the tenant. Slots are granted for a set term and cannot be extended, and the rent is nominal precisely so that the award means something. Committee decisions are posted with reasons. The plaque list at the promenade's entrance records every business that has held a slot, and the names nobody recognises outnumber the ones they do.

Grand Waypoint and Cargo Exchange.name: Grand Waypoint and Cargo Exchange
Grand Waypoint and Cargo Exchange.basicInfo: The largest Corsair logistics site outside Helvyra's flagship network centre, handling cargo, delivery, commercial routing, emergency supply and the disputes that follow all four. The Lunar Gates move travelers; this complex moves the capital's material life. It is fast, tightly organized, extremely loud and socially chaotic at every hour of the shift cycle. The site is built for load rather than for looking at: star-metal decks and ramp halls under a roof of ribbed panel, floors painted in route colours that are relaid as the handling arrangements change, with older conduit runs reused to carry deck lighting and the cold stores. Its bones are older than its function, and a Genesis foundation, a Dravon service corridor and a Corsair-built gantry all carry traffic in the same building. Corelight enters through high slots and marks the shift pattern, the heaviest movement running before it reaches full daytime intensity and again on the evening change, with maintenance taken in the low window. Everything is charged: shipping, storage, priority, insurance, the locker a small trader keeps stock in. What arrives here is visible in the Grand Market within days, and what fails to arrive is visible faster.
Grand Waypoint and Cargo Exchange.hiddenInfo: Everything the city consumes is legible from these floors before it is visible anywhere else. Route conditions posted in the Commercial Route Gallery are already showing a supply line under strain, and cargo workers in the Commons have worked out what it means several days ahead of any representative. A consignment of emergency medical cargo has gone missing between manifest and pickup, and the Lost Parcel Department's file on it is thinner than it should be. Private house shipments have been misdelivered to the wrong compound twice this season, which is either incompetence or a very cheap way to read a rival's supplies. The Quiet Reroute Office is the site's real vulnerability: legitimate emergency rerouting authority, minimal oversight, and the single access smugglers most want. A legal route has become politically impossible to run, and the workaround being arranged is legal in only the narrowest sense. Xyren interests have again approached the site about modifying or removing the Grand Xyren Sign, and the request was refused in terms nobody bothered to soften.

Grand Relstaris Waypoint.description: The public commercial counter and network hub of the whole complex, a high hall of live route boards, booking desks and Corsair staff working several conversations at once. Anyone can ship from here. The noise is constant and the queue moves faster than it looks. The hall is wide and hard-floored, its ceiling carried on a Corsair gantry that still takes load, with the booking desks ranged under the boards and a weighing and handling line running down one side. Rates are posted by route and class and change with conditions. Consignments are checked, labelled and taken at the counter, and nothing leaves without a manifest. The floor paint at the head of the queue has been worn down to bare deck and repainted so many times that the current line does not quite match the one beneath it.

House Cargo Exchange.description: Major-house and institutional shipments handled on separate floors with their own manifests, seals and handling crews. Volume here dwarfs the public counter. Rival houses' cargo passes within metres of each other, which is why the routing is deliberately opaque. The floors are reached by their own ramps and worked by crews who are assigned rather than chosen, under lighting brighter than the public hall so that seals can be checked at a glance. Contracts are negotiated in offices above the deck and the rates are not published. Handling is charged by weight, class and priority, with a premium for discretion. The seal store behind the supervisor's office is inventoried at every shift change, and a discrepancy in it stops the floor until it is resolved.

Courier Flight Deck.description: Launch and return for priority local delivery, an exposed deck of marked lanes where couriers drop in, load and are gone inside a minute. Flight discipline is absolute and enforced by the deck crew. Couriers rank each other informally and viciously on turnaround times. The deck is a broad plate platform with numbered bays, screens along the outer edge and a crew station at the centre that controls every movement onto it. Couriers are registered, insured and paid by the consignment. Loads are handed over at the bay and signed for on the spot, since nothing is left standing on the deck. The bay numbering was changed once, years ago, and half the couriers still use the old numbers, which the crew have long since stopped correcting.

Diplomatic Shipment Hall.description: Protected Republic, Citadel and representative cargo, moved under seal with a documented chain of custody and its own secure dock. Contents are not declared to handlers. The hall's paperwork survives longer than most of the governments that generate it. The hall is plain and controlled, a short run of deck behind a barrier with its own dock door and a records office that never has more than two people in it. Access is by authorization and the authorization is checked against a list that is updated daily. Handlers move sealed units and are not told what they contain. The custody register is kept in bound volumes rather than only in the systems, a redundancy introduced after an incident that the current staff know about only from the volumes themselves.

Independent Cargo Lockers.description: Small-business and individual storage in racked units rented by the month, from a single crate to a whole bay. Traders stage Market stock here. The lockers are the cheapest legitimate way to hold goods in the capital and are consequently always full. The store is a deep hall of caged racking under strip lighting, reached from the public hall by a ramp worn smooth by handcarts, with an attendant at the entrance who checks every departure against a ticket. Rentals are paid in advance and access runs through posted hours. Insurance is offered, declined by most and regretted by some. The waiting list is kept at the attendant's desk on a clipboard, and everyone who asks is told the same estimate regardless of how long it actually takes.

Emergency Supply Office.description: Medical, infrastructure and disaster-priority routing, with standing authority to bump commercial cargo off a route without negotiation. During a crisis this office effectively runs the site. Between crises it maintains reserves and argues with everyone about storage space. The office is a control room and a reserve store on the same level, the room plainly fitted with a status wall and the store kept locked, stocked and rotated on a schedule that nobody is permitted to defer. Priority is granted against criteria that are published, which does not stop the arguments. Bumped consignments are recorded and compensated under the site's own rules. The reserve store's rotation log hangs inside the door, and the initials on the last line are checked by the next person before anything is moved.

Premium Delivery Hall.description: High-value speed and security contracts, handled by vetted crews in a hall with its own access control and insurance desk. Clients pay for guaranteed timing and mostly get it. Failures here are expensive enough that the Damaged Cargo Court keeps a dedicated list. The hall is smaller and cleaner than the general floors, finished to a standard clients can see, with its own dock, its own scales and an insurance desk that is part of the sale rather than an afterthought. Crews are vetted, named on the contract and rotated to prevent familiarity with any one client. Timing guarantees carry penalties that are actually paid. The client waiting room has a window onto the dock, deliberately, so that a nervous shipper can watch their own consignment being loaded.

Lost Parcel Department.description: Misrouted, disputed, unidentified and politically inconvenient packages accumulate on deep shelving under numbered claims. Investigators work the backlog steadily. A few items have sat here long enough that their original senders no longer exist in any registry. The department is a long room of shelving behind a counter, lit unevenly, its aisles arranged by the date an item arrived rather than by anything useful. Claims are made against description and a handling charge, and a disputed claim is referred to the cargo court. Investigators trace routes backward through manifests that are frequently incomplete. The oldest aisle at the back is not swept as often as the others, and the dust on it is the department's most honest measure of its own backlog.

Damaged Cargo Court.description: Inspection, responsibility, insurance and compensation decided in a court with the goods present as evidence, crates opened in front of both parties. Verdicts are quick. Carriers, senders and insurers all lose here often enough to keep taking the process seriously. The court is a hard-floored chamber with an inspection bench, a drain and a public bench along one wall, built so that a damaged consignment can be brought straight in from the deck. Filing costs little and the court hears it quickly. Assessors are drawn from the site and from outside it, and their reports are given to both parties in writing. The bench is scarred from decades of crates being levered open on it, and nobody has ever proposed replacing it with something more dignified.

Commercial Route Gallery.description: Live route conditions and supply risk displayed across a long wall of boards, updated as fast as reports arrive from every city on the planet. Merchants read it like weather. A route going amber here moves prices in the Grand Market within a day. The gallery is a raised walk facing the board wall, with standing room, a rail and a row of desks where traders work directly from the display. Access is free and the gallery is busiest at the shift changes. The boards carry conditions and risk rather than promises, and the distinction is stated in the heading of every column. The chalk ledge below the boards is used by traders to keep their own running notes, and the site cleans it once a cycle and never more often than that.

Restricted Goods Review.description: Legal review of controlled materials before they move, staffed by inspectors with the authority to hold a consignment indefinitely. Documentation is checked against the goods themselves. Most holds are paperwork failures; a small and memorable minority are not. The review floor is a sealed bay with an inspection table, a secure hold and an office where the paperwork is worked through line by line while the shipper waits outside. Reviews are charged and scheduled, and a consignment that arrives without its documentation simply waits. Inspectors work in pairs and sign jointly. The hold cage at the back carries items that have been there long enough to acquire their own file numbers, and the inspectors refer to some of them by those numbers alone.

Cargo Worker Commons.description: Shift meals, labour organization and route gossip in a wide canteen that never empties, tables claimed by crew and held across generations. The food is heavy and cheap. More is accurately known about the capital's supply situation in this room than in the Republic Forum. The commons is a low hall with a serving counter along one end, long tables, a wall of lockers and a labour association board that management has learned not to interfere with. Meals are subsidized through the site's own arrangement rather than free. Crews come in at the change of every shift and leave in the same groups they arrived with. The table nearest the door belongs to the deck crews by an arrangement nobody wrote down and nobody has successfully challenged.

Grand Xyren Sign.description: The most formal and devastating anti-Xyren sign on Nexara, mounted where every arriving crew must pass it, displayed as a civic requirement nobody can remember officially approving. Its wording is precise and merciless. Attempts to alter or remove it are made and refused with some regularity. The sign is cut into dark star-metal and set at the head of the main handling approach, lit from above so that it is legible at every hour of the shift cycle. It is cleaned as part of the site's routine maintenance and has been recast at least once, in the same wording. Crews pass it without comment and visitors stop in front of it. The stone beneath the mounting is worn in a shallow arc where people have stood to read the whole of it.

Quiet Reroute Office.description: Legitimate emergency rerouting, handled discreetly so that a diverted shipment does not become a public incident. The authority is real and the oversight is thin. It is, by common agreement across the underworld, the single access at this site most worth acquiring. The office is two rooms off a service corridor, unmarked except by a number, with a desk, a terminal and a filing cabinet that is not the site's main record system. Reroutes are authorized by a single officer on duty and logged afterward rather than before. The work is genuinely necessary and genuinely difficult to audit. The corridor outside carries no traffic except people going to this door, which is the one detail that makes the office hard to visit unnoticed.

Public Pickup Hall.description: Crowded civilian parcel collection, a hall of numbered windows and a queue that reaches the doors on delivery days. Families, students and small traders collect here in person. The staff have heard every possible explanation for a missing claim slip. The hall is plain and hard-surfaced with a barrier rail steering the queue past the windows, its noticeboards carrying collection rules that are read while waiting and forgotten at the counter. Items are held for a period and then charged storage. Identification is required and a nominated collector can be registered in advance, which almost nobody does until the first time they need it. The seating at the side is occupied by people waiting for someone else's queue number, and by children who have been told to sit there and stay.

Open Contract Hall.name: Open Contract Hall
Open Contract Hall.basicInfo:
The capital's central place for jobs, apprenticeships, public contracts and independent work, connecting workers, professionals, students, houses, businesses and institutions in one enormous hall. It is one of the clearest expressions of Relstaris's promise that anyone can become anything, and one of the clearest demonstrations of how easily opportunity turns into exploitation. Ambitious, crowded, hopeful and entirely transactional. The building is a single great volume of pale grey stone and star-glass on a star-metal frame, galleries stacked around an open floor, its listing boards mounted on panels that were cut into a Dravon-era corridor wall and never fully disguised. Old conduits carry the board lighting, and the brass rails along the galleries have been polished by hands rather than by staff. Corelight falls through the high glazing onto the public floor and marks the hiring day, the crowd thickest before it reaches full daytime intensity and thinning as it drops, with the immediate queue still standing well into the evening shift. Registration is free and most of what happens here is not: credential checks, contract reviews, arbitration filings and the cost of the days spent waiting.

Work on offer here: Relstaris — The Signed Shift (ask Branna Sol).
Open Contract Hall.hiddenInfo: The Hall's rules are good; enforcement depends on who complains. The Fair Contract Review Office is tracking a contract template circulating on the public floor that is legal, comprehensible and designed to trap the signer in unpaid obligation, and it has already appeared under three different employer names. Sol contractors continue to be offered a disproportionate share of dangerous work through the Sol Contractor Board, and an organizer is building a case out of the Disputed Payment Court's records to prove the pattern rather than the individual incidents. A major house is recruiting a specialist away from a family business that will not survive the loss. Underworld recruiters are copying public listings word for word and running interviews two streets away, which is why the Reputation Verification Desk has started checking employers as well as applicants. The Closed Contract Archive holds the files on failed jobs, injuries and disappearances, and someone has been requesting rather too many of them.

Public Job Floor.description: The Hall's open heart: banks of listings, direct interview booths and a crowd that turns over completely between morning and evening. Work is offered and accepted the same hour. The board refreshes constantly and people watch it the way others watch a match. The floor is a wide stone expanse under the galleries, its listing banks arranged in rows with standing room between them and interview booths built into the side walls. Listing here is free to employers and registration is free to workers, which is why the floor is the busiest room in the district. Terms are shown on the listing and rarely improve in the booth. The rail in front of the central bank has been worn to a different colour at the height where people rest their hands while reading.

Professional Contract Gallery.description: Specialist work in medicine, engineering, law, security, education and administration, posted with real terms and negotiated in private rooms off the gallery. Credentials matter here more than anywhere else in the Hall. Employers court candidates rather than the reverse. The gallery runs above the public floor behind a brass rail, quieter and better finished, its negotiation rooms small and glazed so that a meeting is visible without being audible. Listings carry stated terms and an employer who posts here is expected to honour them. Candidates are checked at the verification desk before a meeting is arranged. The seating along the gallery is comfortable, which is the clearest signal in the building about who the room is designed to keep waiting and who it is not.

Apprenticeship Court.description: Training placements with businesses, houses and independent masters, arranged face to face in a court where the master and the applicant both have to show up. Terms cover years. The court keeps a standing register of masters who have been struck off it. The court is an open square of tables under a lower ceiling than the main floor, set out so that each conversation happens within sight of the clerks. Placements are registered, and the terms, hours and conditions are recorded rather than left to memory. A family member or advocate may sit in and frequently does. The struck-off register hangs by the entrance where every applicant passes it, and the clerks will read out the reasons for any name on it to anyone who asks.

Independent Contractor Hall.description: Short-term work, consulting, protection, investigation and technical service, listed by contractors advertising themselves rather than by employers. Rates are public and undercut openly. Half the capital's freelance professionals keep a permanent listing on this wall. The hall is a long room with the listing wall down one side and a run of hire desks down the other, noisier than the galleries and considerably more direct. A listing carries a term fee and can be amended daily. Contractors are expected to display certification where the work requires it, and the desks check. The most contested space is the eye-level strip at the centre of the wall, which is allocated by a rotation the hall enforces because the alternative was worse.

Civic Service Desk.description: Public jobs supporting Relstaris infrastructure and institutions, from transit maintenance to clinic administration, offered with stable terms and unexciting pay. The desk never runs short of vacancies. Its staff are frank about which posts will still exist in five years. The desk is a plain counter with a vacancy board behind it and a short bench in front, tucked off the main floor where the noise drops enough to hold a conversation. Applications are made here and processed through the institutions themselves, which is slower than the public floor and more reliable. Capitol Service terms are listed alongside permanent posts and explained without varnish. The vacancy board is updated in the morning and again at the shift change, and the older cards are left up until they are filled.

Academy Graduate Lane.description: Entry-level professional recruitment aimed squarely at new Academy graduates, with employers from every district taking tables in term-end season. Offers are compared out loud in the aisle. Graduates without a sponsor negotiate hardest, because nobody is negotiating for them. The lane is a run of numbered table bays along one gallery, booked and paid for by the employer, with the graduate side of each table deliberately left without a chair so that conversations stay short. Traffic is seasonal and the lane is half empty for much of the cycle. Offers are made verbally and confirmed in writing at the verification desk. The chalk board at the lane entrance lists which employers are present today, and graduates photograph it rather than trust their memory.

House Recruitment Rooms.description: Private rooms where major and minor houses seek talent, each with its own door and its own style of persuasion. Offers include housing, standing and obligations rarely written into the contract. People leave these rooms having agreed to more than the salary. The rooms open off a panelled corridor above the main floor, each fitted out by the house that holds it, so the corridor runs from austere to lavish within a few doors. Rooms are leased by the cycle and the leases are public even when the meetings are not. Candidates are invited rather than admitted. The corridor has a bench at each end and no seating between, which means anyone waiting is waiting where the whole corridor can see them.

Sol Contractor Board.description: Work commonly offered to Sol Starians, including the dangerous jobs others avoid, posted on a board that everyone in the Hall recognizes without explanation. Pay is better than the equivalent elsewhere, for reasons. Organizers gather near it and take notes. The board is a tall panel set slightly apart from the general listings, with its own rail and its own standing space, and the listings on it name conditions that the public floor's listings usually leave out. Postings are checked against the fair contract rules and are frequently found compliant and still appalling. The notes taken nearby are kept by people building a pattern rather than a complaint. The board's frame is old star-metal, and the bolt holes around it show that it has been moved at least twice.

Fair Contract Review Office.description: Free legal review of any contract before signing, with exploitation-prevention staff who will read a document line by line for anyone who asks. Their annotations are blunt. Employers who object to their clients using this office generally reveal exactly why it exists. The office is a counter and three reading rooms off the main floor, plainly furnished, with a queue that is longest in the hour before the floor closes. Review is free and confidential, and staff will annotate a copy for the worker to keep. They advise rather than refuse, since the decision belongs to the person signing. The sample contracts pinned along the corridor are real, with the names removed, and each one is marked up in red where the trap is.

Disputed Payment Court.description: Unpaid work, changed terms and dangerous conditions heard by arbitrators with power to order payment and bar an employer from the Hall. Workers usually appear without representation. The court's records are the best evidence in the capital of how bad work actually gets. The court is a plain chamber with a table, a witness chair and a public bench, kept deliberately informal so that an unrepresented worker is not immediately at a disadvantage. Filings cost little and are heard in order. Arbitrators can order payment, amend terms and bar an employer from listing, and the bars are posted publicly. The record shelves along the back wall are open to inspection, and organizers work through them with a persistence the court has never discouraged.

Reputation Verification Desk.description: Confirms credentials and employment records while permitting a formal response to a disputed entry, so that one bad season is not permanent. Checks run both directions now. Employers with a pattern of complaints are flagged to applicants who ask directly. The desk is a counter with screened booths behind it, positioned between the public floor and the professional gallery so that both use it. Checks are charged to whoever requests them and the fee is the same regardless of outcome. A disputed entry carries the subject's own written response attached to it permanently. The card at the counter explaining the right of response is printed in larger type than anything else on the desk, which was a decision somebody had to argue for.

Second Career Pavilion.description: For people changing professions, leaving house roles or rebuilding after a public failure, with counsellors who treat a career change as ordinary rather than as a confession. Retraining referrals are handled here. The pavilion is busiest in the weeks after any major closure in the city. The pavilion is a separate room with soft seating and a side entrance, the only part of the Hall that does not open directly onto the noise of the floor. Sessions are free and unhurried, and nothing discussed in them is recorded on any employment file. Counsellors refer people to the Open Circuit, the trade schools and the civic desk depending on what they actually want. The tea point in the corner is maintained by the counsellors themselves and is the room's most commented-upon feature.

Anonymous Talent Demonstration Rooms.description: Applicants may demonstrate skill before revealing house identity, behind screens that hide everything except the work. Employers commit to an assessment before the name is given. A number of the capital's better careers began with someone refusing to be judged on their surname. The rooms are small and identical, each divided by a screen with a working surface on the applicant's side and a viewing position on the other, lit so that neither party can read anything from posture or dress. Sessions are booked in advance and run to a fixed length. An employer who withdraws after the name is given has that withdrawal recorded. The screens are plain panel, replaced when they wear, and the room keeps no decoration at all that could hint at anyone's origin.

Closed Contract Archive.description: Records of failed jobs, injuries, disappearances and unresolved liability, held under access rules and requested more often than the Hall would like. The files are complete and unflattering. Anyone building a case against an employer starts in this room. The archive is a low room of closed shelving behind a counter, with two reading desks and a clerk who logs every request and every file released. Access is granted against a stated purpose, and the categories of person who may ask are posted at the counter. Copies are charged by the page. The request log itself is not public, which is the single question visitors ask most often and the one the clerk has a fixed form of words for.

Immediate Work Queue.description: Fast hiring for urgent needs, filled from a standing line of people who need money today and cannot wait for a review. It solves genuine emergencies and produces frequent abuse. Everyone in the Hall knows which of those any given morning is about. The queue forms along a marked line by the side entrance, in the open, under a lamp that is left on through the night because the line begins forming long before the Hall opens. Employers take workers from the front and are required to state the work and the rate before anyone leaves the line. Payment is same-day and is the entire attraction. The chalk mark on the wall where the line starts has been redrawn in the same place for years and nobody now knows who first put it there.

Maker's Reach.name: Maker's Reach
Maker's Reach.basicInfo: The production, repair, design and small-industry district where Relstaris builds and fixes much of what it consumes, from civic infrastructure to clothing to kitchen systems. Less prestigious than Academy research and far less controlled than Vexorath engineering, its strength is practical work done to real deadlines by independent specialists and minor-house crafts. Busy, noisy, inventive and physically grounded. The district is built low and heavy in soot-darkened stone and plate over an older star-metal frame, its workshop rows running under gantries that were hung for a different trade entirely, with reused conduit carrying power to benches that were never in any original plan. Colour comes from the shutters: every unit is painted by whoever holds it, and the rows change palette from one frontage to the next. Corelight reaches the yards in a broad wash and sets the working day, the foundry and repair crews starting before it reaches full daytime intensity and the quieter benches working on through the evening shift, with heavy draws scheduled into the maintenance window. Materials, bench rent, certification and tool hire all cost money, and the district's oldest argument is over who pays for the parts when a repair goes wrong.
Maker's Reach.hiddenInfo: The district solves problems the prestigious institutions have failed at, and resents having to say so politely. A civic repair crew here has just fixed something the research campus modelled incorrectly for two cycles, and neither side is handling the credit well. Counterfeit certification is the district's live scandal: forged Contair-standard marks have appeared on locally made components, and the Standards Office is working out whether the source is a workshop or an inspector. A prototype abandoned in the salvage yard has turned out to be valuable to people who do not shop in the Prototype Market, and its inventor has started being approached in the street. Redevelopment pressure is rising on the older workshop rows, with construction contracts already drafted for housing that would displace whole families of makers. An apprentice and a master are in open dispute over whose design a successful piece actually was, and the Under-the-Table Repair Door has relocated again, one step ahead of an inspection it knows the schedule of.

Independent Workshop Rows.description: Rows of open-fronted workshops making tools, furniture, equipment, clothing and custom fabrication to order, each with its own bench, its own smell and its own regulars. Commissions are agreed by handshake and drawing. Most makers here have worked the same unit for decades. The rows are narrow and continuous, shutters folded back through the working day so that the whole street is one long workshop, floors laid in plate where the heavy trades sit and worn stone where they do not. Units are leased from the district and the leases pass between makers more often than through the office. Prices are quoted against materials and hours. The drawing boards propped at the front of each unit carry the current commissions in pencil, and customers read their neighbours' as a matter of course.

Civic Repair Yards.description: Public infrastructure and emergency repair staged from open yards stacked with conduit, panel and transit components. Crews roll out at any hour to failures across the city. The yard foreperson's judgement about what can wait is effectively municipal policy. The yards are open plate aprons behind heavy gates, racked with salvaged and new stock in equal measure, lit hard at every hour because the work does not observe the Corelight. Crews are civic staff on rotating shifts and are dispatched from a board in the yard office. Materials are drawn against a job number and accounted for afterward. The chalk board by the gate lists the open faults across the city, and the order in which the foreperson rewrites it in the morning is watched closely by anyone who has been waiting.

Star-Metal Foundry Hall.description: Controlled shaping and structural work in star-metal, done behind heat shielding in a hall that glows through its roof vents at night. Output goes into buildings, bridges and civic frames. The foundry crews are among the best-paid and most closely regulated workers in the district. The hall is a single tall volume with shielded bays along one side and a moving gantry overhead, its floor plate replaced in sections and its walls dark with decades of work. Draws are scheduled and licensed, and the heavy ones are taken in the maintenance window when the supply is steadiest. Nobody enters the bay floor without clearance and gear. The shift bell at the end of the hall is old enough that it was inherited with the building, and the crews still work to it rather than to any posted clock.

Textile and Garment Court.description: House fashion, professional clothing, performance costume and straightforward repair, made in a bright court of cutting tables and pattern displays. Commissions arrive from compounds and conservatories alike. A torn formal coat can be saved here in an afternoon, at a price. The court is glazed along its upper wall so the light falls evenly on the cutting tables, the floor swept constantly and the air full of the particular quiet of people concentrating. Work is priced by the piece and rush work is priced higher, openly. Fittings are held behind curtains at the back and the schedule for them is the court's most contested document. The rail of finished commissions by the door is covered against dust, and each piece carries a ticket with a name and a collection date.

Food Systems Workshop.description: Kitchens, preservation systems, market equipment and restaurant design, built and tested by people who consult working chefs before drawing anything. Installations go into venues across the capital. The workshop keeps a functioning kitchen purely to break its own products in. The building is part fabrication floor and part test kitchen, tiled where it needs to be and plated where it does not, with extraction running through ducting that has been extended by three different owners. Designs are quoted, built and installed under contract, with maintenance sold separately and taken up by most buyers. Chefs come in to argue with the drawings. The test kitchen's equipment is visibly abused, and the workshop shows it to clients on purpose rather than tidying it away before a visit.

Flight Equipment Bay.description: Civilian movement gear built, fitted and maintained in a bay with a test lane running out over the terraces. Safety checks are mandatory and logged. Couriers and daily commuters queue here on the same mornings and complain about each other cheerfully. The bay is open-fronted onto the lane, racked with gear along both walls and fitted with a bench where every item is checked before it leaves. Fitting is charged, checks are charged, and the log entry is free and compulsory. The test lane is netted and marked with the same symbols used on the city's public corridors. The board above the bench lists the items currently withdrawn from service by type, and the couriers read it before they read anything else in the room.

Contair Standards Office.description: Verification for any system claiming technical compatibility, issuing or refusing the marks that let a component be sold legally. Inspectors visit workshops unannounced. Their refusals are quietly the reason most of what this district builds can be trusted. The office is a plain civic-standard suite with a counter, a test bay and a records room, finished in grey and deliberately unlike every workshop around it. Submissions are logged, charged and examined in the order they arrive. Inspectors are rotated between rows so that no maker deals with the same one repeatedly. The mark itself is struck rather than printed, and the office keeps the retired dies locked in the records room where the inspectors can point at them during an argument about forgery.

Prototype Market.description: Small creators sell early designs directly to the public from portable stalls, with the maker standing behind every piece explaining what it does not yet do. Buyers accept the risk knowingly. Several now-standard civic tools were first sold from this pavement. The market runs along a widened stretch of pavement under a run of gantries, stalls set out at posted hours and packed away at the close, with pitch fees charged by the day. Sellers must state what is untested and most of them enjoy doing it. Buyers get a written note of what the maker will and will not stand behind. The pitch nearest the corner is the most valuable and is allocated by a rota that the market's sellers administer themselves, with predictable results.

Apprentice Work Court.description: Practical education outside the Academy, where apprentices learn on real commissions with real consequences and a master watching the first hundred mistakes. Places are contested. Graduates of this court often out-earn Academy-trained peers within a few years. The court is a shared floor of benches under a high roof, with each master's group working its own corner and the whole of it visible from a walkway above. Placements are registered through the Open Contract Hall and the terms are recorded. Apprentices are paid a little and charged for materials they ruin, which is an education in itself. The offcut bin at the centre of the floor is picked over daily, and the rule that anything in it belongs to whoever reaches it first is enforced with some vigour.

Failed Design Salvage Yard.description: Useful parts and harder lessons pulled from unsuccessful work, sorted into bins anyone may search for a small fee. Students, makers and scavengers pick through it daily. Occasionally something in here turns out to have been abandoned too early. The yard is an open plate lot behind a mesh fence, its bins ranked by material rather than by origin and its aisles muddy with metal dust. The fee is paid at a hut by the gate and buys a full day of searching. Anything taken is weighed and recorded, which is how the yard keeps track of what leaves. The bin at the back that nobody has sorted in years is the one experienced searchers go through first, and they do not advertise the fact.

Construction Contract Office.description: District growth, housing and public works contracted from an office whose noticeboard decides which streets change next. Residents attend the postings in numbers. Redevelopment disputes start here long before anything is built or demolished. The office is a plain frontage with a public room at the front and drawing offices behind, its noticeboard glazed and lockable and mounted where a crowd can gather without blocking the lane. Contracts are advertised, tendered and awarded in public sessions. Objections are received in writing and have a stated period in which they must be made. The board's glazing was fitted after the notices were repeatedly removed, and the office has never said by whom.

Emergency Fabrication Floor.description: A standing capacity activated during shortages and city crises, idle and fully equipped the rest of the time. When it runs, the district works in shifts around the clock. Its output during the last supply collapse is still cited in Republic briefings. The floor is a large clear hall with machinery held under covers, its power fed through heavy conduit tapped from the district's oldest supply and tested monthly whether or not anything is running. Activation is authorized by the district and paid for afterward, which is an argument deferred rather than avoided. Crews are drawn from the workshop rows on a standing list. The covers are removed and replaced as part of the test, and the crews who do it treat the ritual with more respect than they admit.

Quiet Inventor Rooms.description: Affordable rented workspaces, small and private, let by the month to people working on something they are not ready to show. Some rooms stay occupied for years. The corridor rule is that nobody asks what is behind a closed door. The rooms run off a plain internal corridor with a shared power point at each end and no windows onto the lane, which is exactly why they let so quickly. Rent is modest, paid monthly, and includes nothing beyond the space and the supply. Tenants sign for their own waste and their own insurance. The corridor noticeboard carries only practical notices about the power and the water, and any attempt to use it for anything else is quietly removed overnight.

Under-the-Table Repair Door.description: An unlicensed modification business that relocates the moment it is inspected, currently trading behind a different frontage two streets from the last one. The work is fast, cheap and uncertified. Its customers include people who cannot explain what they need repaired. The current premises are a single deep unit with the shutter half down through the working day and a bench visible from the lane only if somebody is looking for it. Payment is taken on completion and no record is kept beyond what the customer takes away. The tools are good and the operator is genuinely skilled. The previous frontages are still identifiable along the row by the bolt holes where a sign used to hang, and the district's makers can point out every one of them.

South Service Terraces.name: South Service Terraces
South Service Terraces.basicInfo: Stepped residential terraces housing the gate, market, cargo, maintenance and service workers who keep Relstaris moving while remaining nearly invisible in formal accounts of the city. Housing, childcare, clinics and transit here are organized around rotating shifts rather than daylight. It is practical, crowded, strongly communal and consistently undervalued by the districts it serves. The terraces step back in courses of grey-green stone over an older star-metal frame, linked by public stairs, lifts and walkways, with reused conduit run up the outside of the blocks to feed rooms and stairwell lamps that were added long after the buildings were finished. Frontages are painted by the households that hold them and no two courses match, which residents regard as the point. Corelight reaches the lower terraces briefly and the upper ones for longer, so the district reads the shift pattern off its own lamps as much as off the light, and the maintenance window is when the water pressure drops and everybody knows it. Rent, utilities, childcare and clinic charges are all real costs on a service wage, and the district's institutions exist because those costs are the ordinary pressure of life here.
South Service Terraces.hiddenInfo: The terraces know how much leverage they have and are increasingly willing to use it. Labour action here would halt the Gate Hub and the Grand Market within a day, and the Service Association Rooms — called the Service Union Rooms by Branna Sol and the service workers themselves, the same place under a working name — are currently weighing exactly that over shift conditions on the cargo floors. A routine maintenance contract has been found to contain assignments far more dangerous than its terms admit, and the worker who noticed is deciding who to take it to. Redevelopment out of Maker's Reach is displacing families from the older terraces, and the Rent Dispute Office is fighting cases faster than it can win them. A service worker who cleans a compound in the east has overheard something political they were never meant to hear and has told nobody outside their own stair. The Supply Shortage Kitchen has been running longer than usual this season, which means the disruption upstream is worse than the Market is admitting.

Gateworker Housing.description: Residences organized around rotating Gate Hub shifts, with sound-damped walls and stairwells where someone is always asleep. Households coordinate meals across incompatible schedules. Everyone here can report the Hub's real staffing situation better than its records can. The blocks are plain and solidly built, their windows shuttered at all hours and their stair lamps kept low, with a shared drying court at the base of each stack. Tenancies are held by workers and their families and are not tied to the employer, a protection the district fought for. Rent is collected monthly and utilities are metered separately. The rota sheets pinned inside each entrance are the household schedules rather than the Hub's, and neighbours read them to know when it is safe to use the stairs at speed.

Market Staff Rows.description: Housing for vendors, cleaners, security and support workers from the Grand Market, built in long low rows with storage at street level. Stock and personal property share the same lockups. Residents leave before dawn and the rows are silent until mid-morning. The rows are older than most of the district, brick and plate under a continuous walkway, their street level given over to shuttered lockups and their upper floors reached by external stairs. Lockups are rented separately from the dwelling and the rents are a standing grievance. Handcarts stand outside every second door through the night. The walkway above the lockups is where the rows conduct their social life, and the chairs left along it are moved only for repairs.

Maintenance Family Terraces.description: Multi-generation households connected to civic repair work, where three generations of the same family may hold posts on the same crews. Tools live in the hallway. Skills and job referrals both pass down these stairs as a matter of course. The terraces are deep and narrow, built back into the terrace step, with workshops and stores at the lowest level, their stairwells wide enough to carry equipment and worn accordingly. Tenancies pass within families where the district's housing rules allow it. Households keep their own stock of parts and lend it freely. The hooks and brackets fitted along every hallway are the district's most characteristic detail, and a new household is judged quietly on how quickly it puts them to use.

Shift Change Plaza.description: The district's centre: food stalls, news boards, transit stops and labour organizing all crowded into one plaza that surges four times a day as shifts turn over. Announcements are shouted from the steps. It is the fastest place in the south to hear anything true. The plaza is a paved square with a covered edge, stalls along two sides, the transit head at one corner and a set of broad steps that serve as the district's platform. Pitches are licensed and cheap. The surge empties as fast as it fills, leaving the stalls to restock and the boards to be rewritten. The steps are worn hollow at the centre and the district has resurfaced them once, badly, in a slightly different stone that everybody still remarks on.

Worker Food Court.description: Affordable heavy meals served at every hour by cooks who know which shift is coming in next and cook accordingly. Portions are sized for physical work. A worker can eat here for a week on what one meal costs in the entertainment district. The court is a covered run of counters and long shared tables, tiled for cleaning and vented straight up through the roof, warm at every hour and never empty for long. Counters pay a pitch fee to the district and hold their pitches for years. Meals are paid for at the counter and there is a slate arrangement that is never discussed in front of strangers. The table at the far end is kept clear for crews coming off a night shift, by a convention nobody has ever had to explain twice.

Public Childcare Hall.description: Essential support for households whose work hours do not resemble a school day, staffed continuously and organized around shift patterns rather than terms. Children stay overnight when a rota demands it. Without this hall, a large share of the district could not work at all. The hall is low and bright, divided into rooms by age with a quiet room for sleeping and a walled yard that is used at every hour. Places are charged on a sliding contribution and the contribution is assessed privately. Staff are trained, paid and permanently short-handed. The handover book at the door records who brought a child and who is expected to collect them, and it is the single document in the district that is never allowed to fall behind.

Service Association Rooms.description: Worker councils, labour disputes and mutual aid run from plain meeting rooms with a noticeboard older than most of the members. Branna Sol and the service workers call the same place the Service Union Rooms; it is a working name, not a second institution. Decisions made here reach the Gate Hub within hours. The rooms occupy a converted terrace with a hall at the front and smaller rooms behind, furnished in mismatched chairs and lit by lamps the association owns rather than rents. Membership is by subscription and the subscription is small. Meetings are held at the shift changes so that every rota can reach one. The noticeboard carries current disputes, aid appeals and funeral notices on the same surface, and nothing is removed from it until the matter is settled.

Affordable Clinic.description: Routine care and workplace injury treatment at rates a service wage can actually meet, with evening and night hours that match the district's shifts. Its injury log reads as an accurate account of which employers cut corners. The physicians here know every family by name. The clinic is a plain building with a waiting room that opens straight off the plaza, consulting rooms behind and a treatment room fitted for the injuries this district actually produces. Charges are posted and reduced through an access arrangement the desk explains without being asked. The waiting room noticeboard carries employment advice and childcare notices alongside health information, because the staff long ago accepted that people read whatever is in front of them.

Night Transit Station.description: Reliable movement through the small hours, when wealthier districts thin their service to almost nothing. Platforms are lit, staffed and busy at three in the morning. The operators know their regulars and hold a car for someone running from a late shift. The station is a plain covered platform on the district's transit ring, its shelters glazed and its lamps kept at full through the night, with a staffed booth that sells fares and answers questions nobody else is awake to answer. Fares are the same as anywhere on the ring and are paid at the barrier. Services run at intervals that the district negotiated and defends at every review. The timetable board is amended by hand whenever a service changes, and the corrections are trusted more than the printed sheet.

Community Repair Court.description: Shared tools, loaned equipment and practical help, run on a book of favours rather than fees. Neighbours fix each other's homes on rest days. Professional makers from Maker's Reach turn up on their own time and pretend it is nothing. The court is an open yard behind the terraces with a lockup of tools, a couple of benches under a roof and a tap that everyone uses. Tools are signed out in a book and returned; anything broken is replaced by whoever broke it or by the court's own fund. Materials are bought jointly when several households need the same thing. The book itself is the court's institution, and the entries in it run back far enough that people look up what their grandparents borrowed.

Worker School Annex.description: Education timed around family shifts, with classes running early, late and at weekends so children and adults can both attend. Teachers are supplied through the Academy's education institute. Adult literacy and trade certification classes are the best attended sessions. The annex is two floors of classrooms over a shared hall, plainly fitted, with a crèche corner so that a parent can attend a class without arranging anything else first. Classes are free or nearly so, and the certification examinations carry a fee that the association helps with. Teachers rotate through from the institute and the good ones are asked to stay. The certificates pinned along the stair are adult ones, and the school puts them there deliberately where the children pass them.

Public Bath and Recovery Hall.description: Rest, heat, water and recovery after physical work, and the district's main social space for people too tired to go anywhere else. Conversation here is unhurried and frank. Disputes between neighbours are more often settled in this hall than in any office. The hall is warm and tiled, its pools and heat rooms fed from a reused conduit line that the district maintains itself, with benches along the walls and a tea counter by the entrance. Entry is charged by the visit at a rate set low on purpose, and the charge is waived for anyone the attendants recognise as having a hard week. Hours run around the shifts. The attendants keep a basket of spare towels that is refilled by regulars rather than by the district.

Rent Dispute Office.description: Housing pressure, sudden rent increases and displacement fought case by case from a cramped office with more files than shelving. Advocates here know the civic code exactly. They win often enough to matter and lose often enough to stay angry. The office is one room and a corridor, its walls stacked with boxes and its single window facing a stairwell, staffed by advocates who work from a shared desk because there is no room for two. Advice is free and representation is arranged where the case justifies it. Cases are logged and the log is used to show patterns rather than incidents. The map on the back wall marks every building in the district with a redevelopment notice against it, and the pins on it have been moving in one direction for some time.

Supply Shortage Kitchen.description: A community food response activated whenever market disruption reaches the district, cooking bulk meals from whatever the routes actually delivered. It opens faster than any civic programme. How long it has been running is the district's honest measure of how bad things are. The kitchen is a plain hall with heavy equipment, a serving hatch onto the street and a store that is kept stocked between activations by the association's own fund. Meals are free while it runs and nobody is asked to account for themselves. Cooks are volunteers from the food court and the terraces, working rotas pinned beside the hatch. The chalk line on the store wall marks each activation and how long it lasted, and it is the first thing anyone looks at when the hatch opens again.

Starfall Entertainment District.name: Starfall Entertainment District
Starfall Entertainment District.basicInfo: Starfall is the nightlife hub most visitors picture when they imagine Relstaris after dark: an illuminated promenade, elevated clubs, a night market and a permanent crowd. It runs from late afternoon until well after the rest of the city has begun another workday. Students, performers, off-duty workers and the occasional representative share the same bright, loud streets. The district wears its history as decoration. Star-glass venue fronts hang on older star-metal frames, and the light bands that give the promenade its colour run along energy conduits laid down for something else entirely, now carrying amber, green and hot magenta across stonework cut in a custodial era nobody here can name. No single palette governs the street, and nobody wants one. Opening hours are read off the Corelight rather than a posted schedule: as its intensity drops toward evening routing the shutters come up, and the shift back toward morning is treated as closing. Everything on offer is paid for, from covers and drink counters to stall food and the lift fare to a flight-level door, and the distance between a cheap night on Student Club Row and an expensive one above the promenade is legible from the pavement. Queues build before the doors open, fast flight is held to controlled night lanes, and whatever the evening produces ends up on the late transit platforms.
Starfall Entertainment District.hiddenInfo: Starfall is not corrupt so much as useful to people who are. Legal nightlife supplies noise, cash, anonymity and private rooms, and underworld recruiters work the district by offering entertainment jobs first and something else later. Information brokers watch the No-Recording Rooms constantly, since the one place in the city where capture is legally blocked is also the place worth knowing about; at least one venue is suspected of quietly preserving what it promises not to record. The Fame Verification Office is sitting on a growing file of fabricated performance histories, several of them attached to people now being publicly promoted on the Celebrity Walk. A representative photographed in the wrong company here can lose a season of Republic standing before the Forum opens, and the brokers who decide which version of the night reaches the public are drinking two streets away on Nightglass Row.

Starfall Avenue.description: The district's main promenade runs bright under layered light bands and public art that is replaced every season. Venue fronts, ticket kiosks and food carts crowd both edges while the crowd moves in slow currents. On a good night the noise never stops and nobody crosses it in a straight line. Underfoot the paving is worn to a shine down the middle and still rough at the kerbs, where old star-metal edging shows through the newer surface. Touts work the venue doors, buskers claim the gaps between them, and the light from three competing frontages meets in the air above the centre of the street. Public protection walks it in pairs without hurrying. A notice at each end reminds arrivals that fast flight is not permitted over the promenade, which is ignored about as often as it is read.

Public Dance Hall.description: A broad mixed-house hall where light bands follow the music and a live performer or operator sets the pace. Inside are the main floor, a practice edge for people still learning, a screened conversation gallery, a drink counter and a quiet seat near the exit. Floor hosts manage space and consent; a cover applies on booked evenings. The ceiling is high enough to swallow the sound and the floor is sprung, which regulars notice in their legs the following day. Traditions rotate through the programme without settling into one house style, so a step somebody learned at home may be the step everyone is doing by the end of the night or the step nobody recognises. The practice edge is where most of that gets sorted out, patiently and loudly, by strangers who will not exchange names.

Flight-Level Clubs.description: Elevated venues reached only through controlled night flight lanes, their entrances hung off tower faces above the promenade. Music arrives at street level in fragments. Arrival queues stack in the air, and anyone who cannot fly needs a lift platform and a host already upstairs willing to clear them. The doors are narrow ledges of star-glass and rail with a single attendant working a list, and the wind of other people's arrivals is a constant. Prices inside match the difficulty of getting in. Approach order is enforced by lane monitors rather than by the venues, which means the argument about who was holding the line is always with somebody who does not work for the club. From the balconies the whole of Starfall Avenue reads as a single moving band of light.

Celebrity Walk.description: A stretch of frontage given over to appearances, promotions and fan culture, with recording rigs along the rail and hired crowds on the busier nights. Performers, fighters and occasional politicians work the line. The pavement carries names that mattered for one season and are now walked over without a glance. The lighting here is deliberately flatter and whiter than the rest of the district so that faces read cleanly, and the rail is polished where thousands of hands have held it. Managers negotiate the order of appearances with venue staff who have heard every version of the argument. Between promotions the walk is simply a public street, and residents cross it carrying shopping, stepping over reputations without looking down.

Night Market.description: Stalls sell food, clothing, art and performance goods until the Corelight turns, run by vendors who may not be here next week. Grilled Terva smoke hangs in the aisles. Bargaining is loud and mostly good-natured, and a fair share of the more interesting stock has no history anyone will describe. The aisles are narrow and roofed in strung light, so the whole market glows a warm uneven orange from outside. Stall pitches are paid for nightly and the good corners cost more, which is why the same faces hold them season after season while the edges turn over constantly. Somewhere in the middle a vendor is always repairing a trestle. Buyers who ask too precisely where a piece came from are answered politely and sold nothing.

Student Club Row.description: Cheap venues converted from older shopfronts and packed with Academy students spending stipend money. Covers are low, the music is loud enough to feel through the floor, and the queues start early. It is the first place a new student gets taken and the last place they admit to visiting. The conversions are visible: house-era doorframes with cut-price fittings bolted through them, back rooms that used to be storage, and paint in whatever colour the last operator had available. Water costs money like everything else, which the newest arrivals learn on their first night. Staff are mostly students themselves, working the door of one venue and drinking in the next one along when their shift ends.

Public Game Arcade.description: Simulation booths, physical challenge courts and social games ranked on public boards that update in real time. Groups drift between machines arguing about scores and disputed rounds. It is bright, loud and one of the few Starfall venues where being twelve years old is not a problem. Families come early in the evening and clear out as the district fills. The booths are charged by the round, the challenge courts by the session, and the boards are the reason both keep taking money. Attendants reset equipment between rounds and adjudicate the disputes that the boards cannot, which is most of them. One court has been out of service long enough that its notice has gone soft at the corners, and the queue has simply redistributed itself.

Performer Recruitment Court.description: Agents, venue bookers and promoters hold open tables while hopeful artists wait their turn with prepared material. Contracts get signed across those tables faster than anyone should sign them. The court is busiest in the hours before opening, when everyone present still believes tonight is the night. It is a roofed hall rather than a street, with the tables set in rows and a waiting bench along one wall where people run through material under their breath. Advocates work the edges offering to read a contract before it is signed, for a fee most of the people who need it will not pay. Rejections are delivered quietly and at the table, and the walk back past the bench is the longest part of the day.

Late Transit Platforms.description: The district transit stop runs heavy service through the night and into the morning shift. Platforms fill with people celebrating, arguing, weeping or asleep across a bench. Staff know the regulars by face and keep a medical point and a lost-property desk open at every hour. The platforms sit below the promenade and carry its noise down a stairwell, so the space is loud without anything happening in it. Fares are collected at the gate and nobody is carried for free. The night supervisor's habit is to keep the far end of the last platform lit and lightly staffed for anyone who needs to sit somewhere quiet, an arrangement that appears in no published schedule and has never been withdrawn.

Morning Recovery Cafés.description: Terraces that open as the clubs close, serving strong Cyrra, water and something warm to people who have not gone home yet. Conversation stays low and the window seats fill first. Staff are practised at taking an order without remarking on the state of anyone's evening. The terraces face the promenade at the point where the Corelight shift is most visible, and the change in the light does more to empty the district than any closing time. Prices are ordinary and the portions are generous. Shift workers heading in share the tables with people heading home, which produces the district's only reliably civil conversations. A hand-lettered card by the counter has asked for the return of a particular coat since well before anyone currently working there was hired.

Public Rooftop Gardens.description: Planted terraces above the promenade, free to enter, with views down Starfall Avenue and out toward the Corelight. Couples and small groups take the benches; others come simply to stop hearing the music. The lighting is kept deliberately low, and the noise from below arrives softened. The planting is dense and maintained by civic crews who work in the hours the district is closed, and the benches are old enough that their star-metal frames have been repaired more than once. Because entry costs nothing, the gardens fill with people who have run out of money rather than out of evening. Somebody is usually asleep in the far corner, and the keepers wake them gently at the shift rather than earlier.

Fame Verification Office.description: A civic office issuing performance licences and settling disputes over public identity, credits and stolen acts. Its queue mixes working artists with people claiming careers they never had. The clerks hold the record of who actually performed where, which makes them widely disliked and frequently approached. The hall is plain by district standards, lit evenly and furnished for waiting, with a numbered ticket system that nobody has found a way around. Filings carry a fee and a processing period, and neither is waived for urgency. Arguments at the counter are frequent and rarely brief. The clerks have a standing answer for every version of the complaint, delivered in the same flat tone to a promoter and to a first-time applicant alike.

House Night Pavilions.description: Rotating pavilions sponsored by major and minor houses, each running its own cultural evening. A Volen hearth night and a Solvraxis recital can occupy the same structure a week apart. Sponsorship buys visibility, not exclusivity: anyone lawfully in the district may walk in. The pavilions are demountable frames dressed to whatever the sponsoring house wants shown, which means the same floor carries a different colour, a different music and a different idea of hospitality every few days. Costs fall on the sponsor rather than the visitor, so the food and drink are usually free and the queue outside is accordingly long. House staff run the door and district protection watch it, and the line between welcome and display is renegotiated at every handover.

No-Recording Rooms.description: Legally protected privacy rooms, screened against capture and rented by the hour. People use them for negotiations, arguments and relationships they do not want documented. The screening genuinely works, which is exactly why the doors are watched by people counting who books which room. The rooms themselves are unremarkable: sealed star-glass panels, a table, seating, a service call and no window. Booking is by the hour at a rate that rises sharply through the night, and the desk takes payment before the door opens.
