Staff do not ask what a room is for and are trained not to remember faces, a discipline that holds better at the desk than it does in the corridor outside.

The Last Light Corner.description: A corner where street performers keep working until the Corelight shifts toward morning. The crowd thins to a few dozen and the acts get stranger and better. District custom holds that nobody takes the corner from a performer who still has an audience. The pitch is a shallow bowl of paving with a step around it that serves as seating, backed by a wall where earlier venue signage was removed and never fully patched. Nothing is ticketed and everything runs on what the audience puts down. Performers who lose the crowd hand over without being asked, because the custom is enforced entirely by the people watching. The last act is generally still going when the light turns and the promenade behind it has already emptied.

Grand Performance Hall.name: Grand Performance Hall
Grand Performance Hall.basicInfo: The Grand Performance Hall is the most respected public arts venue in Relstaris, hosting music, theatre, civic ceremony, Academy showcases and major competitions. Its stages range from a vast main house to a small room built for experiments nobody is sure will work. A successful appearance here can remake a career; a public failure can define someone for cycles. The building itself has been inherited several times over and repaired by every government that held it: ancient star-metal carries the span of the main house, narrow service corridors run behind the newer walls in a pattern that was plainly cut for security rather than for stagehands, balconies from a later expansion era hang over the auditorium, and the current restoration work is visible in the fresh star-glass around every entrance. The interior palette is deep red and worn bronze, which belongs to no other district. Corelight reaches the plaza outside and the technical floor takes its cue from it, since evening programming begins as the routing shifts. Nothing here is free except the open-air court: seats are ticketed, rehearsal chambers are booked and charged, and the better sightlines cost accordingly. Performers arrive early, crews arrive earlier, and the queue for returns forms long before the doors.
Grand Performance Hall.hiddenInfo: The Hall's programming is quietly contested. Patrons on the balcony fund seasons and then press the director over content, casting and which minor house gets the main stage, and at least one sponsorship is currently being used to keep a work about an earlier Core transfer out of the schedule. The Performer Archive holds records of banned pieces and disastrous nights that several established families would prefer stayed unrequested, and researchers who ask for them tend to be noticed. Backstage, contract and ownership disputes run constantly between Academy-trained performers and the houses that sponsored their training. Sabotage happens here more often than the Hall admits publicly, and it is rarely obvious whether the motive is personal rivalry, commercial pressure or politics. The Emergency Replacement Room is the reason: an understudy who steps out on a ruined night can leave famous, so someone always benefits from a ruined night.

Grand Main Stage.description: The principal house, built for large productions, orchestral work, theatre and public ceremony, with tiered seating that fills to the upper rail on opening nights. Its acoustic systems are tuned before every run. Standing on the empty stage during a technical call is reportedly the loudest silence in the city. The room is high and deep, in dark red and dulled bronze, and the old star-metal ribs of the span are left exposed above the topmost tier where the newer ceiling stops short of them. Seats are ticketed by level and the difference between the levels is not subtle. Latecomers are held at the doors until a break in the programme, a rule the front-of-house staff enforce against representatives and students with the same unbothered courtesy.

Public Performance Court.description: An open-air court outside the main house where accessible programming runs free of charge. Families sit on the steps, students perform between professional slots and the sound spills into the surrounding streets. It is where most Relstaris residents first see anything the Hall produces. The steps are broad, shallow and warm-coloured, cut from stone that predates the frontage behind them, and they are worn into dips where the best sightlines are. Nothing is ticketed and nothing is reserved, so arriving early is the only currency that works. Vendors are permitted at the edges and charge what the district charges. Between slots the court reverts to ordinary use, with children running the steps and someone practising in a corner nobody has asked them to leave.

Minor-House Theater.description: A mid-sized house reserved for smaller-house and independent productions that would never be scheduled on the main stage. Programming is argued over fiercely and changes with the season. A strong run here has repeatedly been the thing that moved a minor name into citywide conversation. The room is plainer than the main house and better liked by the people who work in it, with a shallow rake, a flexible floor and fittings that have been replaced piece by piece rather than all at once. Slots are allotted rather than sold, which makes the allotment itself the contested thing. Companies share the same dressing space and the same technical crew, and a great deal of the district's professional gossip is generated in the corridor between them.

Academy Showcase Hall.description: The venue for student, faculty and alumni performance, run jointly with the Academy's conservatory. Assessment panels sit near the front and family sits behind them. The atmosphere is part concert, part examination, and the applause is never quite an honest measure of what the panel thought. The hall is lit evenly rather than dramatically, because the panel needs to see, and the seating is arranged so that the front rows can be watched by everyone behind them. Attendance is free to family and charged to the public. Students hold the corridor outside in a state of controlled panic for most of the day. Results are not announced in the room, which does not stop the entire audience from reading the panel's faces as they leave.

Artist Dressing Wing.description: A corridor of preparation rooms where nerves, rivalry and backstage politics are concentrated into the hour before a performance. Costume and effect systems line the walls. Who gets the end room is a status question everyone claims not to care about and everyone tracks. The corridor is narrow, warm and permanently over-lit, and its walls carry the layered marks of every fitting that has ever been bolted to them. Room allocation is posted at the head of the wing, which is the first thing any arriving company reads. Somebody is always warming up through a wall. The wing's own custom is that the call is repeated three times and nobody is collected after the third, a rule that has ended at least one career and started several others.

Rehearsal Chambers.description: Practice spaces of varying size, booked in rotation by professionals, students and touring companies. Sound isolation keeps a chamber ensemble and a percussion rehearsal from destroying one another. The booking board is the most closely read document in the building. Chambers are charged by the block and the cheap blocks are the awkward ones, which is why the small hours are populated entirely by students and by people rebuilding a career. The isolation is a retrofit into much older rooms, so the panels stop short of the ceiling in places and a low thud carries through the floor regardless. Overrunning a block is the single most reliable way to start an argument in the Hall, and the board carries a worn notice saying so.

Cultural Festival Plaza.description: A broad plaza attached to the Hall used for seasonal and rotating regional festivals, with temporary staging and vendor rows. Solvraxis, Ignivex and Korrvane seasons all take their turn here. When no festival is running it reverts to an ordinary, pleasant public square. Its paving is pale and hard-wearing, set with anchor points for staging that are invisible until a festival needs them, and the Corelight falls across it unobstructed enough that residents use the plaza to read the shift. Vendor pitches are licensed and charged. Each visiting season brings its own colours, food, music and assumptions about how loud a public space is allowed to be, and the plaza absorbs all of it and then goes quiet again.

Patron Balcony.description: Elevated boxes for sponsors and their guests, with private service and a clear sightline to both the stage and the rest of the audience. Being seen here is half the point. Sponsorship conversations happen during intervals and occasionally during performances, which the performers notice. The boxes are hung from an older expansion and finished in bronze and smoked star-glass, with a separate stair so that arrivals need not cross the public foyer. Attendants work the level permanently and know exactly which box is in use by whom. Access is by sponsorship rather than by ticket, and the Hall depends on it, which shapes how firmly the director is able to decline a request made in one of these rooms between acts.

Performer Archive.description: Records of famous appearances, catastrophes, technical innovations and works withdrawn from performance, held in a climate-stable gallery. Access is public but logged. Archivists can produce a recording of almost any night the Hall has staged, which is a service and a threat depending on who is asking. The gallery is cool and quiet, lined with stacked storage behind glazed star-metal frames, and lit low enough that the reading desks each carry their own lamp. Retrieval takes time and carries a fee for anything outside the open catalogue. The request slip asks for a name, a date and a reason, and the archivists have never once explained what happens to the third field.

Backstage Contract Office.description: Where employment, rights, payment and ownership are settled, or more often fought over, between performers, companies and sponsors. Advocates work from a side room. The office keeps late hours because most disputes surface within an hour of a performance ending. The room is small, functional and set directly off the working corridor, so half its business is conducted by people still in costume. Filings are recorded and copied, and the copies are what the arguments are actually about. Academy-trained performers and the houses that paid for that training account for a standing share of the caseload. The bench outside has been repaired at one end and not the other, which is the detail every regular claimant mentions.

Technical Production Floor.description: Lighting rigs, sound arrays, staging machinery and specialist effect systems are run and maintained from here by crews who know the building better than any director. Cable runs cross the floor in marked lanes. The crew's opinion of a production is generally accurate and never solicited. The floor is loud in the way machinery is loud rather than the way audiences are, and it runs on power drawn through conduits far older than the equipment bolted onto them. Shifts are scheduled around the Corelight's maintenance windows, when the heavier work is done. Spares are ordered, invoiced and waited for like anything else in the city, and one rig has been running on a temporary fix long enough for the fix to acquire a nickname among the crew.

Public Critic Gallery.description: A seating block set aside for reviewers and food for the reputation economy that follows every opening. Debate continues in the gallery bar long after the curtain. A single well-placed review from these seats has closed productions and filled houses in the same season. The block sits at the level where the sound is best and the sightline is honest, which the Hall concedes deliberately. Seats are allocated by accreditation rather than sold. Nothing prevents an ordinary member of the public from buying into the rows alongside, and a certain kind of enthusiast does exactly that in order to argue with reviewers at the interval. The bar stays open past the last performance for no stated reason.

Emergency Replacement Room.description: A small ready room where covers and understudies wait through performances they expect not to appear in. It holds fitted costume, a mirror and very little else. Careers have started in this room, which is why nobody treats a shift in it as wasted time. The room sits close enough to the wings that the performance carries through the wall as a muffled shape without words, and the call system is the only decoration. Shifts in it are paid, modestly. Occupants read, stretch, run lines under their breath and watch the call light. The mirror frame carries initials scratched into it over many seasons, a practice the Hall has never officially permitted and has also never sanded off.

Silent Stage.description: A small black room for experimental work and private previews, named for its policy of no announcement and no recording. Audiences are invited rather than ticketed. Work that would be laughed off the main stage is tried here first, and occasionally survives. The room is unfinished by design, its walls and floor dark, its seating movable, its rig minimal and openly patched into the building's older power runs. Invitations circulate by word of mouth among people who work in the Hall and in the district around it. Nothing is billed and nothing is reviewed. The house custom is that what happens here is not repeated outside, which holds for the work and fails immediately for the gossip.

Nightglass Row.name: Nightglass Row
Nightglass Row.basicInfo: Nightglass Row is the capital's high-end private nightlife district, an elevated promenade of invitation-only clubs, diplomatic lounges and dining rooms with negotiated guest lists. Public figures come here to be seen by the right people and unseen by everyone else. It is elegant, expensive and considerably more dangerous socially than Starfall is physically. The Row is built quiet. Its frontages are smoked star-glass in greys and near-blacks with almost no signage, set into an older star-metal colonnade that was clearly raised for some other purpose and has been refitted rather than replaced, and the lighting is kept low and warm so that a face at a distance stays a shape. Corelight barely enters at street level, which is the point; the venues run their own light and take their hours from the district rather than from the city's routing, opening as the Corelight drops and closing well before it turns. Everything on the Row is charged and most of it is charged twice, once for the service and once for the discretion. Admission is by invitation, membership or the word of somebody already inside, and refusal is delivered courteously at the door by staff who never explain it. Arrivals are received. Noise is a sign that something has gone wrong.
Nightglass Row.hiddenInfo: Privacy on the Row is a product: promised, priced, negotiated and regularly breached. More Republic business is settled in the Diplomatic Lounge and the Confidential Contract Suites than in any Forum committee room, and representatives who will not enter one another's compounds meet in the Major-House Bars instead. Reputation brokers sit one table away from outright information brokerage, and the difference is a matter of paperwork rather than conduct. The Closed Window's absolute ban on recording made its reputation, and the persistent suspicion is that the club has preserved far more private evidence than it destroyed. Blackmail here rarely arrives as a threat; it arrives as a favour. At least one major-house member is running underworld business through the Row's private suites, using legitimate venue security to keep out exactly the people who would notice.

Nightglass Promenade.description: A refined elevated street of dark glass frontages, most of them unmarked, lit low enough that faces are difficult to resolve from a distance. Arrivals are received rather than admitted. The promenade is quiet by design; noise on Nightglass Row is a sign someone has made a mistake. Underfoot the surface is dark, even and kept immaculate by crews who work the hours the Row is closed. Door staff stand back from the entrances rather than in front of them, and a guest who does not know which frontage to approach is already the wrong guest. Public protection may lawfully walk it, and does, unhurriedly and without being welcomed. The only conspicuous thing on the whole street is the occasional stretch of older colonnade where the refit stopped short and the original star-metal is left plain.

Diplomatic Lounge.description: Where representatives and senior staff meet outside formal government, in deep seating arranged so no group overhears another. Service is discreet and constant. Conversations begun here have altered Republic positions before the relevant committee was ever convened. The room is broad and low-ceilinged, divided by screens and planting into clusters that each keep their own sightline to the door, and the light is warm enough to flatter and dim enough to obscure. Attendants circulate without being summoned and withdraw without being dismissed. Staff hold a standing rule against seating two delegations within earshot, which occasionally means a senior figure waits, and waits visibly, until a cluster clears.

Private Gaming Hall.description: Legal high-stakes games, social wagers and reputation risks, played at tables with house-neutral oversight. Stakes are often favours rather than credits. Losing well is admired; losing badly in front of the wrong audience has ended more than one political career. The hall is smaller than its reputation, a single room of dark wood and dulled metal with the tables set far enough apart that each carries its own quiet. Oversight staff stand at the wall and are drawn from no single house, which is the arrangement the Row sells. Buy-in is real money and the favours are recorded nowhere. The custom is that a player may leave a table at any point between hands, and the people who cannot bring themselves to use it are precisely the ones everyone else is watching.

Restricted Performance Club.description: Invitation-only entertainment, small rooms, short runs and performers who are paid well for discretion. Programmes are never published. Getting in requires someone already inside to vouch for the newcomer, which makes the guest list itself the interesting document. The rooms are intimate to the point of discomfort, with the performance close enough that an audience cannot pretend not to be part of it. Performers are engaged by short contract and paid at a rate that reflects the silence expected afterwards. Runs end without notice. Staff destroy the guest list at the close of each night as a matter of house policy, and the standing question on the Row is whether that policy survives contact with anyone willing to pay for the sheet.

Major-House Bars.description: Neutral venues catering to representatives who refuse to set foot inside one another's compounds. Seating is arranged to give every party a clear exit. The staff are chosen for their ability to serve a Dravon and a Castro delegation on the same evening without incident. The rooms are deliberately plain for the Row, with no house symbol anywhere in them, and the neutrality is maintained by the venue rather than by any agreement between the guests. Security is the venue's own and works to the Row's limits rather than to any house's instructions. Bar staff learn early that the correct response to an overheard sentence is to keep pouring, and the ones who manage it are paid well enough to stay for years.

Invitation Dining Rooms.description: Private meals with negotiated guest lists, where the composition of the table is itself the message. Menus are agreed in advance. An unexpected fourth chair at a three-person dinner has been read across the capital as a political announcement. The rooms are sealed, warm and furnished for a fixed number, and the setting of that number is handled between staff days before anyone arrives. Service enters on a call and not otherwise. Cancellation is charged in full, which is why an empty room with a laid table is occasionally left to run its booking. The lists themselves are held by the venue, and the venue's willingness to confirm or deny a name is the reason anyone books here at all.

Rooftop Flight Lounge.description: A high-altitude terrace with controlled access, reached by approved flight lanes and a single lift for ground guests. The view runs from the Corelight to the Southeast rim. Conversations happen at the rail, where the wind makes eavesdropping technically difficult. The terrace is open, pale and much brighter than anything below it, which surprises first-time guests who have come up through the dark of the promenade. Lane clearance is arranged by the venue and can be refused. The single lift is a genuine constraint and a deliberate one, since it means every ground guest is seen arriving by whoever is already at the rail. Attendants keep to the inner edge and leave the rail to the guests.

Private Security Court.description: Venue security coordinates here, handling guest disputes, refusals and discreet removals without involving public protection. It runs its own incident record. The court's standing arrangement with the Row's owners is more valuable to them than any individual client. The room is functional rather than elegant, set behind the frontages with its own access, and it is the only space on the Row that looks like work. Directors from several venues meet in it to agree who is barred and for how long. The record is kept meticulously and shared selectively. Removals are handled through back routes and staff describe them, without irony, as escorting a guest to their transport.

Quiet Exit Passage.description: A protected departure route threading behind the venues for guests who cannot be seen leaving by the promenade. Access is granted, not bought. Its existence is common knowledge; who used it on a given night is not. The passage is narrow, lit at ankle height and finished plainly, running between service walls where the older structure of the Row is entirely undisguised. Venue staff open it from the inside and it cannot be entered from the far end. Use is logged by the venue that grants it, and those logs are the single most frequently requested document on the Row. A worn place on one wall marks where a great many shoulders have turned the same corner in a hurry.

Reputation Broker's Table.description: A permanently reserved table where legal public-relations consultation sits uncomfortably close to information brokerage. Clients arrive with a problem and leave with a version of events. Which version reaches the public first is usually decided over the second drink. The table sits where it can be seen, which is part of the service, and the reservation is paid for continuously whether or not anyone is sitting at it. Consultations are billed by engagement and the fees are not discussed at the table. The work is lawful as written and the paperwork is impeccable. What arrives at the table is a client and what leaves it is a statement, a schedule and a list of people who will be told first.

Confidential Contract Suites.description: Sealed rooms for private business and political agreement, with verification systems and no external record. Witnesses are supplied by the venue. A contract signed here is enforceable and, so far as the rest of the city is concerned, did not happen. The suites are small, windowless and screened, each with its own approach so that the parties need not meet in a corridor. Booking is expensive, timed and refused to anyone the venue does not already know. Verification runs on equipment maintained under contract and tested before every use. The venue's witnesses are salaried, permanent and famously incurious, and their signatures appear on a great many documents that nobody will ever see together.

The Closed Window.description: A club famous for refusing all public recording, its interior known only to those admitted. The refusal is absolute and has been tested in civic court. The persistent rumour is that the ban protects the club's own archive rather than its guests. Its frontage is the darkest on the Row and carries no name at all, only a shuttered panel that gives the place the name everyone uses. Admission is by membership and membership is not advertised. Devices are surrendered at the door without exception, including those belonging to senior figures who have tried the argument and lost it. Members describe the interior in terms that do not agree with one another, which the club has never troubled itself to correct.

Morning Denial Office.description: A daytime service for clients who require the previous night not to have occurred, staffed by people fluent in statements, retractions and plausible schedules. The waiting room is deliberately unmemorable. Most clients are back within the season. The office opens as the Corelight climbs toward work intensity, which is several hours after the Row has emptied and exactly when the consequences begin arriving. Fees are charged by engagement and rise with urgency. Staff take a full account first and correct nothing the client says while they are giving it. The waiting room has one bench, one blank wall and a reception desk positioned so that two clients need never look at each other.

The Nexaran Table.name: The Nexaran Table
The Nexaran Table.basicInfo: The Nexaran Table is a dense dining district rather than a single restaurant, packed with celebrated houses, family businesses, Academy kitchens, street food and rooms representing every major city on Nexara. Locals argue about it constantly and eat in it daily. In Relstaris a name can be built through food as effectively as through combat, scholarship or politics. The district is a working demonstration of the city's refusal of a single palette: each frontage is finished in whatever its kitchen wants to say about itself, so copper, deep green, bare star-metal, smoked glass and painted stone sit shoulder to shoulder down the same run of street, many of them fitted into structures that were something else under an earlier government and still show the old openings. Kitchens take their rhythm from the Corelight, prep beginning as it rises toward work intensity and the long service running through the evening shift, with the all-night rooms carrying whatever is left. Ingredients, equipment, staff and leases all cost money, and a family business here is a genuine financial risk rather than a lifestyle. The smell in the street changes every few paces and never stops entirely, and the loading bays are busy at hours when the dining rooms are dark.
The Nexaran Table.hiddenInfo: The district's fights are cultural before they are commercial. Purists attack The Open Table for combining traditions, The Measured Feast refuses to let Quilrath cuisine be read as Dravon politics, and Dust and Glass is watched for any sign that it is treating frontier hardship as decoration. Critic's Walk holds real power here: a single unfair review has closed a family business inside a season, and at least one current ranking is being quietly paid for. Recipe and technique theft moves through staff poaching rather than documents, so the Restaurant Supply Exchange doubles as the district's rumour exchange. Underworld transactions ride in on supply deliveries, since nobody inspects a crate of ingredients as closely as they inspect a person. Meanwhile the Failed Kitchen Auction keeps producing openings, and the next celebrated chef in Relstaris is currently working a shift at the Academy Culinary Showcase.

The Open Table.description: A Relstaris-born restaurant deliberately combining traditions from several cities, loved by locals and attacked by purists. Its room holds a shared dining run, corner tables, an adaptable family table and a visible finishing counter. Menus name ingredients and the traditions behind them rather than claiming an invented heritage. The room is warm and mid-bright, lined in pale wood and worn metal, with the finishing counter set where every seat can watch it. Service is brisk and the shared run fills first. Bookings are taken for the family table and rarely for anything else. The house answer to the purist argument is printed at the foot of the menu in the same size as everything else, which has offended more people than the cooking ever has.

The Quiet Orbit.description: A Solvraxis-inspired dining hall built for restraint: measured service, low light and table spacing that makes private conversation genuinely possible. Courses arrive without announcement. It is where people come to talk about something difficult over food that will not interrupt them. The room is pale, sparse and acoustically soft, with each table set far enough from the next that a raised voice would be an event. Staff move at a deliberate pace and do not recite. Bookings are held to the stated time and the room is never overfilled, which means the wait for a table can run for weeks and the restaurant declines to do anything about it. Diners leaving tend to be quieter than diners arriving.

The Upper Bracket.description: A Korrvane competition restaurant hung with memorabilia and live match boards, where arguments about brackets and predictions run louder than the music. Tables are booked out on tournament nights. Losing a public prediction here costs a round and a season of reminders. The room is bright, red-lit and deliberately crowded, with the boards mounted high enough that every seat has a sightline and low enough that people stand to point at them. Food arrives fast and in quantity. The walls carry a layered accumulation of signed gear, printed results and photographs, none of it arranged and none of it removed. The house keeps a running board of open predictions, and a name stays on it until it is settled.

Wayfarer's Rest.description: A Corsair-operated restaurant and alcohol hall serving travellers, merchants and people who would rather not register at official lodging. It runs long hours and asks few questions. Route talk at the bar is worth more than the food, which is nonetheless good. The hall is long, dim and built to take luggage, with heavy tables, a rail for coats and a bar that runs most of one wall. Payment is expected and credit is extended selectively by people who remember exactly who has been extended it before. Staff are practised at not hearing a conversation and equally practised at ending one. A board by the door carries messages left for people who have not arrived yet, some of them old enough to have gone soft.

Emberhouse.description: An Ignivex restaurant built around controlled heat tables where guests finish their own food in the open flame. Shared plates and direct conversation are the point. The room is hot, bright and deliberately unsuited to anyone trying to conduct a quiet negotiation. Extraction runs above every table and still loses the argument, so the whole room smells of the cooking and so does everyone who leaves it. Tables are sold by the setting rather than the seat, which makes a small party expensive and a large one sensible. Staff demonstrate the heat table once, firmly, and intervene without apology when a guest handles it badly. The ceiling above the tables carries a permanent darkening that the house has stopped trying to clean.

The Measured Feast.description: A Quilrath cultural restaurant that presents its traditions on their own terms and refuses to have them read as Dravon politics. Service is formal and precisely paced. Staff will explain a custom at length to anyone who asks honestly and not at all to anyone scoring points. The room is ordered and restrained, its settings exact, its lighting even, its decoration limited to a few pieces that are explained on request and labelled nowhere. Courses are timed and arrive in sequence regardless of how quickly a table eats. Prices are firm and the house does not negotiate them. The standing house position is stated once to any guest who raises politics at the table, after which the subject is simply not continued by the staff.

Last Arrival Kitchen.description: An inexpensive all-night kitchen serving students, shift workers and newcomers who arrived after everything else closed. Portions are large and the seating is communal. It is often the first Relstaris meal a new arrival eats and the one they remember. The room is plain, brightly lit and never empty, with long tables, a counter, a queue that moves and no bookings of any kind. Prices are low and posted. The staff work through the Corelight's maintenance window without changing anything about the menu or the pace. Newcomers sitting down with a tray are routinely told, by whoever is beside them, which district they should be looking at for a room and which they should not.

No House Required.description: A Relstaris-born restaurant that refuses to organise its identity around any single lineage, in a city where almost everything else does. The menu is assembled from whatever the kitchen can justify. Its regulars include mixed-house families and people who are tired of being asked. The room carries no house symbol and no city claim, and its fittings are a deliberate mixture with nothing matching anything else. Tables are close, the noise level is comfortable and children are unremarkable. The menu changes without notice and the kitchen will explain any dish on it in detail. The only fixed thing in the room is the refusal, and the house has never once made a statement about it beyond the name over the door.

Dust and Glass.description: A Dustfall-inspired grill using salvage aesthetics without pretending frontier hardship is decorative, its fittings genuinely reclaimed. The cooking is direct and heavily smoked. Dustfall-born customers are the harshest and most valuable judges of whether it has got the tone right. The room is built from reused panel, cut star-metal and mismatched seating, all of it worked rather than distressed, and the grill itself is the brightest thing in it. Portions are direct and the seasoning is not moderated for the district. The house keeps its sourcing plain when asked. Nothing in the room is labelled as a relic, and a guest who treats a fitting as a prop is corrected by the staff without much warmth.

The Verified Plate.description: A Vexorath-influenced precision kitchen where every process is measured, logged and displayed, and no customer is permitted to adjust the equipment. Plating is exact. The house position is that consistency is a courtesy, and it will not be argued out of it. The room is cool, pale and clinically lit, with the working line visible behind glass and the logs shown as a matter of routine rather than display. Timings are held. Requests for modification are received politely and declined, and the decline is the same for a critic, a representative and a first-time guest. The equipment is serviced on a published schedule and the kitchen closes rather than run it out of specification.

Hundred Family Court.description: A covered court of rotating minor-house food stalls, the roster changing through the season so no family holds a pitch permanently. Competition between neighbouring stalls is open and loud. A strong run here is how a minor name gets noticed in the capital. The court is a high roofed space over plain paving, lit from above, with the stalls set in a ring and shared seating in the middle. Pitches are allotted and paid for, and the allotment is the subject of more argument than the cooking. Families bring their own colours, their own signage and frequently their own relatives to work the counter. The centre tables are shared by everyone, which is how the competition stays loud and stays civil.

Academy Culinary Showcase.description: A student-run restaurant where careers begin and fail in public view, staffed on rotation by the Academy's culinary programme. Bookings are cheap and the standard swings wildly. Instructors sit at the back and say nothing until service is over. The room is a proper dining room rather than a teaching kitchen, which is the point, and the students run the front of house as well as the line. Diners are told plainly that the standard varies and book anyway. A bad service is visible to everyone in the room, including the student responsible, and the district's established kitchens send people to watch for exactly that reason. The rota is posted where the queue can read it.

Critic's Walk.description: The stretch where reviewers, food media and public rankings concentrate, with disputes conducted as openly as the reviews themselves. Restaurateurs walk it deliberately to be seen unbothered. A verdict formed on this pavement can travel the district before dinner service ends. It is an ordinary stretch of street with an extraordinary function, lined with terrace seating that is more expensive than its food justifies because of what can be overheard from it. Rankings are posted and updated where everyone can argue with them. Arguments here are public, frequent and occasionally settled in a civic office elsewhere. Kitchens send junior staff to stand and listen, a practice everyone knows about and nobody admits.

Restaurant Supply Exchange.description: Ingredients, equipment, staff hiring and emergency purchasing, trading from before dawn until the last kitchen has what it needs. Crates move continuously through the loading bays. Half the district's news and most of its poaching happen while someone waits on an order. The exchange is a working hall of bays, counters and cold rooms, lit hard and floored for wheels, and it is loud in the hours when the district is otherwise asleep. Orders are placed against credit and settled on terms that vary with how long a kitchen has been trading. An emergency purchase costs more and everyone knows exactly how much more. Nobody inspects a crate as closely as they inspect a person.

Failed Kitchen Auction.description: Equipment, fittings and leases from closed restaurants, sold off in front of the people who lost them and the people who will replace them. Bidding is brisk and quietly brutal. Every successful kitchen in the district has bought something in this room. The room is bare, the lots are laid out on the floor in the order they will be called, and the seating is arranged so that everyone can see who is bidding. Lots are paid for on the day and removed the same evening. Former owners attend more often than outsiders expect, sometimes to bid and sometimes only to watch the line go. The auctioneer reads each lot in the same even tone, including the ones that still carry a kitchen's own marks.

Private Family Dining Rooms.description: Bookable rooms used for birthdays, negotiations, breakups and political meals, with service that arrives only when called. Soundproofing is ordinary but sufficient. The district's standing joke is that more is decided in these rooms than in any Concourse negotiation chamber. The rooms sit behind or above the dining floors of several houses along the street, each furnished for a single table and a fixed number of settings. Booking carries a minimum charge whether or not the party eats. Staff knock and wait. The rooms see birthdays and inheritance arguments on the same evening, and the district's servers can generally tell which is which from the state of the table when they are finally called back in.

Convergence Festival Grounds.name: Convergence Festival Grounds
Convergence Festival Grounds.basicInfo: The Convergence Festival Grounds are the open district Relstaris built so the whole of Nexara can be celebrated without forcing every large event into the civic centre. Fields, pavilion rings, competition courts and a food mile fill and empty with the festival calendar. On a major convergence the crowd runs into the hundreds of thousands; between festivals it is a large, pleasant public park. The ground itself is deliberately plain: pale hard-wearing surfacing, low star-glass service housings, anchor points and power taps set flush and left uncovered, and long runs of old conduit reused to feed the temporary grids. Colour arrives with the delegations and leaves with them, so the same field is red and gold one season and something else entirely the next, and nothing here is finished in a palette the grounds own. Corelight falls across the open ground unobstructed, and the festival programme is built around its routing, with the heavy work of raising and striking staging done in the maintenance windows. Pitches, pavilion slots and market frames are let and paid for. Between events the fields are used by families, by flyers practising, and by cleanup crews still working through the last convergence.
Convergence Festival Grounds.hiddenInfo: Regional rivalry is the engine here. Pavilion placement in the ring is negotiated months ahead and read as a statement about standing, and a minor house granted a prominent slot can find itself unexpectedly known across the planet. Sabotage of rival programming happens most seasons and is almost never traced, because the Temporary Market Grid and Festival Worker Camp turn over thousands of unregistered short-term staff. Crowd Response keeps a standing file on politicians attempting to attach themselves to civic celebrations they did not organise. The genuine danger is scale: a lost child or a missing performer inside a crowd this size is a serious emergency, and the Response Hall's coordination with the Public Protection District is tested at every convergence. After the crowds go, the cleanup crews routinely turn up property, evidence and occasionally people who never left.

Grand Festival Field.description: The central open field, large enough to hold a citywide celebration with room to move, surfaced to survive both crowds and controlled flight. Staging is raised and struck by the season. Standing at its centre when full is the closest most residents come to seeing the whole city at once. The surface is pale, slightly textured and laid over anchor channels that show as faint lines when the field is empty, and the whole expanse is open to the Corelight with nothing built high enough to shadow it. Access is free and unticketed for civic events and charged for private ones. Crowd lanes are marked on the ground and enforced by stewards rather than barriers. When the field is empty it is disconcertingly quiet, and the marks of the last staging are still legible underfoot.

Regional Pavilion Ring.description: A ring of temporary structures assigned to Solvraxis, Korrvane, Quilrath, Vexorath, Helvyra, Ignivex, Dustfall and minor-house delegations. Each is built and dressed by its own people. Position in the ring is negotiated hard and read closely by everyone who understands the order. The frames are standard and everything hung on them is not, so the ring runs through eight incompatible ideas of how a building should look within a short walk. Delegations bring their own staff, their own food and their own rules about entry, within the grounds' limits. Slots are allotted well in advance and cost money. The service road behind the ring is where the delegations actually talk to one another, out of sight of the frontages they have just spent a season arguing over.

Public Competition Court.description: Courts and stages for noncombat competition: culinary contests, art, flight skill, technical demonstration and games. Scoring is public and disputes are settled on the spot. It is the one arena in Relstaris where reputation is won without anyone being struck. The courts are hard-surfaced and ringed with standing room, with the scoring boards raised where the whole crowd can argue with them. Entry fees are modest and the prizes are mostly recognition. Judges are drawn from several houses and independents, which is the only reason the on-the-spot rulings hold. A competitor who disputes a result is heard once, publicly, and the crowd's reaction is generally a better predictor of the outcome than the argument is.

Festival Food Mile.description: A long run of temporary vendors mixed with recurring stalls that have been returning for decades. Smoke, steam and competing music fill the length of it. Queue length is the only ranking that matters, and everyone pretends not to be watching it. The run is lined on both sides and roofed only in patches, so the smoke drifts across the walkway and the noise of one stall's music is never entirely free of the next. Pitches are let by the day and the returning stalls pay for the same ground every season, which is why they hold the best of it. Prices rise toward the centre of the mile. Somewhere along it a queue has formed for a stall nobody in the queue can yet see.

Family Recreation Gardens.description: Planted grounds with play structures, shaded seating and youth activity spaces, kept open between festivals as ordinary public parkland. Families use it as a meeting point. It is deliberately placed where the noise of the main field arrives as a distant sound. The planting is mature and maintained by civic crews, and the paths are wide enough for the traffic a convergence pushes into them. Entry costs nothing. Between festivals the gardens belong entirely to the neighbourhood that walks to them, and the play structures carry the wear of constant ordinary use rather than the wear of events. A meeting point post near the main path has accumulated a layer of handwritten notes that nobody removes until the season turns.

Open Flight Showcase.description: A marked aerial volume for controlled performance flight and movement display, with ground viewing along its boundary. Routines are cleared in advance by flight control. Academy students and independent flyers compete here for attention rather than prize credits. The volume is bounded by marker beacons rather than structure, so from the ground it is simply the piece of air where everyone is looking. Clearance is free to apply for and routinely refused for anything the controllers consider unsafe over a crowd. Viewing is unticketed and the boundary is held by stewards. Agents, venue bookers and training programmes watch from the boundary, which is the actual reason most of the flyers are here.

Minor-House Celebration Court.description: A mid-sized venue for events too large for a housefront but too particular for the whole city, booked far in advance. Recognitions, namings and anniversaries fill the calendar. A packed court here has changed how a minor house is regarded in the capital. The court is a walled open space with a raised end, plain enough to be dressed into whatever the booking family wants and durable enough to be dressed again a few days later. Bookings are charged and the good dates cost more. Families cater it themselves or bring a kitchen from the district. Because the calendar is public, the capital can read at a glance which minor names are spending and which have not booked in several seasons.

Temporary Market Grid.description: A serviced grid of powered pitches let by the day for seasonal goods and festival commerce. Stalls appear and vanish inside a single cycle. Because turnover is total, it is the easiest place in Relstaris to sell something once and never be found again. The grid is laid out in numbered lanes with power taps and water points at the corners, fed through conduit that predates the surfacing above it. Pitches are paid for in advance and the paperwork asks for little. Stewards walk the lanes and intervene in disputes rather than in trading. At the end of a convergence the whole grid is bare within a day, and the only trace of a given stall is a mark on the paving where its frame stood.

Public Rest Terraces.description: Quiet stepped terraces set into the ground's edge, screened from the main field, for people who need to sit down inside an enormous crowd. Water and shade are provided. Parents, older residents and the overwhelmed find each other here without conversation. The steps are broad and low, finished in pale stone that stays cool, and the screening is planted rather than built so the sound arrives as a wash rather than as music. Nothing here is charged for and nothing is sold. Response staff pass through on a loop and stop for anyone who looks unwell. The unspoken custom of the terraces is that nobody is asked what is wrong, and somebody always sits within reach anyway.

Emergency Crowd Response Hall.description: The coordination centre for medical response, protection, lost persons and evacuation across the entire grounds, staffed heavily during events. Screens track density across every sector. Its standing assumption is that something will go wrong and the only question is how early it is seen. The hall is functional, hard-lit and loud with overlapping traffic, set where crews can reach the field from it without crossing a crowd. Medical, protection and steward leads work the same room by design. Coordination with the Public Protection District runs continuously during a convergence. The lost persons desk is the busiest position in the building and the one that is never left unstaffed, including through the quietest part of the night.

Festival Worker Camp.description: Temporary accommodation for staff, performers, vendors and logistics crews who arrive with a festival and leave with it. Shifts run around the clock. The camp has its own economy, its own rules and very little interest in explaining either to visitors. It is a dense block of stacked temporary units, shared washing points, a canteen that never closes and a great deal of equipment stored wherever it fits. Beds are allocated against a work assignment and charged against pay. Because shifts run continuously, a proportion of the camp is always asleep and the noise discipline is enforced by the workers themselves. Newcomers learn the camp's rules quickly, mostly by getting one of them wrong.

After-Festival Grounds.description: The fields as they stand once the crowds have gone: cleanup crews, lost property, dismantled staging and whatever was abandoned. Work continues for days. Crews here find things at a rate that keeps a protection liaison permanently assigned to them. The ground is stripped back to its pale surfacing in uneven stages, with sections still under staging while others are already swept, and the whole district is quiet enough that a dropped frame carries across it. Crews are paid by the shift and the work is unglamorous. Lost property is logged and held. The liaison's desk is set up in whatever structure has not yet been taken down, and it moves several times before the clearance is finished.

Low Relstaris.name: Low Relstaris
Low Relstaris.basicInfo: Low Relstaris is the lower-city residential hub that exists beneath and between the celebrated districts: older foundations, dense affordable housing, utility corridors and neighbourhoods the capital rarely films. Most residents are ordinary people living in the cheaper, older part of the largest city on Nexara, and they run their own schools, markets, clinics and festivals. It is worn and overlooked, and the people who live here are not apologetic about either. The district is built into and around what earlier governments left: ancient star-metal supports carry whole blocks of newer housing, old energy conduits run through kitchens and stairwells because it was cheaper to build around them than to remove them, and the star-glass here is thick, scratched and rarely replaced. Nothing matches. Panels are patched in whatever colour was available, so a single frontage can carry four, and the district reads as mixed rather than poor from any distance. Corelight arrives second-hand, cut by the structures above, and residents read the work and maintenance shifts off it like everyone else in the city while paying for power and water at ordinary cost. The stairwells are loud, the repairs are local, and a stranger walking through is noticed and placed within a block.
Low Relstaris.hiddenInfo: Low Relstaris is the district where civic neglect becomes visible first. Drainage and utility failures along the Flooded Foundation Walk have been reported for cycles without funded repair, the clinic operates past its capacity on outreach staffing borrowed from the Myralis Capitol Clinic, and the schools run on local effort rather than allocation. A landlord consolidation is currently moving through the Lower Residential Rows, and the Rent Defense Rooms are organising against a displacement that would clear several blocks at once. The harder problem is competition for legitimacy: criminal protection offers faster help than the city does, and the Community Protection Office has to keep proving it is the better option without the funding to guarantee it. Officials arrive after a crisis becomes visible from above, which residents note every time. The Deepways surface somewhere in this district, and everyone local knows roughly where.

Lower Residential Rows.description: Dense family housing stacked into converted older structures, with shared stairwells, patched façades and laundry lines strung between flight wells. Generations live within a few doors of one another. The rows are noisy, close and defended fiercely by the people who grew up in them. The conversions are obvious once looked at: doorways cut into what were plainly service walls, floors added inside rooms built to a much larger scale, and star-metal framing left bare where the cladding was never finished. Rent is the cheapest in the capital and still a serious monthly problem for most households. Stair landings serve as porches, workshops and negotiation space. A repair one household pays for tends to benefit three, which is the arrangement the rows run on and argue about constantly.

Old Conduit Housing.description: Apartments built around disused or rerouted city infrastructure, where a bedroom wall may be a decommissioned power channel. Rent is low and the layouts are strange. Residents know which conduits are genuinely dead and which are only supposed to be. Rooms bend around channel runs, ceilings drop without warning and some flats are reached through what was once an access hatch. The star-metal of the conduits is warm in places and cold in others, and every household knows which of its own walls is which. Landlords let the oddest layouts cheapest. The building custom is that a resident who finds a live channel reports it to the neighbours before the owner, because the neighbours will act on it first.

Community Market.description: Food, clothing, repairs and services traded from permanent stalls under a patched canopy, with prices set by people who know their customers. News moves faster here than through any civic feed. Nothing in it is fashionable and almost all of it is cheaper than the upper city. The canopy is a long assembly of mismatched panels over a paved run, and the light under it is uneven and warm where it comes through the coloured sections. Stalls are held by the same families for years and passed on rather than sold. Credit is extended by memory and settled the same way. A stallholder who overcharges a neighbour hears about it from three other stallholders before the end of the day.

Public Repair Court.description: A shared yard of tools, benches and fabrication equipment maintained collectively for household and building repairs. Skills get taught while work is being done. What the city will not send a crew for, the court fixes on a weekend. The yard is open-sided, floored in worn surfacing and lined with racked tools that are signed out on a board and generally returned. Equipment is bought collectively and repaired more often than replaced. Anyone may use it and everyone is expected to clean up. The court's running argument is about who is allowed to take the heavier fabrication equipment off site, a dispute that has been settled several times and has never stayed settled.

Underfunded Clinic.description: Legitimate medical care operating permanently beyond its resources, with a waiting room that fills before opening. Staff are competent, exhausted and short of almost everything. Myralis outreach staff rotate through, which keeps the doors open and does not solve the problem. The clinic occupies a converted frontage with a plain intake desk, a long bench, treatment rooms behind a curtain wall and a back room where supplies are counted more carefully than anyone would like. Care is charged at rates the district can nominally meet, and the arrangements made for households that cannot are handled quietly at the desk. Triage is honest and the wait is long. The notice about the referral process has been amended by hand twice and is still out of date.

Lower Schools.description: Public education with fewer resources than any Academy-adjacent institution and a strong local identity that teachers defend openly. Classes are large and equipment is old. Graduates who reach the Academy are named on a board in the entrance hall. The buildings are older structures adapted room by room, with high ceilings, hard floors and environmental systems that work unevenly along a corridor. Teachers buy materials out of their own pay and say so. Families contribute what they can and the school is careful about how it asks. The board in the entrance hall is polished, added to rarely and read by every parent who walks past it, and nobody in the district treats it as a small thing.

Worker Gathering Hall.description: A large plain hall used for meetings, celebrations, disputes and mutual aid, booked continuously and rarely empty. Chairs get rearranged several times a day. Decisions made here reach the whole district faster than any official notice would. The hall is a single high room with a raised end, plain walls and a floor that has been resurfaced in patches, and its acoustics are poor in a way that forces people to stand up and speak clearly. Booking is free to residents and charged to anyone from outside. A meeting, a naming and a rent organising session can share the same afternoon. The keys are held by a rota of residents, and the handover happens in the doorway with the next booking already waiting.

Shared Kitchens.description: Communal cooking and food-support spaces where households pool ingredients and cook in rotation. Nobody is asked to explain why they came. Portions go out to residents who cannot attend, carried by whoever is walking that way. The kitchens are long rooms of scrubbed surfaces, mismatched equipment and heat units that are serviced by the repair court rather than by any contractor. Ingredients come from the community market at prices the stallholders adjust without discussing it. Rotas are posted and mostly kept. The rule that nobody is asked anything is enforced by the people who run the room rather than written down, and a visitor who asks anyway is answered by somebody changing the subject.

Flooded Foundation Walk.description: A low corridor where drainage and utility failure have left standing water against original city foundations. Boards and raised walkways cross the worst of it. Residents have reported it for cycles; the repair has been scheduled and deferred more times than anyone has counted. The foundations here are ancient star-metal, cut on a scale nothing above them matches, and the water sits dark against them and does not drain. The corridor is cold, echoing and lit by whatever fittings residents have run down to it. The boards are maintained locally and remade whenever they rot through. A copy of the most recent deferral notice is pinned at the entrance, and somebody has written the date of the previous one beside it.

Community Protection Office.description: A local safety office working alongside, and sometimes instead of, city protection, staffed largely by residents. Response is fast because the responders live here. Its authority is informal, which is both its strength and the reason it can be pushed aside. The office is a converted shopfront with a desk, a wall of contact rotas and a back room used for conversations that should not happen at the counter. Volunteers work shifts around their actual jobs. Training comes partly from the city's public emergency programme and partly from experience. The coordinator's standing difficulty is that criminal protection in the district promises help faster than the office can guarantee it, and everyone in the room knows the comparison is being made.

Lower Flight Wells.description: Vertical shafts cut through dense older construction, used as flight routes between levels where no lift exists. Lighting is uneven and the updrafts are unpredictable. Local children learn them early and outsiders misjudge them badly. The shafts are irregular, walled in mismatched construction from several eras, and hung with lines, cabling and the occasional improvised platform at a level somebody needed one. Air moves through them from the conduit runs below, which is where the updrafts come from. Nothing about them is maintained as flight infrastructure because officially they are not flight infrastructure. The marks scratched at each landing level are the district's own wayfinding and correspond to no published map.

Rent Defense Rooms.description: Offices where residents organise against displacement, predatory ownership and quiet reclassification of their buildings. Records, tenancy documents and case histories fill the walls. The work is slow, legalistic and has stopped at least two clearances outright. The rooms are cramped and papered with filings, with a long table where cases are read aloud and a locked cabinet holding originals. Advocates work unpaid or nearly so, and the copying alone is a real expense. Residents arrive with notices they do not understand and leave with a date, a form and someone who will come with them. The wall carries a map of the district marked with buildings under pressure, and the marks are added to more often than they are removed.

Neighborhood Festival Court.description: A paved court for local celebrations that city media never cover, decorated by whoever is hosting that season. Food comes from the shared kitchens and music from whoever owns equipment. It is the district at its best and it is never filmed. The court is plain paving between residential blocks, with power taps at two corners and hanging points that have been used so often the fixings have been replaced twice. Decoration is improvised and reused. Nothing is ticketed and contributions are collected in a tin that circulates. Children take the middle of the court and are not moved out of it for the performers, which visitors from other districts find disorganised and nobody local intends to change.

The Upper View.description: A narrow public terrace at the district's edge where residents can see the prosperous city built above them, lit by Corelight they pay for and do not receive. Benches face outward. People come to think, argue or simply look, and nobody asks which. The terrace is a strip of paving behind a star-metal rail, worn bright along its top edge, with the structures of the upper city rising directly across from it. The light changes across the view as the Corelight shifts through its routing, which is the whole reason people time their visits. It costs nothing to stand here. The benches are old, repaired by the repair court, and the far one is understood to belong to whoever reached it first and needs it most.

The Vein Market.name: The Vein Market
The Vein Market.basicInfo:
The Vein Market is the best-known name for a market that never occupies one permanent shape, moving between old service spaces, closed legal businesses, hidden cargo routes, private residences and abandoned structures. Everyone in Low Relstaris knows it exists and knows how to ask after it; almost nobody knows where it will be next. It sells restricted goods, information, discreet services and emergency supply, and it can help people the official systems will not. Because it borrows its rooms, it has no architecture of its own: one cycle it fills a stripped service hall lined in old star-metal, the next a shuttered shopfront with the fittings still in place, and the colour of any given pitch belongs to whatever building is hosting it. What travels with the Market is the lighting, portable and harsh, and the layout, which always leaves sightlines to every entrance and a clear run toward the exit. Trading begins after the Corelight drops toward evening routing and thins before the maintenance windows, when crews are moving and attention is cheap. Everything is paid for, mostly in credit and sometimes in obligation, and the second kind is the expensive one. The Market's rules are real, locally enforced, and the only reason it is survivable.

Work on offer here: Relstaris — The Deepways Passenger (ask Kessa Ruun).
The Vein Market.hiddenInfo: Only the Market's current pitch is concealed; the Market itself is common knowledge, and its reputation is the reason people find it. Its rules are real and locally enforced, which is what makes it survivable: the Underworld Food Hall is neutral ground, the Moving Exit is relocated on a schedule that defeats raids, and the peacekeepers protect customers the law failed. The cost is the Debt Ledger Hall, where informal loans convert into obligations and, eventually, into people used as collateral. Civic officials depend on the Scarcity Auction more than any of them will state publicly, and legal supply failures in the capital are followed within hours by price movements here. Right now the Reputation Knife Desk is running a fabricated-evidence campaign against an Academy student whose family cannot afford to contest it, and the Quiet Return Counter is holding house property nobody can be seen to reclaim.

Restricted Technology Stalls.description: Modified, stolen, prohibited and simply unsafe systems laid out on folding tables that can be gone in minutes. Sellers demonstrate rather than document. Provenance is never discussed and the buyer is expected to understand exactly what they are accepting. The tables are arranged in a loose run with power drawn from whatever the host building still carries, and the demonstrations are the only light some of the pitches have. Prices are high and firm, and nothing carries a warranty of any kind. Sellers will say what a unit does and refuse to say what it was. A buyer who asks the wrong question is answered with silence and a folded table, and the pitch beside it will not trade with them either for the rest of the night.

Information Broker Court.description: Political, commercial, academic and personal information traded in a cleared space with sightlines to every entrance. Brokers work from memory, not records. Price depends less on what is being sold than on who will be damaged when it moves. The court is kept deliberately empty of furniture beyond seating, so that every approach is visible and no conversation is closer to another than the brokers permit. Transactions are verbal and payment is immediate. A broker who is wrong twice is finished here, which keeps the standard higher than the setting suggests. The court's own rule is that nobody is sold information about a person standing in the room, and it is enforced by everyone present at once.

Unlicensed Medical Room.description: Discreet treatment with no official record, run by practitioners whose licences are suspended, surrendered or never granted. Equipment is better than anyone expects. Patients here are usually people for whom an entry in a medical file is more dangerous than an untreated injury. The room is scrubbed, bright and better organised than the rest of the Market, with a curtain, a working table and supplies kept in a case that travels. Treatment is charged and the rates are not low, because the supplies are bought at Market prices. Practitioners take a history and do not write it down. Serious cases are referred onward with a name and a route, and the referral is the part of the service the patient is least likely to use.

False Credential Office.description: Employment histories, Academy records, travel documents and identity papers produced to a standard that survives ordinary inspection. Work is slow and expensive. The office refuses commissions it judges likely to bring protection investigators down on the Market. The working space is small, screened and equipped with more care than anything else the Market moves between sites. Commissions are taken in person, quoted by difficulty and paid partly in advance. Turnaround is measured in cycles rather than hours, and pressing for speed raises the price and lowers the quality. The refusals are the office's real reputation: it has turned away work that would have paid extremely well and has explained itself to nobody.

Hidden Cargo Exchange.description: A transfer floor for goods removed from legal Waypoint oversight, worked by crews who unload fast and ask nothing. Crates arrive labelled as something else. Volume rises sharply whenever inspection tightens on the legitimate cargo network. The floor is whatever the current site offers with enough clearance for a loader, usually an old service bay with doors at both ends and the marks of previous handling all over the surfacing. Crews are paid per load and rotate constantly. Nothing is stored here longer than it has to be. The only paperwork that matters is the receiving label, and the standing instruction to every crew is that a crate that has been opened does not move on.

Smuggler's Passage.description: The Market's working connection to the Deepways and to a handful of selected surface businesses, guarded at both ends. Guides take a fee per crossing. Which passage is live changes with the Market, and using last season's route is a well-known way to disappear. The live passage is whatever inherited corridor the current pitch can reach, so it may be stripped transit tunnel, conduit run or the back of a legal premises with the staff paid to look elsewhere. Guides carry their own light and set the pace. Fees are per person and per load, payable at the near end. Nobody is taken through who cannot keep up, and the refusal is made at the entrance rather than partway along.

Stolen House Goods Market.description: Property whose ownership is politically inconvenient: compound fittings, archives, ceremonial items and pieces that cannot be openly sold. Buyers are often connected to the houses that lost them. Nothing here is displayed with a name attached. Pieces are laid out on cloth or left in their transport cases, and a great deal of the stock is worth more for what it proves than for what it is. Viewing is by appointment within the trading period. Prices are negotiated privately and settled the same day. House marks are covered rather than removed, because a buyer who wants the piece usually wants the mark intact and a buyer who does not is in the wrong room.

Vein Market Contract Rooms.description: Sealed rooms where investigation, intimidation, recovery, theft and violence are commissioned in plain language. Terms are agreed in person only. The Market takes a cut and disclaims everything, which has been tested and held. The rooms are small, screened and furnished with nothing that could carry a record, and each is approached separately so that two clients need not meet. Nothing is written and nothing is repeated. The Market's cut is collected before the work begins. Contractors and clients are introduced by an intermediary who leaves before terms are discussed, an arrangement that exists precisely so that the intermediary can say, accurately, that they were not present.

Underworld Food Hall.description: A neutral eating space protected by local rules that hold even between crews actively in conflict. Food is cheap, hot and surprisingly good. Violence inside the hall ends a crew's welcome in the Market entirely, and everyone has seen that enforced. The hall runs on long shared tables and a single serving counter, lit warmer than the rest of the Market and kept clean by staff who have been doing it for years. Payment is at the counter and nobody eats on credit. Weapons are not collected, because the rule is about conduct rather than equipment. Crews who will not sit together sit at opposite ends and the staff seat them there without being asked, a piece of routine that is the hall's entire security arrangement.

The Moving Exit.description: The Market's primary escape route, relocated on a rotation known only to those who need it, marked each cycle by a changing sign. Crowds thin toward it when anything goes wrong. Its whole value is that no raid has yet arrived faster than the rotation. The exit is always a real route out of the host structure rather than a hiding place, kept clear, and checked before trading opens. The sign is a small, unremarkable mark placed where regular traders will find it and a first-time visitor will not. Anyone may use it. The rotation is maintained by a handful of people who are paid to do nothing else, and who are the only members of the Market permitted to close a pitch on their own authority.

Scarcity Auction.description: Emergency goods sold at open bid whenever legal supply fails in the capital: medicine, parts, water filtration, rations. Bidding is fast and merciless. Civic buyers attend through intermediaries and would deny it under oath. The auction is called from a crate or a counter with the lots stacked behind it, and it runs for as long as there is stock and no longer. Payment is immediate and goods leave with the buyer. Prices track the failure above almost exactly, which is why the Market learns about a supply collapse before most of the districts affected by it do. Nothing is reserved, and a bidder who is buying for a clinic gets no consideration for it whatsoever.

Reputation Knife Desk.description: Fabricated evidence, rumour placement and public humiliation sold as a service, with rates by target and reach. Work is commissioned discreetly and delivered publicly. It is the Market's most despised desk and one of its most reliably profitable. The desk is a single table set apart from the busier pitches, staffed by people who are polite, unhurried and entirely willing to explain the pricing structure. Commissions are quoted by how visible the target is and how far the material is meant to travel. Payment is staged against delivery. Other traders do not sit near it, do not eat with its staff and do not refuse its money when it is spent at their pitches.

Quiet Return Counter.description: Stolen goods handed back for payment without anyone admitting who took them, a service that solves problems for thieves and victims alike. No names are recorded. A surprising amount of major-house property has passed across this counter and been quietly reinstalled. The counter is plain, positioned where both parties can approach without crossing, and staffed by people whose entire professional skill is failing to look closely. Items are described rather than identified. The fee is a share of the assessed value and is taken from the returning payment rather than charged separately. Goods held for collection are kept in a locked case behind the counter, and the case is the most closely watched object in the Market.

No Questions Workshop.description: Unauthorised repair and modification of equipment, prosthetics, flight gear and systems whose warranty conditions forbid exactly this. The work is skilled. The workshop's only stated rule is that it will not knowingly build something designed to fail under its user. The bench is properly equipped and better lit than anything around it, with tools racked in order and parts in labelled trays, because the technician working it is a professional whatever their licensing situation. Work is quoted by hour and part. Jobs are queued and the queue is honest. The rule is repeated to every new customer in the same words, and the work refused under it has included commissions from clients nobody in the Market would willingly disappoint.

Debt Ledger Hall.description: Where informal loans, obligations and favours are recorded and enforced, in a room lined with ledgers that do not exist legally. Repayment terms are flexible until they abruptly are not. People appear in these ledgers as collateral, and getting a name removed is the Market's hardest transaction. The hall is quiet, orderly and furnished like an office, which is a large part of what makes it frightening. Entries are read back aloud when a loan is taken so that the borrower cannot claim not to have understood. Terms are renegotiated freely and the renegotiations are recorded too. The ledgers travel with the Market in locked cases, and the keepers carry them personally rather than trusting a crew.

The Deepways.name: The Deepways
The Deepways.basicInfo: The Deepways are a hidden transit and infrastructure network older than the modern district map, made of abandoned transit rings, Core conduits, former security routes, sealed passages and maintenance shafts. Their routes are omitted from the official city map and no single group controls the network. People use them to travel unseen, to move cargo, to escape, and occasionally to live where the maps show only corridor. The network is the clearest record the capital has of how it was built: ancient star-metal structure carrying loads nothing above it needs carried, energy conduits still live inside walls that later construction simply sealed over, security fittings from one administration bolted through the work of another, and expansion-era stonework finished to a standard the modern city no longer bothers with. Light comes from the conduits themselves, from failing civic fittings and from whatever people carry. Corelight reaches almost none of it, so time down here is kept by the maintenance windows above, when crews move and the network is at its busiest and least private. Nothing is charged for and everything costs something: a guide takes a fee, a map is sold at whatever the buyer's situation will bear, and a route that was safe last season may be the reason somebody does not come back.
The Deepways.hiddenInfo: Nobody holds the Deepways, and that is the whole problem. Maintenance crews have legal routes through it, smugglers have agreed neutral passages, and the two overlap without anyone negotiating; the Deepways Map Exchange sells competing, incomplete charts at high prices, which regularly sends two groups who each believe they are alone into the same hall. Someone is currently running an Illegal Gate Relay Room, attempting to redirect or imitate transit infrastructure, which is a Contair-grade engineering problem that no Contair engineer has been asked to look at. The Lost Citadel Stair still connects toward a former government wing, and what survives at the Sealed Dravon Checkpoint includes working systems from a prior administration. Beneath Low Relstaris the Flooded Utility Trench is worsening, and the residents of The Wrong Turn Residence live in a space the city does not record and therefore will not repair.

Abandoned Transit Ring.description: A former public transit loop, its platforms stripped and its tunnel still structurally sound, now used unofficially by anyone who knows the entrances. Old signage survives in patches. Movement through it is fast, quiet and entirely undocumented.
