The tunnel runs wide and level with the old running surface still in place, and the platforms stand bare except for the mounting points where everything removable was taken. Sound carries the full length of it, so an approach is heard long before it is seen. The surviving signage names destinations in the layout of an earlier city, several of which no longer exist under those names. Those who use the ring regularly navigate by the stripped platforms rather than by the signs.

Core Conduit Walk.description: A narrow path running alongside old power channels, warm and faintly lit by the conduits themselves. It is the most direct route through the network and the most dangerous. Experienced guides time crossings against the channel cycles rather than trusting the shielding. The walk is a ledge with a rail on one side and the channel casing on the other, close enough that the warmth is constant and the light shifts along the wall as the routing changes above. Nothing here was built for people to stand in for long. The shielding is original, patched in places by crews whose work is decades apart and visibly different. Guides charge more for this route than any other and will refuse it outright during a maintenance window.

Hidden Freight Route.description: A cargo path sized for loaders and crates, bypassing every street-level checkpoint between the lower city and the district edges. Wheel tracks are constant in the dust. Whoever maintains its lighting has never been identified and has never stopped. The route runs flat and straight for long stretches with turning space cut at the junctions, which is the detail that gives away its original purpose. The surfacing is worn in two continuous bands. Loads move through it on a rhythm that has nothing to do with the legal cargo network and everything to do with when inspection tightens above. The lighting is sparse, functional and replaced quietly, and every crew that uses the route has a theory about who is paying for it.

Old Corsair Passage.description: A route cut during an earlier expansion era, still carrying Corsair route marks on its walls and better built than anything around it. Merchants used it legitimately once. It now serves people who value a passage whose original builders left good documentation nobody else has. The stonework is squared, the drainage still runs, and the passage keeps its section where later tunnels sag and patch. Route marks are cut into the wall at intervals in a system that remains legible to anyone who has learned it. Nothing about it is hidden except its entrances. The quality of the build is the reason it is still in use, and it is also the reason several parties have tried to work out what else the same builders left down here.

Sealed Dravon Checkpoint.description: A former security control point with barriers down and some of its systems still drawing power after decades. Scanners occasionally register a passer-by and log it somewhere unknown. Getting through is straightforward; getting through unrecorded is not. The structure is heavy and deliberately narrow, with mounting brackets where equipment was stripped and housings where it was not, and the surviving fittings hold a dull indicator light that changes without apparent pattern. Power reaches it through a conduit run that nobody has been able to trace. Regular users pass on the far side of the corridor and move quickly. What the logs are, where they go and whether anyone still reads them are three separate questions and nobody has answered the first.

Forgotten Genesis Reinforcement Tunnel.description: A heavy structural route built for defence, with load-bearing work far beyond ordinary civic construction. It has survived collapses that took the levels above it. Those who shelter here during infrastructure failures do so because nothing has ever brought it down. The tunnel is wide, low and entirely without ornament, its star-metal ribbing set close and its surfaces bare. Sound deadens in it rather than carrying. Because it is known to hold, it accumulates the marks of people who have waited here: bedding stores, water containers, and levels scratched into one wall at the heights different groups of children reached in different years. Nobody claims it and nobody has ever successfully closed it.

Maintenance Worker Paths.description: Legal service routes known to city crews, marked with current signage and equipped with functioning emergency points. Crews pass through on shift rotation. They see far more of the network than their work orders cover and report only a fraction of it. The paths are the only part of the Deepways that looks maintained, with current markings, working call points and lighting that is replaced on a schedule. They cross the rest of the network constantly, because the infrastructure being serviced does not respect the distinction between documented and undocumented routes. Crews are paid for the work on their orders and nothing else. A supervisor's standing instruction is that anything unusual is reported at the end of a shift, which is why so much of it is not.

Illegal Gate Relay Room.description: An unauthorised installation attempting to redirect or imitate transit infrastructure, assembled from stripped components and running hot. The engineering is ambitious and unstable. Anyone who understands what is being attempted here is either alarmed or extremely interested. The room is a converted chamber packed with racked components, improvised cooling and cable runs spliced directly into an old conduit, and the noise of it is audible in the corridor outside. The heat is the first thing a visitor notices and the reason the work is done in short sessions. Parts are bought through the Market at prices that suggest serious funding. Nothing in the assembly is documented, and whoever is building it has left no indication of what a success would be used for.

Underworld Safe Passage.description: A temporarily neutral corridor maintained by agreement between crews who otherwise have no reason to cooperate. Passage is granted, not taken. The agreement has broken down twice in living memory and both times the network became unusable for a season. The corridor itself is unremarkable, which is part of the point: it is kept clear, kept lit at the junctions and kept empty of anything worth fighting over. Crews post their own people at the ends rather than relying on any shared authority. Granting passage is a favour that is recorded informally and called in later. The agreement covers conduct in the corridor and nothing whatsoever about what happens to anyone at either end of it.

Collapsed Core-Era Hall.description: An ancient civic space cut off by later construction, its ceiling partly down and its original purpose still legible in the surviving stonework and fittings. Nothing has been catalogued. Historians who have seen it describe it as the best-preserved record of the city before the current map. The hall is large, cold and half filled with the material that came down into it, and what remains standing is built to a scale that later construction never matched. Fittings survive on the intact walls in a form that is clearly civic rather than domestic. Reaching it requires a route nobody publishes. Those who get in are a mixture of researchers, guides and people sheltering, and all three groups tend to leave the fallen section undisturbed.

Lost Citadel Stair.description: A long ascending stair that once connected to a government wing no longer shown on any plan, its upper reaches sealed but not filled. The steps are worn in the centre. Where exactly it emerges is a question several parties would pay a great deal to answer. The stair is narrow, turning and finished to a standard that marks it as an official route rather than a service one, with a handrail worn smooth on the inner side. The seal at the top is later work, solid, and installed from the far side. Nothing about the stair is dangerous except the interest in it. Guides who know the lower entrance charge for it and decline, consistently, to discuss the upper one.

Flooded Utility Trench.description: A hazardous water-filled trench beneath Low Relstaris, deepening as drainage above continues to fail. Crossings require gear and nerve. The failures that fill it are the same ones flooding the foundations residents keep reporting. The trench runs between service walls with the water standing dark and still against original foundation metal, and the cold of it carries into the corridors on either side. The footing below the surface is uneven and cannot be seen. Crossings are made on improvised lines and boards that are replaced by whoever needed them last. The level is measurably higher than it was, which the maintenance crews have recorded, and the record has gone into the same queue as every other deferred repair.

Unmarked Surface Doors.description: Exits opening inside legal districts, disguised as service panels, storerooms and the backs of ordinary premises. Some businesses know what they are hosting and some do not. Each door is a standing relationship between the network and somebody upstairs. The doors are unremarkable by design, fitted into walls where a panel is expected, and most of them open only from the Deepways side. Which doors are live changes as businesses close, change hands or lose patience. A proprietor who knows is generally paid, in credit or in goods delivered without paperwork. A proprietor who does not know usually finds out when somebody comes through in a hurry, and what happens to the door afterwards depends entirely on them.

The Wrong Turn Residence.description: An inhabited community built into a space official maps record as empty corridor, with power tapped, water carried and its own local order. Children have grown up here. The residents are unregistered, which means they have no services and no protection they did not build. The space is a wide section of old structure partitioned with salvaged panel into rooms, walkways and a shared middle ground, lit by fittings spliced into a conduit that still carries. Water is fetched and heated. Repairs are made collectively and recorded in nobody's system. The community keeps a watch at each approach, and outsiders are met, spoken to and turned back or brought in according to a judgement the residents make quickly and do not explain.

Deepways Map Exchange.description: A trading point for charts of the network, all of them partial, several of them deliberately wrong, sold at prices that reflect desperation rather than accuracy. Buyers compare fragments openly. Two good maps disagreeing is the most reliable warning the Deepways offer. The exchange occupies a junction wide enough for several sellers to lay out their work without crowding, lit by portable fittings and marked only by the fact that people are standing there. Charts are drawn, copied and annotated by hand. Sellers will let a buyer compare before purchase, because a comparison usually sells two maps rather than one. Nothing is guaranteed and nothing is refunded, and every seller says so before taking payment.

The Hollow Ring.name: The Hollow Ring
The Hollow Ring.basicInfo: The Hollow Ring is a secretive illegal combat and training district built for fighters and spectators who want results official institutions will not permit. It does not replace Korrvane tournament culture, the Academy or the Open Circuit; it offers money, secrecy, forbidden conditions, unlicensed technique and a faster route to a reputation, or to destroying someone else's. Its locations are not advertised and admission runs through people already inside who are willing to vouch. The district occupies inherited structure rather than anything built for it: heavy old halls with star-metal ribbing overhead, security corridors from a former administration used exactly as they were intended, and later partition work thrown up in whatever material was to hand. Almost everything is dark, and the light is concentrated hard onto the floors where money is being made, so the district reads as black and white with a red spill from the betting boards. Nothing here follows the Corelight except by inversion; matches are timed to the maintenance windows, when crews are occupied and the city above is at its least attentive. Entry, gear, treatment and information are all paid for, and the most expensive thing on offer is leaving.
The Hollow Ring.hiddenInfo: The Ring runs on debt and on reputation, and it manufactures both. The Debt Fight Queue is full of people fighting because they owe the wrong person, and the Match-Fixing Office turns those obligations into outcomes that are sold before the fight begins. Fixing here does not stay here: results have already distorted at least one official competition, and a house reputation was damaged this season by cheating arranged three levels away from anyone who could be named. The Recruitment Balcony is where criminal organisations, private security firms and major-house intermediaries do their scouting, which is how an Academy prodigy ends up fighting under a second name. Hidden Viewing Rooms hold spectators who cannot be recognised, including at least one public protector. And the Clean Exit Program is real but rationed: fighters can leave, if they are valuable enough and willing to pay what leaving costs.

Main Illegal Ring.description: The primary combat floor, a sunken ring under harsh lighting with standing room packed to the walls and no medical requirement before a match. Rules are announced fight by fight. The noise at the decisive moment carries further through the structure than the organisers would like. The floor sits below the standing level in what was plainly built as something else, and the surfacing has been replaced often enough that the patches are a record of the district's worst nights. Heat and noise build with the crowd and there is no ventilation worth the name. Admission is charged at the door and paid in advance. The announcement of conditions is made from the floor itself, and a fighter hearing a rule they did not expect has the length of that announcement to decide.

Aerial Cage Volume.description: A restricted vertical match space enclosed in field barriers, where flight combat continues past every limit the Academy imposes. Falls are part of the format. Fighters who make their name here are rarely permitted to compete legally afterwards. The volume is a tall shaft of inherited structure with the barriers generated across its open faces and the audience on galleries at several levels. The equipment producing the barriers is maintained by one technician and everybody knows it. Air moves badly at the top. Because falls are expected rather than prevented, the floor of the shaft is prepared for them, and the preparation is the single most honest piece of engineering in the district.

Fighter Holding Rooms.description: Preparation cells where fighters wait alone with a medic, a handler and whoever has come to apply pressure. Contracts get amended in these rooms. What is agreed between the door and the floor decides more matches than technique does. The cells are small, bare and lined in old panel, with a bench, a water point and a door that is watched from outside. Sound from the floor comes through the wall as a rhythm rather than as words. Medics do what they can in the time allowed and are paid by the organisers rather than by the fighter. The handler's job is to have the fighter on the floor at the called time, and every other consideration in the room is subordinate to that.

Unlicensed Recovery Clinic.description: A treatment room that keeps fighters functional without asking how the injuries happened or recording that they did. Equipment is scavenged and the practitioners are genuinely skilled. Its standing referral to Myralis outreach is used more often than the Ring's operators know. The room is clean in a way the rest of the district is not, with the working surfaces scrubbed and the scavenged equipment kept in better order than its origins suggest. Treatment is charged and deducted from a fighter's purse before they see it. Practitioners work fast because the queue between matches does not wait. The referral is given quietly, in a form a patient can use somewhere else, and nothing about it appears in the room afterwards.

Betting Gallery.description: Tiered viewing with public odds boards, private books and credit extended far too easily to people already losing. Odds move on information, not performance. A sudden shift in the gallery is the clearest signal in the district that a match has been arranged. The gallery is stepped, crowded and lit by the boards themselves, which throw a red wash across the faces watching them. Public books take stakes at the rail and private books work the upper steps. Credit is offered readily and settled without flexibility. The board operators have a practised gesture for suspending a market, and the sound the gallery makes when they use it is recognisable from the far side of the district.

Private Challenge Chamber.description: A closed room for personal grudges and discreet matches with no audience beyond the parties and their seconds. Terms are set in advance and honoured. It is the one part of the Ring that operates closer to formal challenge tradition than to spectacle. The chamber is plain, evenly lit and sized for the match rather than for a crowd, with a marked floor and nothing on the walls. Use is booked and paid for, and the fee is high because the room's value is that nothing about it is sold to anyone. Seconds hold the terms and hold each party to them. The district's operators do not take a position on what is settled in here, which is precisely why it is used.

Recruitment Balcony.description: An overlooking gallery where criminal organisations, private security firms and major-house intermediaries watch for usable talent. Offers are made before a fighter has left the floor. Nobody on this balcony introduces themselves by the name they use in daylight. The balcony runs above the standing room with its own stair and is furnished for people who intend to stay for several matches. Drinks are served and nothing is charged, because the cost of the balcony is carried by the people who benefit from it. Watchers take notes in forms that mean nothing to anyone else. An approach made from here is made through an intermediary, and the fighter frequently never learns who was actually asking.

Equipment Lockers.description: Storage for legal and prohibited gear, sorted by who is permitted to know it exists. Some of it would end an Academy career on sight. The locker attendant's real function is deciding which fighter gets which enhancement on a given night. The room is racked floor to ceiling with cases and cages, catalogued in a system the attendant carries in their head. The front racks hold ordinary training gear and the back ones do not. Gear is signed out against a fighter's purse and returned before they leave the district. Fighters ask for particular equipment and are given what the attendant decides, and the argument that follows is always lost by the fighter.

Hidden Viewing Rooms.description: Screened boxes for wealthy spectators and political figures who require anonymity, with separate access and no line of sight from the floor. Service is silent. What the boxes pay for is the certainty that nobody below will ever be able to name them. The boxes are set into the old structure above the ring, reached by a corridor that does not connect to the public approach, each one closed and screened so that the occupants cannot see one another either. Attendants enter only when called. The fee is the largest single source of income the district has. The screening is checked before every event by the same person who checks the barriers, which tells anyone paying attention what the operators consider critical.

Match-Fixing Office.description: Where outcomes are arranged through bribes, threats and manufactured narratives, and reputations are built or destroyed to order. The ledgers are kept in a code that changes monthly. It is the most profitable room in the district and the most dangerous to enter uninvited. The office is small, well furnished and set behind two doors, and it is the only room in the Ring with a proper desk. Arrangements are discussed in terms that would be unremarkable in a legitimate business. Payment moves before the match and settlement afterwards. Nothing arranged here stays inside the district, and the people who work the room are entirely aware of how far the results travel.

Emergency Escape Route.description: A cleared exit path used during raids, betrayals and matches that exceed their agreed limits, kept unobstructed as a condition of the Ring's continued operation. Routes tie into the Deepways at more than one point. Everyone employed here is drilled on it. The route runs through service width corridors and down into inherited structure, marked by fittings that read as ordinary maintenance signage to anyone who does not know better. It is checked before every event and anything left standing in it is removed without discussion. Fighters are shown it once. The condition is enforced by the operators against their own staff more harshly than any other rule in the district.

Ruin Board.description: A wall recording fighters whose public careers collapsed after Ring involvement, maintained as both a memorial and a warning. Names are added without ceremony. Some fighters visit it before their first match and go through with it anyway. The board is a stretch of old wall near the approach to the holding rooms, lit by a single fitting, the names cut or written directly onto the surface in whatever hand was available at the time. Nothing is dated and nothing is explained. Names are never removed, including the ones belonging to people who are still alive and working elsewhere. Fighters stopping in front of it are left alone, which is the closest thing to courtesy the district maintains.

Second Name Desk.description: Where fighters obtain aliases, concealed identities and the paperwork to keep a legal career separate from an illegal one. The work is good enough to survive casual checking. Every prodigy fighting here has stood at this desk first. The desk is set in a side room with a screen, a working unit and a chair on the applicant's side, and the whole transaction takes less time than a fighter expects. Names are chosen by the fighter and vetted by the desk against names already in use. The fee is charged once and the maintenance of the identity is charged again. The desk keeps a record of which legal name sits behind which second name, and that record is the most valuable object in the district.

Debt Fight Queue.description: A waiting area for people fighting because they owe someone who prefers repayment in matches. The queue is orderly and quiet. Nobody in it chose the opponent, the conditions or the night, and the holders of those debts are not present. The area is a corridor with a bench along one wall and a handler at the end of it calling names off a list. People wait in ordinary clothes with their gear in a bag. Some have fought here many times and some have never fought anywhere. Conversation is sparse and practical, mostly about how many matches a particular obligation is understood to be worth, a figure that several people in the queue have discovered is not fixed.

Clean Exit Program.description: A rare arrangement that helps a valuable fighter leave the Ring with their identity and health intact, at a cost set by the people they are leaving. Terms are enforced rather than negotiated. It works, and it is offered to almost no one. The arrangement is handled in an office no different from the ones where fights are bought, by the same people, in the same tone. Terms cover what is paid, what is surrendered and what the fighter agrees never to be able to say. Compliance is verified afterwards for as long as the operators consider necessary. The programme's existence is what makes the rest of the district survivable to think about, which is a service the operators understand they are providing.

Forgotten House Ward.name: Forgotten House Ward
Forgotten House Ward.basicInfo: The Forgotten House Ward is a quiet, worn district of compounds built by houses that declined, vanished, merged, lost recognition or moved away. Some buildings stand empty; most hold tenants, informal communities, workshops, descendants without legal ownership or caretakers still waiting for families that will not return. It is politically abandoned rather than derelict, and the people living in it have built something real inside unresolved property law. The ward is the most colour-faded part of the capital and still not one colour: house blues, deep reds and greens survive in patches on stonework that has not been recoated in generations, and where a facing has been repaired the new star-glass sits bright and obviously wrong against everything around it. Ancient star-metal shows at the foundations of compounds built long after it. The Corelight reaches the ward at ordinary intensity and residents read the shifts off it like anyone else, but the ward keeps its own rhythm, since almost nobody here commutes to the districts that set the city's working hours. Utilities are paid for through arrangements as unresolved as the tenancies. Sound carries a long way down avenues built for processions that no longer happen.
Forgotten House Ward.hiddenInfo: Ownership here is the live question. The Disputed Property Office processes claims against records lost across three changes of government, and the Old House Archive holds damaged documents that could restore a family name or destroy one; both legal and criminal inheritance brokers are working those rooms now. Developers want the ward cleared and are applying pressure through tenancy reclassification rather than eviction notices, while the Resident Community Court governs the ward in practice and has no standing anyone above it recognises. At least one former compound has been taken over by an underworld crew who found the walls and the privacy convenient. The Sealed Custodian-Era Building predates the surrounding ward and has never been properly reopened, and its connection to an earlier Core holder is the sort of historical evidence that would change legal status for several families at once.

Empty Housefront Avenue.description: A formal processional avenue of house entrances still maintained by caretakers, with no political presence behind any of them. Stonework is cleaned, banners are absent. Walking it is unsettling precisely because everything is in good order and nobody is home. The avenue is wide, straight and paved for ceremony, with approach steps at each frontage and mounting points where standards were once carried. Caretakers work to schedules set by families who no longer send instructions, funded by arrangements that in several cases nobody has reviewed in decades. The doors are locked and the fittings are polished. Sound travels the whole length of it, so a single set of footsteps is audible from either end, which is the detail visitors remember.

Occupied Former Compounds.description: Old house properties subdivided into dense housing, with reception halls turned into shared kitchens and delegation rooms into apartments. Families have lived in them for generations. The architecture is far grander than the tenancies attached to it. Ceilings are high, doorways are wide, and the partitions dividing them are thin panel put up by residents rather than by any owner. Original fittings survive in odd places, a carved surround around a kitchen door, a floor pattern under a bed. Rent is paid to whoever currently claims the right to collect it, and in some buildings that question is genuinely open. Households maintain the structure themselves because no owner has repaired anything here within living memory.

Collapsed Representative Hall.description: The ruined civic structure of a family nobody now represents, its roof partly down and its chamber open to weather. Salvage has taken the fittings. Residents leave it standing because demolition would require an owner, and there is not one. The chamber floor is scattered with fallen material and the surviving walls still carry the shape of a formal seating arrangement. Mounting scars mark where every removable fitting was taken, in stages, over many years. Children use the outer steps and are told to stay off the floor. The ward's position is that nothing further should be taken from it, an agreement reached at the resident court and enforced entirely by the neighbours who can see the building from their windows.

Hidden Family Shrine.description: A small memorial space kept by descendants who hold no formal recognition, tended quietly and not advertised. Offerings are current. Finding it requires being shown it by somebody who has decided the visitor should know it exists. The space is a single room behind an ordinary door, lit low, with the memorial set against the far wall and seating for very few. Everything in it is maintained by hand and replaced at the tenders' own cost. Nothing is written down about who keeps it. The room is kept clean and the fittings are old, and the one recent addition is a repair to the doorframe made by a neighbour who has never been told what the room is for and has never asked.

Unclaimed Residential Tower.description: A tall structure occupied by people whose legal right to be there has never been resolved, and never been tested. Utilities run through informal arrangement. Its residents keep a shared record of their occupancy in case a claim is ever brought. The tower is sound, plain and built to a house standard that has outlasted the house, with a central stair, wide landings and window bays of thick scratched star-glass. Power and water reach it through connections made by residents and maintained by them. The record is kept by a rota of households and copied more than once. Nobody in the building has received a demand or a notice, and the absence of one has become its own quiet source of anxiety.

Illegal Workshop Court.description: Businesses operating out of abandoned infrastructure without licence, permit or rent, producing real goods for real customers. Power is drawn creatively. The workshops are tolerated because the ward needs what they make and because nobody has jurisdiction to stop them. The court is a yard between old service structures, filled with benches, racks and equipment under improvised cover, and the noise of it starts early and continues past the maintenance window. Power comes off conduit runs that were never decommissioned properly. Work is honest, priced and warrantied by reputation alone. The court's own rule is that nothing is made here that would bring an investigation into the ward, and the workshops police it among themselves.

Disputed Property Office.description: A civic office drowning in claims, counter-claims and lost records spanning several governments. Files are stacked past their shelving. Clerks here can trace a contested compound through three legal systems and still be unable to say who owns it. The office is one long room with a counter, a bank of readers and paper accumulating on every horizontal surface, lit flat and permanently short of space. Filings carry a fee and a waiting period that nobody attempts to defend. Clerks are patient, precise and openly resigned. The standing advice given across the counter is that a claimant should gather everything they have before filing, because a file that has been opened and found incomplete goes back to the end of a queue measured in cycles.

Forgotten House Archive.description: Damaged records of vanished families: genealogies, contracts, recognitions and grants, much of it water-marked or partly unreadable. Access is supervised. A single legible page in this room has both restored a name and destroyed one within the same season. The archive is cool, quiet and arranged by no system that survives from its original ordering, with damaged material stored flat in trays and handled under supervision on a cleared table. Requests are made in writing and take time. Fees apply to copying. The archivists know which trays hold material that people have asked after repeatedly, and they have their own quiet view about which of those requests came from a family and which from a broker.

Resident Community Court.description: Where the ward governs itself: tenancy disputes, shared repairs, boundaries and conduct, decided by residents under no formal authority. Decisions are recorded and generally respected. The court's legitimacy comes from the fact that nothing else arrives. It sits in a hall that was built for a house's own business, with the original seating still in place and a table brought in for the people currently hearing the matter. Attendance is open. Cases are heard in the order they were raised and the record is read back before anything is settled. The court has no power to enforce anything, which its members state at the opening of every session, and which has not yet stopped a decision from holding.

Sealed Custodian-Era Building.description: A structure older than the ward around it, closed since before current property law and never properly reopened. Its seals are original. What it was built to hold is a matter of speculation that historians and inheritance brokers pursue for different reasons. The building is squat, heavy and built from star-metal and stone at a scale that makes the compounds around it look decorative, with no windows at ground level and a single sealed approach. The seals are intact and have been examined more than once by people who concluded that opening them is not a small job. Nothing about it is maintained. Residents treat it as a landmark, and the ward's directions are routinely given in relation to it.

Name Removal Wall.description: A long wall marked where house symbols were taken down, chiselled out or stolen, leaving outlines that remain legible. Some removals were official and some were not. Residents can date the ward's decline by reading along it. The wall runs beside a public way, its surface a sequence of clean rectangles, rough gouges and shapes still faintly coloured where a symbol shaded the stone beneath it. Nothing has been recut and nothing has been filled. The difference between a careful removal and a violent one is obvious at a glance. People stop at it, and the ones who stop longest are usually looking for a particular outline rather than reading the whole run.

Inheritance Broker Rooms.description: Offices where legal specialists and outright opportunists pursue dead-house property, sometimes in the same building. Clients arrive with fragments of documentation and hope. The honest brokers and the predatory ones use identical letterhead. The rooms are fitted out to look like practices and mostly are, with a waiting bench, a consulting room and a wall of reference material chosen for its appearance as much as its use. Consultations are charged and the fee schedules are posted. Work is taken on contingency where the property is worth it. A claimant who cannot afford the filing costs is offered an arrangement, and the arrangements offered by the two kinds of broker in this ward are very difficult to tell apart on the page.

Returner's Gate.description: The entrance used by people claiming descent from a vanished house, watched by residents who have seen many such arrivals. Claimants are received politely and verified slowly. Occasionally one of them is telling the truth, and the ward has to decide what that means. The gate is a formal approach with a stair, a screen wall and a receiving space that was designed for a household's own guests. Residents keep somebody at it during ordinary hours, not as security but as courtesy. Claimants are offered a seat, asked what they have brought and directed to the archive and the property office. Nobody is turned away at the gate itself, which is a decision the community court has revisited and upheld.

Public Salvage Boundary.description: A disputed line marking what may lawfully be taken from abandoned structures and what may not. Salvagers and residents argue over it continuously. Both sides cite the same ambiguous civic ruling, which has never been clarified. The boundary is marked on the ground in paint that has been reapplied by both parties in slightly different places, so in several stretches there are two lines and an argument between them. Salvage crews work with equipment and a stated reading of the ruling. Residents work with presence. Disputes are taken to the community court, which has no jurisdiction over the salvagers, and to the property office, which has no answer, and they are generally settled by whoever is standing there at the time.

Mixed-House Residential Wards.name: Mixed-House Residential Wards
Mixed-House Residential Wards.basicInfo: The Mixed-House Residential Wards are the capital's main civilian housing network, home to the majority of residents who are neither visitors nor occupants of major-house compounds. Coreworkers, Republic staff, Academy graduates, multi-generation families and retired civic workers live along the same streets under a dozen different lineages. Life here is ordinary in the way the rest of Relstaris is not: schools, markets, gardens, clinics and neighbours who know each other by name. The wards are not one place and do not look like one: a street of low old houses in warm sandstone gives onto a run of pale new towers, and a terrace of civic housing in blue-grey star-glass backs onto a court that has been painted by its residents in whatever they agreed on. Older blocks stand on star-metal foundations laid for something larger, and several ward streets follow the line of a conduit run rather than any plan. Households read the Corelight for the work and maintenance shifts and complain about the evening routing in the same terms their neighbours use. Rent, tuition, power and water are all real monthly expenses, and a good address in these wards is expensive enough that families stay put for generations to keep one.
Mixed-House Residential Wards.hiddenInfo: These wards are where Republic decisions stop being abstract. A vote on utility allocation or transit funding reaches residents as rent, as clinic waiting times, as whether the Night Transit Walk is lit for shift workers coming home, and the Community Debate Hall fills whenever one of those lands badly. Interhouse Family Services handles the questions the houses would rather not discuss in public: marriages, inheritance and naming across lineages whose customs directly contradict each other, and their caseload is growing faster than any house will acknowledge. Residents are visibly tired of being treated as background by major-house visitors and Academy tourists. The quieter tension is demographic: children raised here take house rivalry far less seriously than their parents expect, and older residents are split on whether that is the ward's greatest achievement or the beginning of something being lost.

Coreworker Terraces.description: Stepped housing for Citadel staff, utility technicians and civic administration workers, built close to the transit lines that get them to shift on time. Balconies face inward onto shared courts. Half the people on a terrace can explain how the city actually runs, and none of them are quoted anywhere. The terraces step back as they rise so that every level gets light into its court, and the courts are furnished by the households rather than by any landlord. Allocation follows employment, which means neighbours change with the rosters. Because the work runs to the Corelight's maintenance windows, somebody on every terrace is asleep at an hour the rest of the city is awake, and the noise discipline in the courts is enforced by residents with genuine feeling.

Republic Staff Housing.description: Residences for public employees and representative staff, plain and well-maintained, allocated by service rather than lineage. Neighbours work for rival representatives and share a stairwell anyway. Political discretion here is a household habit rather than a rule. The buildings are unornamented, evenly finished and kept in better repair than most of the ward, because the maintenance is contracted rather than left to households. Rent is deducted against the post and the tenancy ends with the service. Children from opposing offices attend the same school and walk there together. The convention on the stairwell is that nothing anyone is working on is discussed above the ground floor, and it holds well enough that its occasional failures are remembered for years.

Young Professional Towers.description: Compact towers full of Academy graduates and specialists in their first independent homes, with shared workspaces and a permanently overbooked roof terrace. Furnishings are new and minimal. The turnover is high and the friendships formed in them are not. The flats are small, efficient and finished in the same pale scheme throughout, and the shared floors are the reason people take them. Rent is high for the space and is the largest single cost most residents carry. The booking board for the terrace is a standing grievance. Doors along a corridor stay open in the evenings because most of the people behind them arrived in the capital knowing nobody, and the tower is the arrangement that fixed it.

Old Relstaris Homes.description: Low multi-generation houses predating the current district plan, with irregular plots and additions built by successive generations. Families have held some for centuries. Their owners are courteous to developers and have never once sold. The houses sit at odd angles to the streets that were laid around them, in materials that were local and ordinary when they were built and are now noticeably unlike everything adjacent. Additions are obvious and unapologetic. Maintenance is constant and paid for out of household income. The plots carry rights that predate the present arrangement of the ward, which the property office confirms periodically and which the families themselves tend to describe in terms of who planted what and when.

Mixed-House Commons.description: Shared neighbourhood centres offering meeting rooms, activity space and a hall that can be booked by anyone in the ward. Programming is decided locally. A Volen naming, a Solvraxis recital and a school assembly can occupy the same room in one week. The buildings are plain and flexible, with movable partitions, a kitchen that everything depends on and a noticeboard by the door that is the most-read surface in the ward. Bookings carry a small charge and the calendar is public. Programming committees are elected and argue. The commons are shared ground in practice as well as in name, and the standing house rule is that no booking may exclude a lawful resident of the ward from the building itself.

Public School Court.description: General education outside the Academy, teaching children of every house background in the same classrooms. Facilities are decent and unglamorous. Teachers here are noticeably better at cross-house mediation than most civic professionals. The buildings surround a paved court used for assembly, games and collection, and the whole site is finished in the hard-wearing, unremarkable materials civic building uses everywhere. Places are allocated by ward and fees are modest against Academy tuition. Staff deal daily with families whose customs about authority, competition and apology contradict one another. The court's own convention is that a dispute between children is settled in front of both households, which the parents find far more difficult than the children do.

Family Market Court.description: Daily food, childcare, repair and small businesses arranged around a paved court where everyone shops at the same hours. Stallholders know households by name and order. It is the ward's real information network and does not pretend otherwise. The court is roofed at its edges and open in the middle, with permanent units around the perimeter and day pitches in the centre, and it is busiest in the hours either side of the Corelight's shift into evening. Prices are ordinary capital prices and credit is a matter of how long a household has shopped there. The childcare arrangement runs off a rota kept behind one of the counters, and half the ward's parents depend on it entirely.

Night Transit Walk.description: A lit, monitored pedestrian route between the transit stops and the residential blocks, built specifically for shift workers and students returning late. Emergency points sit at intervals. Residents notice immediately when a section of its lighting is left unrepaired. The route runs wide, straight and deliberately overlooked by windows rather than screened from them, with the surfacing kept even and the planting kept low. Its lighting is independent of the Corelight routing, which is the whole point of it. The emergency points connect directly to civic response and are tested on a schedule. A failed section is reported to the ward council within a shift, and the council's record of how long each repair took is read aloud at the debate hall.

Neighborhood Gardens.description: Public growing plots, recreation lawns and event space maintained by residents on a rota. Produce goes to the households that worked the beds. Plot allocation disputes are the ward's longest-running and least serious political conflict. The gardens are walled, gated and open to anyone in the ward, with beds laid in ranks, a shared tool store and a water point that costs the association money every cycle. The rota is posted and honoured unevenly. Events are held on the lawn and cleared by the people who held them. The allocation list is maintained by one household at a time, in a book, and every keeper of the book has been accused of favouritism by somebody within a season of taking it on.

Local Clinic.description: Routine medical care, vaccinations, checkups and minor injuries, staffed adequately and used constantly. Waiting times are reasonable. It refers serious cases onward to the Myralis Capitol Clinic and handles everything short of that competently. The clinic is a single-storey building with an intake desk, a waiting room built for families and treatment rooms along one corridor, lit softly and kept quiet. Care is charged and the schedule is posted at the desk. Staff know most of the households by name and a great deal about them by inference. The referral conversation is handled in a side room rather than at the desk, a practice adopted after a complaint and never written into any procedure.

Community Debate Hall.description: A hall for local issues that do not require Republic-level politics: rents, school funding, transit, development. Attendance spikes when something lands badly. Representatives who show up here without being invited are heard out and rarely thanked. The hall is plain, raked slightly and sized for a crowd it only occasionally gets, with a speaking position at the front and a recording clerk beside it. Sessions are free to attend and open to any ward resident. The agenda is set in advance and amended loudly. The clerk's record is posted afterwards, and the ward's habit of quoting it back to civic officials, accurately and at length, is the reason the hall is taken more seriously than its size suggests.

Interhouse Family Services.description: Offices handling marriage, inheritance, naming and household custom where lineages cross and their traditions do not agree. Mediators work from precedent and patience. Most of the capital's genuinely difficult family law passes through these rooms without ever becoming public. The offices are quiet, comfortably furnished and arranged so that two families can arrive separately and leave separately. Sessions are booked, charged on a scale and often run over. Mediators hold a working knowledge of customs from every major house and a long file of precedents that exist nowhere else. The caseload is growing and the waiting period with it, which the service reports each cycle in terms that nobody above it has yet acted on.

Retired Resident Row.description: Housing for older workers, former representatives and longtime neighbourhood anchors, at ground level and close to the market court. Doors stay open in the afternoons. Anyone wanting to know what the ward was like before the current district plan asks here. The row is single-storey and stepless by design, with wide doorways, a continuous frontage of small gardens and seating set where the Corelight reaches the path at working intensity. Tenancies are long and the allocation favours people who have lived in the ward for decades. Neighbours check on one another without making a system of it. The row's collective memory is the ward's most consulted resource and its least formally recorded.

The Unremarkable Street.description: A perfectly ordinary residential street, famous among locals precisely because nothing historically important has ever happened on it. There is a small unofficial sign saying so. Residents defend its record with more energy than the joke strictly deserves. The street is a short run of mid-height housing in mismatched but harmonious frontages, with a repair shop at one end, a transit stop at the other and nothing between them that anyone has needed to write down. The sign is hand-made and has been replaced at least twice. Residents track near-misses with genuine attention, and the standing argument is whether an incident in an adjoining street counts, a question the ward has never settled and enjoys too much to settle.

Public Protection District.name: Public Protection District
Public Protection District.basicInfo: The Public Protection District is the capital's centre for safety, investigation, mediation and emergency response, operating under the Republic rather than under any single house. Its personnel are drawn from multiple houses, independent professionals and specialist responders, with civilian review built into the structure. Its stated purpose is to protect shared civic ground without imposing one house's culture on the city, and it is tested on that constantly. The District is built to be approached rather than defended: pale grey-blue star-glass, wide unscreened frontages, public counters set close to the street and no house symbol on any of it, all of it fitted into older civic structure whose star-metal framing is left visible where the refit ran out of reasons to hide it. Shifts turn with the Corelight, the heavier briefings falling at the change into evening routing and the maintenance windows staffed for the incidents that come with them. Services at the counters are free to residents and the District's costs are argued over in the Republic every cycle. Protectors, mediators, reviewers and clerks share the same corridors, and the queue in the complaint hall is visible from most of them.
Public Protection District.hiddenInfo: The District's independence is contested from several directions at once. Protectors are pressured by their own houses to interpret incidents favourably, Dravon publicly accuses the force of political bias, and the House Security Liaison Floor has to coordinate with private compound forces without handing them public authority. Evidence here disappears through legal influence rather than theft, which is precisely why the Evidence Integrity Vault was built and why its logs are watched. The Underworld Investigation Wing is currently working the supply chains that connect the Vein Market to legitimate businesses, and it knows some civic offices are relying on illegal supply during shortages. Missing Persons carries the District's heaviest and least funded caseload: newcomers, students and workers who vanish into the city, some into the Hollow Ring under new names and some into the Deepways. Community responders in Low Relstaris keep arriving before formal deployment, which the Civilian Review Chamber treats as a finding rather than an anecdote.

Civic Protector Hall.description: The District's administrative centre, handling deployment, duty rosters and public-facing service at a long open counter. Protectors from several houses share the same briefing floor. The hall is deliberately unfortified, which is a policy statement the force has had to defend more than once. The room is high, plainly finished and lit evenly from above, with the counter running most of its length and the briefing floor behind it in full view of anyone waiting. Rosters are posted publicly. Residents come in to report, to ask and to complain, and are dealt with in the order they arrived. The counter has been rebuilt once after an incident and rebuilt to the same open specification, which the commander at the time explained in a public session and has not been asked about since.

Emergency Flight Deck.description: Launch platforms for rapid response across the vertical city, with crews on rotation and equipment staged for immediate departure. Flight lanes clear on alert priority. Response times across Relstaris are measured from this deck and published quarterly. The deck is open, hard-surfaced and marked out in launch positions, with equipment racked where a crew can reach it at a run and a controller's position overlooking the whole platform. Crews rotate through rest, ready and standing states. Lane clearance is coordinated with civic flight control and is the part of the system most likely to fail under load. The published figures are read closely by the wards with the worst coverage, who bring them to their own debate halls.

Gate Incident Response.description: A specialist unit for the Grand Lunar Gate, trained in arrivals, crowd containment, contraband and transit failure. Its officers rotate through the Gate itself. Most of what they handle is confusion rather than crime, and they treat the distinction seriously. The unit's rooms hold briefing space, equipment for crowd work and a wall of current arrival patterns that is updated every shift. Officers are chosen partly for languages, customs and patience. A great deal of the work is explaining a procedure to someone who has never used a Gate before and has just been separated from their belongings. The unit's own training material opens with the reminder that a frightened arrival is not a suspect.

Public Mediation Court.description: Rooms for de-escalation and conflict resolution before a dispute becomes a criminal matter, open to any resident. Mediators are trained across house customs. A substantial share of the capital's potential violence ends in these rooms instead. The rooms are small, neutral and furnished without a raised position for anyone, with separate approaches so that parties need not meet in a corridor before they are ready. Sessions are free and booked. Mediators work to no fixed script because the customs in the room may contradict each other about who speaks first, what an apology is and whether a third party may be present. Agreements are written down, read back and signed, and the copies go home with the parties rather than into a case file.

Cross-House Security Room.description: Coordination space used during disputes involving compounds or representatives, with representatives of each involved party present. Protocols are strict and rehearsed. Getting rival house security to accept the same operational picture is the room's entire purpose. The room is built around a shared display table with fixed positions, and the positions are assigned by protocol rather than chosen. Nothing in it belongs to any house. Access is logged and the logs are available to the civilian review. The protocols cover who speaks, in what order and with what standing, and they are rehearsed often enough that the rehearsals themselves have become a recognised part of the District's relationship with the compounds.

Detainment Review Office.description: Independent review of every custody decision and use of force, with access to complete incident records. Reviewers are outside the chain of command. Its findings have ended careers and its existence is the main answer the District gives to accusations of policing excess. The office sits apart from the operational floors with its own entrance and its own records access, and its staff do not share a briefing with the protectors whose work they examine. Review is automatic rather than triggered by complaint. Findings are written, published in summary and delivered to the officer concerned before anyone else reads them. The working relationship between the office and the duty commanders is professional, cold and entirely deliberate.

Disaster Coordination Center.description: The operations floor for Core outages, fires, structural failure, crowd emergencies and evacuation, running live feeds from across the city. Seats are assigned by agency. During a citywide incident this is where Contair engineering, Myralis medicine and civic response sit at one table. The floor is tiered toward a wall of feeds, kept dim so the displays read, and loud in a controlled way that visitors find unsettling. Positions are staffed continuously at a low level and filled out on alert. Agencies bring their own people and their own authority, and the centre coordinates rather than commands. The standing rehearsal schedule is resented by everyone required to attend it and has never been allowed to lapse.

Academy Incident Unit.description: Handles student safety, serious misconduct and coordination with Academy administration, staffed by officers who understand campus politics. Cases are sensitive by definition. The unit's difficulty is that the Academy prefers to resolve things internally and the law does not always allow it. The unit works from a modest floor with interview rooms furnished for young people and families rather than for suspects. Officers are experienced and selected for their tolerance of institutional pressure. Cases arrive through the Academy, through families and sometimes through a student walking into the complaint hall. The unit's standing practice is to record every request from the Academy to handle a matter internally, and that record has become one of the most sensitive documents in the District.

Underworld Investigation Wing.description: Long-term investigation into organised crime, trafficking, market manipulation and hidden supply chains, working from case walls rather than fast response. Officers here are rotated for their own safety. Their files reach further into legitimate business than the District states publicly. The wing occupies a closed floor with restricted access, its rooms lined with case boards that are worked over months and cleared only when a matter ends. Officers work in small teams and do not discuss cases across them. Rotations are mandatory and unpopular. The wing's difficulty is not finding the connections but proving them in a form that survives the influence brought to bear once a name from a legitimate business enters a file.

Public Complaint Hall.description: Where citizens report incidents and file misconduct complaints against protectors, with clerks who record everything regardless of how it will look. The queue is public and visible. Making complaint intake impossible to hide was a deliberate design decision. The hall opens directly off the street with seating, a numbered queue and a row of clerks at an open counter, and the whole room is visible from the frontage. Filing costs nothing. Clerks take a statement in the complainant's own words and read it back before it is entered. Complaints against named officers are logged identically to every other kind, and the running count of open matters is displayed on the wall where the queue can read it.

Civilian Review Chamber.description: A hearing room for independent oversight, holding public sessions on conduct, policy and contested incidents. Panel members are civilians. Protectors give evidence under the same conditions as anyone else, which is the point and remains unpopular internally. The chamber is arranged with the panel at one end, a table for evidence and public seating that is genuinely open, and sessions are held at hours ordinary residents can attend. Panel members are appointed from the wards and serve fixed terms. Sessions are recorded and the record is public. The chamber has begun treating repeated findings as patterns rather than incidents, which has changed how seriously its recommendations are taken and how much they are resisted.

Missing Persons Office.description: Casework on newcomers, students, workers and residents who disappear into the largest city on the planet. The wall of open cases is long and old. Investigators here work closely with arrival wards and lower-city contacts and are permanently short of staff. The office is cramped, overfull and organised around the wall, which is maintained by hand because no display has ever suited the way the work is actually done. Reports are taken without a waiting period. Investigators carry more cases than they can work and say so in every funding session. Families come in to ask after cases that have been open for years, and the practice is that somebody sits down with them properly rather than answering across a desk.

House Security Liaison Floor.description: Coordination with private compound forces, conducted on public ground and on public terms. Liaison officers negotiate access constantly. The floor exists to cooperate without surrendering civic authority, and the line moves under pressure every season. The floor is deliberately modest, with meeting rooms sized for small delegations and no space that could host a house force. Liaison officers are senior, rotated and briefed to record every request. Access to shared ground, movement of armed personnel and response to incidents crossing a compound boundary are the recurring subjects. Each agreement is written, dated and filed, and the accumulated file is what the District produces whenever a house claims a precedent that does not exist.

Community Response School.description: Public training in emergency response, first care, evacuation and crowd safety, open to any resident. Classes fill quickly in districts with poor coverage. Its graduates are often the first competent people on the scene anywhere in the lower city. The school runs from practical rooms with equipment that is used hard and replaced on a cycle, and its instructors are working responders taking teaching shifts. Courses are free and the places are allocated by application. Classes mix students, shift workers, shopkeepers and retired residents. The instructors' standing observation is that the districts sending the most applicants are the ones the District reaches slowest, and they have stopped presenting that as a coincidence.

Evidence Integrity Vault.description: Secured storage protecting physical and recorded evidence from house influence, tampering and quiet loss. Access is logged and independently audited. It was built because evidence used to vanish legally, and the vault's audit record is itself evidence of that history. The vault is a controlled floor of sealed storage with a single entry, an examination room and a handling procedure that slows every investigation using it. Items are logged in, logged out and photographed at each transfer. The audit is run by people who report outside the District. The procedure is widely complained about by investigators under time pressure, and no commander has ever proposed relaxing it in a session that was being recorded.

Myralis Capitol Clinic.name: Myralis Capitol Clinic
Myralis Capitol Clinic.basicInfo: The Myralis Capitol Clinic is the most respected neutral specialist medical institution in Relstaris, following the clinical standards of the Myralis Continuum in Vexorath while serving residents of every house, including Dravon. It covers trauma, recovery, prosthetics, neural medicine, clinical ethics and Core-holder monitoring, and its authority comes from trust and consent rather than political alignment. Its halls are calm, technically advanced and deliberately unaffiliated. The building is finished in pale green and white star-glass with the light kept soft and even, and the older structure it occupies has been restored rather than replaced, so ancient star-metal framing runs through wards fitted out to current clinical specification and a decommissioned conduit run carries cabling along a corridor that was built for something else entirely. No house symbol appears anywhere inside. The Clinic works to clinical time rather than to the Corelight, staffed continuously through every shift and every maintenance window, though the intake hall fills predictably as the city's working intensity ends. Care is charged, and the arrangements made for patients who cannot meet the cost are handled where the queue cannot hear them. The corridors are quiet, the floors are clean, and somebody is always waiting.
Myralis Capitol Clinic.hiddenInfo: The Clinic's neutrality is under constant, polite pressure. Houses attempt to shape diagnoses, sponsors and employers try to adjust health records, and the Medical Records Integrity Office spends most of its time refusing people who are certain they are entitled. The Core Holder Health Suite monitors the current holder without any authority over the Core itself, a distinction that matters enormously whenever rumours about the holder's health begin circulating. Ethics cases are accumulating in the Synthetic and Biological Interface Review around prosthetics, dependency and consent, and the Clinical Ethics Court is hearing disputes the Academy would prefer stayed internal after an injury scandal in its training programme. The Unlicensed Practice Liaison quietly brings underworld patients and practitioners toward safe care without automatic punishment, which works and which the Public Protection District has never formally endorsed. Records held here could also prove that a public defeat involved sabotage.

Public Intake Hall.description: The Clinic's main entrance and triage floor, assessing everyone who arrives regardless of house, record or ability to pay immediately. Staff move quickly and speak plainly. Nobody is asked for a lineage before they are asked what is wrong. The hall is wide and low-lit, with an assessment counter, seating that fills from the doors inward and treatment bays screened along one side. Arrivals are seen by condition and not by order, which is explained to the room repeatedly and resented anyway. Billing is handled after assessment and never before it. The written notice at the counter stating that no patient is refused assessment has been reprinted in larger type at least once, and staff still point to it several times a shift.

Cross-House Trauma Center.description: Major injury treatment conducted without political separation, so rival-house patients are stabilised in adjacent bays as a matter of course. Surgical suites run continuously. The unit's standing rule is that house security waits outside and does not negotiate about it. The floor is bright, hard-surfaced and arranged for movement, with the bays open to a central working aisle and the suites beyond a controlled threshold. Equipment is standardised to Continuum specification and checked between cases. Staff work in mixed teams by roster rather than by lineage. The rule about security is stated at the threshold by whoever is senior on the floor, in the same words every time, and it has been stated to delegations from every major house.

Core Holder Health Suite.description: A dedicated monitoring facility for the current Core holder, equipped for continuous assessment and rapid intervention. Access is tightly limited. The suite observes the holder's health and has no authority over the Core, a boundary written into its charter. The suite is small, self-contained and quieter than anywhere else in the building, with its own approach, its own records handling and a standing clinical team rather than a rotation. Equipment is maintained under a separate contract and tested on a schedule that does not vary. The charter is displayed inside the suite rather than outside it. Nothing observed in this room is released, confirmed or denied, which becomes considerably harder to sustain whenever rumours about the holder begin moving through the capital.

Academy Recovery Wing.description: Long-term rehabilitation for student injury, overtraining and affinity strain, coordinated with Academy instructors. Recovery schedules are enforced against student impatience. A worrying share of admissions here involve training nobody has officially authorised. The wing is built for stays rather than visits, with rehabilitation floors, assessment rooms and seating for families, finished warmer than the clinical areas around it. Instructors attend by appointment and are told what the schedule permits rather than consulted about it. Costs fall on families, sponsors or the Academy depending on the case, and the difference matters. Clinicians record the training history behind every admission, accurately, whatever the student has been advised to say.

Prosthetics and Adaptation Institute.description: Recovery technology, artificial organs, mobility support and the long adjustment that follows them, with fitting bays and a workshop floor. Patients test devices in a realistic mock-up street. The Institute treats adaptation as a life, not a procedure. The workshop is a working fabrication space with benches, tooling and components racked in order, noisier than the rest of the Clinic and open to the patients whose devices are being made in it. The mock-up street includes uneven surfacing, a transit step, a market stall counter and a stair, because those are the things patients report going wrong. Fitting is charged, and the adjustment appointments that follow are charged separately, which the Institute states plainly at the first consultation.

Continuum Transfer Liaison.description: Coordinates high-risk cases, specialist consultation and patient movement with the Myralis Continuum in Vexorath. Transfers are arranged around gate scheduling. The liaison's judgement about when a case exceeds capitol capability is rarely contested twice. The office is small and permanently in use, with communication equipment, case files in transit and a board tracking who is waiting on what. Transfers depend on gate clearance, safe transport and receiving capacity, and any of the three can stop one. Consultations run in both directions. The liaison's working principle is that moving a patient is itself a clinical intervention, and the argument that follows from it is the one they have most often with families in a hurry.

Synthetic and Biological Interface Revie.description: Clinical ethics work on prosthetics, artificial systems, identity, dependency and consent, conducted by mixed panels including patients. Cases are slow and heavily documented. The questions it handles have no settled answers anywhere on Nexara. The review sits in plain rooms with a table, a recording clerk and seating arranged so that the patient members are not placed apart from the clinicians. Cases are read into the record in full before discussion. Documentation is exhaustive because the panels expect to be read by people facing the same question later. The caseload is growing, and the panels have begun keeping a separate record of the questions they could not answer at all, which is now the more closely read of the two.

Clinical Ethics Court.description: Hears disputed treatment, consent, experimental care and attempts by houses to influence clinical decisions. Proceedings are recorded and partly public. Its rulings are binding within Myralis practice and have shaped medical conduct across the capital. The court sits in a formal room with a raised panel position, a table for the parties and a public gallery that is opened for the parts of a hearing that can be heard openly. Parties may bring advocates. The record of a closed session is sealed to the panel and the parties alone. Rulings are published with the clinical reasoning intact, which is why they are cited by practitioners who have no obligation whatsoever to follow them.

Neutral Medical Arbitration Rooms.description: Where conflicting medical claims and professional reviews are settled between practitioners, houses and insurers. Panels are drawn from outside the parties involved. Both sides accept the process because the alternative is the Republic Forum. The rooms are functional and deliberately unimpressive, with a table, a display for records and no seating that confers standing on anyone. Panels are appointed case by case and the appointments are disclosed to both parties beforehand. Sessions are charged to the parties and the fees are shared. Findings are written, reasoned and final within the process, and the standing observation of the arbitrators is that most of what reaches them is a dispute about money wearing a dispute about medicine.

Public Recovery Gardens.description: Planted grounds for rehabilitation walking, physical therapy and quiet family time, with graded paths and sheltered seating. Patients set their own pace. It is the one part of the Clinic where nobody is being assessed. The paths are laid at deliberately varied gradients with handrails on the steeper runs and rest points at intervals that therapists chose rather than gardeners. Planting is dense, low and maintained by Clinic staff. Entry costs nothing and is open to families whether or not they are visiting a patient. The unwritten arrangement is that clinicians walking the gardens do not stop to look at how a patient is moving, and the patients who have noticed them not looking appreciate it.

Emergency Flight Intake.description: A direct aerial arrival platform for critical patients, feeding straight into trauma without passing through the public hall. Crews hand over on the deck. Priority here is determined by condition alone and the Clinic publishes that it is. The deck is open, marked out for approach and lit hard, with a covered threshold leading directly onto the trauma floor and equipment staged at the doors. Crews from civic response, house services and independent operators all land here on the same terms. Handover is verbal, fast and recorded. The published priority statement exists because it has been tested, and the Clinic's account of the occasions on which it was tested is part of the same public document.

Low Relstaris Outreach Clinic.description: The base for staff and resources sent into underfunded districts, running rotations into the lower city's own clinic. Supplies are packed here and carried out daily. Outreach staff are the Clinic's clearest statement about who its medicine is for. The base is a working room of shelving, packing benches and transport cases, with a rota board that is the most argued-over object in the department. Supplies come out of the Clinic's own budget and the volume is never enough. Staff rotate through on top of their ordinary duties. The coordinator's standing difficulty is that the outreach keeps a lower-city clinic open without changing anything about why it needs keeping open, and the department says so in every review.

Confidential Care Floor.description: Protected treatment for politically sensitive patients, with restricted access and separately secured records. Presence here is not disclosed. The floor exists because the alternative is patients who need care choosing an unlicensed room instead. The floor is reached by a controlled approach and is otherwise an ordinary clinical ward, which patients arriving in fear find reassuring and their households find inadequate. Records are held under a separate system audited by the records office. Staff are assigned rather than rotated. The Clinic will not confirm that a named person is on the floor to any enquirer, including a house, including a representative, and including, on at least one occasion, a family.

Medical Records Integrity Office.description: Prevents houses, sponsors and employers from altering or extracting health records, maintaining audited files that cannot be quietly edited. Requests to amend arrive constantly. Its refusals are the main reason the Clinic's neutrality is believed. The office is small, closed and equipped with records systems that log every access alongside the name and standing of whoever made it. Amendments require a clinical reason recorded by the clinician responsible. Requests arrive politely, in writing, from people who are entirely certain of their entitlement, and are refused in a standard form that has not been softened in years. The audit trail is available to the ethics court and to nobody else.

Disaster Treatment Hall.description: A large hall kept equipped and empty, activated during citywide emergencies for mass casualty care. Drills run through it regularly. Its readiness is coordinated directly with the Public Protection District's disaster centre. The hall is a bare floor marked out in treatment positions, with supplies sealed in bays along the walls, power and water runs terminated at every position and lighting kept at a low holding level. Nothing is stored in it that would have to be moved. Drills bring in staff from across the Clinic and from civic response, and the hall is at its noisiest when nothing is wrong. The stock in the sealed bays is rotated on schedule and the rotation is the department's least popular standing duty.

Unlicensed Practice Liaison.description: Encourages patients and practitioners from underground medicine toward safe care without automatic punishment, on the principle that a treated patient matters more than a prosecution. Conversations are confidential. It is the Clinic's most pragmatic and most legally awkward service. The liaison works from a plain room with its own entrance away from the intake hall, furnished for conversation rather than examination. Nothing said in it is recorded unless the patient asks for it to be. Practitioners come in for supplies, for advice and occasionally to hand over a case they cannot manage. The service has no formal endorsement from the Public Protection District, a silence that both institutions have found it convenient not to disturb.

Family Waiting Commons.description: A shared waiting space where political rivals sit within a few seats of one another because injury ignores house boundaries. Refreshment and information are provided without charge. Staff have seen more genuine cross-house civility in this room than anywhere in the capital. The commons is broad, softly lit and furnished in clusters rather than rows, with a counter offering water and something hot and a staffed information point that gives the same answer to everyone. Nothing in the room is allocated by standing. Families wait for hours and the room accumulates coats, bags and sleeping children. The counter is restocked through the night, and the person doing it is generally the one who notices first when somebody has been waiting alone too long.

High Relstaris.name: High Relstaris
High Relstaris.basicInfo: High Relstaris is the elevated district crossing above several sections of the capital, holding the highest public flight routes, observatories, communications terraces, gardens and landing decks. It is open, luminous and exposed, with the Corelight rising through it and the whole city grid legible below.
