Wealthy residents, flight controllers, researchers, service crews and ordinary visitors share the same platforms, which is not always comfortable for the residents. The district is built light: pale star-glass, thin structure, open decks and long spans that read as almost nothing from below, much of it anchored into star-metal masts that were raised for earlier purposes and reused rather than rebuilt. Cabling and service runs are threaded through old conduit that was never intended to climb this far. Because the Corelight passes through the district rather than reaching it second-hand, its shifts are more visible here than anywhere in the capital, and the platforms fill and empty accordingly. Public ground is genuinely public and free, which is precisely what the district's residents are contesting; private residences, landing rights and lane clearances are expensive and allocated rather than bought. Service crews work the same structures the views depend on, and most visitors never see them.
High Relstaris.hiddenInfo: High Relstaris is where the capital watches, listens and plans. The Signal Anomaly Room is working unexplained long-range transmissions that nobody has yet been able to classify or dismiss, and the Future Orbital Planning Office is studying what an official capitol-to-orbit connection would require, with Republic, Contair, Corsair and civic specialists at the same table and no finished platform approved. Neither project has settled conclusions, and both attract interest well beyond their remit. Politically, the district's residents are pressing to restrict public access to the overlooks and the High Civic Garden, which would turn shared civic ground into private amenity and has drawn a Republic objection. The Skyline Service Platforms are worked by crews maintaining structures most residents only admire from below, and their conditions are the district's quiet scandal. Flight emergencies up here are managed from Emergency Sky Control, and at this altitude margins are small.

High Flight Crown.description: The city's highest sanctioned flight lanes, marked by light beacons and cleared for controlled high-speed movement. Traffic is routed continuously by sky control. Flying the Crown at speed is the closest thing Relstaris has to a public spectacle nobody had to organise. The lanes are defined by beacon lines rather than by structure, so the Crown is a shape in the air that experienced flyers read instantly and newcomers misjudge. Clearance is required, granted by lane and revocable without discussion. Spectators watch from the overlooks below, which is unregulated and free. The beacons are serviced by the skyline crews on a rotation, and a beacon that has gone dark is reported by flyers long before the maintenance schedule reaches it.

Planetary Observatory.description: Instruments for Nexaran sky study alongside a public education floor with viewing sessions for residents and school groups. Researchers work through the night cycle. The observatory insists on the public floor because it argues the sky is civic property. The instrument halls are cold, dark and kept apart from the public floor, which is bright, busy and built for children who have been brought in by their schools. Sessions are free and booked out well ahead. Researchers give the public talks on a rota and complain about it in a way that fools nobody. The argument about civic property is made formally every time the district's residents propose restricting access to anything, and the observatory's director makes it in writing each time.

Long-Range Communications Terrace.description: Arrays for planetary communication and signal monitoring, spread across an exposed terrace and tended by technicians in weather gear. Traffic passes through here for the whole capital. The equipment is Contair-standard and audited more often than anything else in the district. The terrace is open, hard-surfaced and laid out around the arrays with walkways between them and a control room set back behind glazing. Technicians work in pairs and sign on and off the terrace every time. The audits are scheduled, unannounced and conducted by people from outside the district. A fault here is felt across the capital within minutes, which is why the spares store is the best-stocked room in High Relstaris and the one nobody is permitted to borrow from.

High Civic Garden.description: An elevated public park with planted terraces, benches and unobstructed views across the entire city grid. Entry is free and deliberately so. It is the single most contested piece of ground in High Relstaris, because residents keep proposing to restrict it. The garden is laid in stepped beds with paths wide enough for the crowds it draws, planting chosen to hold in the exposure, and benches set along the outer edge facing the view rather than each other. Civic crews maintain it and the cost appears in the Republic's accounts every cycle. Families, students, workers and residents use it together, in numbers the residents describe as a problem and the Republic describes as the point. The gate has never been fitted with a lock.

Diplomatic Landing Deck.description: A formal aerial arrival platform for major delegations, with reception space and controlled approach lanes. Ceremony here is precise and brief. Which delegation lands on which pad is a protocol question that has caused real diplomatic friction. The deck is finished to a standard the rest of the district does not attempt, pale and immaculate, with marked pads, a covered reception hall and staff who rehearse an arrival before it happens. Lane clearance is arranged in advance and timed to the minute. Nothing about the pads is functionally different from one another, which the protocol office explains regularly and which has never once resolved the argument. A delegation kept waiting on approach is a message, and everyone involved knows it.

Emergency Sky Control.description: The operations room managing flight across the city during incidents, able to close lanes, ground traffic and clear corridors for response craft. Controllers work in short rotations. At this altitude a mistaken instruction has consequences within seconds. The room is dim, tightly laid out and lined with position displays showing traffic across the vertical city, and it is quiet in a way that is entirely unlike calm. Rotations are short and enforced by supervisors who remove people from position without argument. Authority to close a lane rests with the controller holding it. The room coordinates with the Public Protection District during citywide incidents, and the handover protocol between them is rehearsed more often than either institution finds comfortable.

Weather Observation Gallery.description: Monitoring of wind, pressure, storm systems and the environmental conditions that affect flight and structure across Relstaris. Forecasts issue directly to sky control. The gallery's advisories close the High Flight Crown several times a season. The gallery is a long room of instrument feeds and working displays, staffed continuously, with its sensor arrays mounted out on the structure where the crews have to reach them. Advisories go out on a standing authority that does not require anyone else's agreement. The staff are used to being argued with by people who have somewhere to be and have never yet withdrawn an advisory because of it. The record of every closure and its basis is published, and the flight community reads it closely.

High Relstaris Residences.description: Expensive skyline homes with extraordinary views and full exposure to wind, cold and the constant traffic of the Crown. Residents pay for altitude and then complain about it. It is also the constituency pushing hardest to limit public access nearby. The residences are pale, glazed and built out along the structure in small numbers, each with its own landing point and a service approach residents prefer not to think about. Costs are extraordinary and recurring, since everything up here is carried, maintained and serviced at a premium. Households are small and mostly absent. The residents' association meets, files objections and is heard out by the Republic, which has so far declined every proposal it has made about the public ground.

Public Corelight View.description: The best safe vantage on the Corelight and the city grid at night, with railed platforms and standing room for a substantial crowd. Visitors arrive continuously after dark. Free access to this platform is treated locally as a civic right. The platforms are tiered so that the back rows can see over the front, railed in star-metal worn bright along the top, and lit only at the footing so that nothing interferes with the view. Nothing is charged and nothing is bookable. The crowd turns over continuously and its noise level rises and falls with the Corelight's routing. Somebody is always explaining the shifts to a visitor, usually a resident, usually inaccurately, and usually corrected by a stranger within a few moments.

Silent Overlook.description: A quiet platform away from the main viewing decks, used for reflection, private conversation and dates that need somewhere unobserved. There is no lighting beyond the safety strips. Custom holds that people here are left alone. The platform is small, plain and reached by a walkway that discourages casual arrivals, with a rail, a few benches and nothing else built on it. It is not signposted and not concealed. Because it is dark, people arriving take a moment to see who is already there, and the convention is to choose the far end. Nobody speaks across the platform. Civic crews check it on their rounds and do not linger, which residents count as part of the custom rather than as an exception to it.

Academy Sky Laboratory.description: High-altitude research and teaching space used by Academy students and staff for observation, atmospheric work and flight science. Equipment is shared with the observatory. Student projects run here that would be impossible at ground level. The laboratory is a working floor of benches, instrument mounts and a sheltered external platform where equipment can be set up in the exposure it is meant to measure. Time on the shared instruments is booked and contested. Students come up on scheduled flights and stay for the session. Projects are supervised loosely and fail visibly, and the wall by the door carries a long list of results that did not work, kept deliberately and added to at the end of every term.

Signal Anomaly Room.description: A small monitoring suite investigating unexplained long-range transmissions, with recordings that have so far resisted classification. Analysts work carefully and publish nothing. The room's existence is public; its current caseload is not discussed outside it. The suite is a single closed room off the communications terrace, equipped for recording, comparison and storage, with acoustic treatment and its own power feed. Access is limited to the analysts and to the terrace's senior technicians. Recordings are catalogued, cross-checked against known traffic and set aside when they cannot be explained. The set-aside catalogue is longer than it was, which the analysts state in their reporting without offering any interpretation of it whatsoever.

Future Orbital Planning Office.description: Republic, Contair, Corsair and civic specialists study what an eventual official capitol-to-orbit connection would require, in models, cost projections and structural assessments. Nothing has been approved or built. The office is deliberately clear that it is planning, not constructing. The working space is a long room of model tables, structural assessments and projections pinned where everyone at the table can dispute them. Specialists attend from their own institutions and bring their own assumptions. Sessions are minuted and the minutes are available. The office states its own limits at the opening of every session, partly as discipline and partly because the number of people who arrive believing a decision has already been taken has not decreased in any cycle so far.

Skyline Service Platforms.description: Working platforms and gantries where maintenance crews keep the district's structures, arrays and lighting operational in wind and cold. Shifts are long and physically demanding. Most residents have never seen the platforms they depend on entirely. The platforms are open gratings and rails hung off the structure below the finished surfaces, reached by service lifts and ladders and stocked with equipment stores at intervals. Crews work in teams, tethered, through shifts timed to the Corelight's maintenance windows. Pay, hours and rest arrangements are the subject of a dispute the crews have raised repeatedly. The mess room at the top of the service lift has a view most of the district would pay for and a floor that has not been replaced in a very long time.

High Challenge Route.description: A legal endurance and flight course threading through the district's structures, timed and publicly ranked. Attempts draw spectators along the overlooks. A successful run is visible across much of Relstaris, which is most of the appeal. The route is marked by beacons and gates set through the district's spans, cleared with sky control before every attempt and closed to other traffic while a runner is on it. Entry is registered and charged. Times are posted publicly and disputed loudly. The course is legal, supervised and genuinely difficult, and the marshals who hold the gates have the authority to stop a run at any point, which they use more often than the rankings would suggest.

Solvraxis.name: Solvraxis
Solvraxis.basicInfo:
Solvraxis is House Castro's city on Nexara: white stone, dark star-glass, silver-blue light and violet accents, immaculately maintained and openly proud of it. It is smaller than Relstaris and smaller than Helvyra, and it has never tried to be either - selective and carefully kept rather than sprawling, with large open spaces where another city would have built. The hub is the city's public face, a run of walks, courts and gardens around the core transit interchange, where nobody carries a weapon and nobody finds that strange. Surfaces are pale and level underfoot, lighting is soft rather than bright and comes from the architecture instead of from signage, and the air above the walks is kept clear enough that residents drop out of it onto a court without anyone breaking stride. Most movement is personal flight; the Public Transit Rings carry anyone who would rather stay on the ground, and neither choice is remarked on. An ordinary day here is errands, meetings, students being collected, and long conversations in places built to hold them. Everything is observed socially rather than officially: people notice each other, remember, and mention it later. It is a haven and expects to be treated as one, which is less a rule than a set of manners a newcomer picks up within a day of arriving.

Work on offer here: Solvraxis — Counting on No One Armed (ask Neressa Valcoro).
Solvraxis.hiddenInfo: The hub's calm is genuine, but it is also an export. Solvraxis sells education, verification and trust to cities that cannot generate their own, and every polished walk is part of that argument. The most consequential room here is the smallest: The Veyth Notary, a thin-income premises belonging to a faded minor House with no district, no civic seat and no political weight beyond the authority of its seals. Its family archive is said to hold a contract a wealthy family would pay heavily to bury; which family, what it proves, how old it is and who else knows all remain unanswered, and the Veyths themselves are notaries rather than schemers. The hub keeps other loose ends in plain view. Nobody agrees what Corelight names. The Gravitic Gardens' gravitic character is never explained. Luminous Gatecourt's relationship to the Lunar Gate District is asserted by no one, despite the name. The Civic Peace Stations here are the city-core instance of a service that runs citywide, and how many others exist is not published. A visitor who mistakes the quiet for emptiness tends to discover that Solvraxis is socially observant long before it is forgiving.

Luminous Gatecourt.description: A bright public court of white stone under silver-blue light, wide enough that a crowd never feels like one. The paving is pale and seamless, seating runs in low stone benches around the edges, and the open air above it is unobstructed enough for someone to arrive from it without disrupting the people below. This is where people wait: students being collected, relatives comparing arrival times, newcomers turning a wrist interface until the city finally makes sense. Orientation happens here by accident as much as by design, because someone always ends up explaining something to a stranger. Waiting is comfortable and nobody moves anyone along. A resident who has agreed to meet here will usually name a bench rather than the court, since there are more of them than a newcomer expects.

City Core Walk.description: A prominent public walk through the city core, paved pale and kept immaculate. Civic frontages in white stone and dark star-glass run along it, the lighting is set into the architecture rather than hung above it, and the walk is wide enough for people to stop in the middle of it without becoming an obstacle. Residents use it for exactly what it looks like: walking, being seen, running into someone they meant to message. For a visitor it is usually where the weapon-free law stops being a rule and becomes obvious, because nobody here is carrying anything. Maintenance happens early and thoroughly, which is why nothing on it ever looks repaired. Conversations started here tend to move somewhere with seating, and everyone knows where the nearest somewhere is.

Starfall Promenade.description: A broad promenade given over to unhurried social life, with violet light strung along its edges once the daylight goes. It is open along its length, with planted margins, room to walk several abreast, and enough seating that a group can settle without arranging anything in advance. Friends meet here without a plan, families take the long way home, and conversations run past the point anyone intended. Nothing about it is scheduled, which is rather the point. The mood shifts through the day from crossing traffic to lingering, and the lighting change is what marks the turn. People arrive from the air and from the ground in roughly equal numbers. The stone at the edges of the seating is worn smooth in the places everybody sits, and polished everywhere else.

Gravitic Gardens.description: Public gardens the city calls gravitic, a description offered without explanation and rarely questioned. What visitors actually find is planting, low terraces and quiet: students revising on the grass, elderly residents with favoured benches, children sent outside to burn off an afternoon. The terraces step gently, the paths between them are wide and even, and the planting is dense enough to soften voices without hiding anybody. Refinement here is simply pleasant. Gardeners work the beds through the day and are used to being asked what the name means; the answers they give vary, and none of them is authoritative. Nothing about the gardens asks visitors to behave in any particular way, and they are used as heavily on an ordinary afternoon as on any other.

Still Court.description: A small civic court kept deliberately quiet, with stone seating and shallow water at its centre. The water is a hand's depth and unmoving, the seating faces it rather than the entrances, and the court is small enough that arriving is a noticeable act. People come here to say something carefully, or to sit after news they were not ready for. It offers no privacy and claims none; voices carry as they would anywhere. What it offers is permission to take a while about it. Nobody hurries anybody here, and someone already seated will move along a bench without being asked. The water is skimmed and cleared each morning, which is the only maintenance the court visibly needs.

Corelight Walk.description: Another of the hub's public walks, running between civic frontages under the same steady silver-blue lighting. It is pale stone underfoot, level and well kept, with the same unhurried width as the city's other walks and the same soft light worked into the buildings along it. Ordinary use: errands, commutes on foot, a conversation that needed somewhere to go. People cut through it at every hour and nobody treats it as a destination. Ask a resident what Corelight actually names and the answer varies from one person to the next, because the city has never settled it. The question surfaces most often when a visitor asks it, and locals enjoy the disagreement more than they would enjoy an answer.

Public Transit Rings.description: The city-core interchange for Solvraxis's local circulation loops: enclosed cabins on fixed public routes, boarding from a clean, well-lit concourse. The concourse is white stone and dark star-glass like everything around it, with level boarding, clear signage and space to stand with luggage without blocking anyone. Children still learning to fly, elderly and injured residents, student groups, anyone carrying luggage, and anyone who simply prefers the ground. Confident fliers skip it, and neither choice draws comment. Cabins arrive, fill and leave without ceremony, and staff on the concourse answer questions all day for people who have not used it before. It is an easy connection point rather than a technical hub, and it is deliberately built to be understood at a glance.

Civic Peace Stations.description: The hub's civic protection presence, open-fronted and staffed rather than fortified. The frontage is literally open: a counter, seating, good light, and nothing between the street and the people working it. This is where a lost child is brought, where directions get asked for, where someone reports that something felt wrong. There is no armed presence because there are no arms; the calm is the service. Staff talk people down, walk them somewhere, or make the call that connects them to whoever they actually need. Most of the work is small and none of it is dramatic. Stations like it exist across the city, and a resident can generally say where the nearest one is without thinking about it.

The Veyth Notary.description: A narrow notarial premises with a worn counter, a rack of seal stock and lighting that has not changed in decades. The room is one deep space with the counter running most of its length, ledgers and reference material shelved behind, and a single chair for anyone waiting. Seals, appraisals, certified copies, witnessed signatures: constant, unglamorous work for a House that is faded rather than powerful. Malkor Veyth or one of his relatives will take a customer's document without hurrying, read it properly, and say plainly what can and cannot be certified. The work is precise and the income is thin, and the premises look exactly like that. The counter is worn deepest at the spot where documents are set down to be signed.

Castro Citadel.name: Castro Citadel
Castro Citadel.basicInfo: House Castro's protected seat in Solvraxis: star-glass halls, a family council chamber, private training courts and terraces open to the air. The building is white stone and dark star-glass like the city around it, older than most of what surrounds it and maintained rather than restored, and it is impressive without announcing anything about rank. There is no gate and no checkpoint. The approach rises to a threshold, visitors walk up, and someone notices them. This is where Castro authority actually lives, as family authority exercised by elders and argued over at a table. Inside, the halls are large, quiet and well lit, with footsteps carrying far enough that nobody arrives unannounced. The household runs ordinary days: guests received, correspondence answered, training worked through in an enclosed court, family members passing one another on stairs and stopping to talk. Elders set the tone and younger members are expected to listen longer than they would like, which holds until somebody disrupts it and everyone is relieved. Formal but not royal, and at some effort not a palace: nothing here is a throne, and the family works at keeping it that way.
Castro Citadel.hiddenInfo: Nothing here is sovereign, deliberately, but the Citadel still holds more than it shows. Darkstar Castro's Solvraxis seat is a seat and not a residence: he lives at the Relstaris Citadel as Core Holder and returns regularly, and the household does not advertise how often the room is used. The Protected Family Archives keep records the family did not lodge with Ravello Archive House, and the division of archival responsibility between the two has never been written down, so pre-Darkstar politics and Relstaris Core history both surface there in fragments. In the private training court, Castro movement is worked without an audience, and what is practised there that Valcoro Academy does not teach publicly is implied rather than defined. Vega Castro receives delegations in his own chamber while holding no exclusive citywide diplomatic authority. Most visitors experience none of this directly. What they get is the approach, a wait, and a courteous sense of having been assessed by people who never said so.

Castro Citadel Approach.description: The open approach to House Castro's Solvraxis seat, a rise of white stone that reads as a threshold rather than a gate. It is broad, shallow-stepped and entirely open, with no barrier across it and nothing built to funnel anyone, so the act of arriving is simply the act of walking up. There is no checkpoint and no barrier; arriving is largely a matter of walking up and being noticed. People arrive from the air as readily as from the ground and land short of the rise out of habit rather than instruction. Visitors are sometimes left to wait here, which is a message delivered very politely. The stone is swept early and the sweeping is the only routine anybody performs on it.

Star-Glass Entry Hall.description: The formal receiving hall, walled in dark Solvraxis star-glass that takes the daylight and gives back something deeper. The hall is tall and largely empty, with seating set well back from the centre and a floor of pale stone that makes the walls read darker still. Guests are met here and the family's restraint registers immediately: the room is unmistakably powerful and announces no rank at all. There are no banners, no displayed honours and nothing indicating who ranks where. Footsteps carry, so nobody arrives unannounced. Household staff meet arrivals at the threshold and take them onward at a walking pace. Delegations who expected a show of force tend to spend their first minute here looking for one.

Family Council Chamber.description: A ringed chamber where the Castros decide things together, around a council table rather than beneath a throne. The seating runs continuous around the table with no head to it, the light is even, and nothing in the room's arrangement tells a visitor who holds the most weight. Elders argue, younger members are expected to listen longer than they want to, and authority here is family authority rather than sovereignty. Sessions run long, break for food, and resume. Disagreement is normal and open, and a decision is reached rather than announced. It is also where formality most reliably collapses once Nina is in the room. The table surface carries generations of small marks, and nobody has ever suggested resurfacing it.

Darkstar's Solvraxis Seat.description: Darkstar Castro's seat in the city, which is his place here and not his home. He resides at the Relstaris Citadel as Core Holder and returns to Solvraxis regularly, and how often the room is occupied is not something the household advertises. The room itself is restrained: a working chamber, well lit, with seating for a small number of people and none of the display a visitor might expect. It is kept ready either way, with the particular quiet of a space that expects him. Staff maintain it on the same rhythm whether or not he is in the city, and they answer questions about his movements pleasantly and without content. Anyone shown in here is being told something by the choice of room.

Vega's Diplomatic Chamber.description: Where Vega Castro conducts diplomatic business and formal meetings in Solvraxis: a working chamber with seating arranged for conversation rather than audience. Chairs face each other across a low table, the light is soft and even, and there is no raised position anywhere in the room. Delegations are received on Castro terms, which means courteously and without theatre. Meetings start on time, refreshment is offered as a matter of course, and the pacing is deliberately unhurried. The room carries no exclusive citywide authority; the man's attention is what people come for. Notes are taken by whoever needs them rather than by an attending secretary, and a session that ends without agreement ends just as politely as one that does not.

Castro Private Training Court.description: An enclosed court where Castro movement is practised without an audience, distinct from anything Valcoro Academy teaches in public. It is a plain space with a worked floor, clear air above it and walls high enough to close it off entirely, with nothing in it but the surface and the room to use it. The floor shows use. Sessions are held between family members and whoever is invited, and the invitation is the whole of the access arrangement. Exactly what is worked here that is not taught downhill in the city is never explained to guests, and the difference is easier to feel than to be told. The court is swept and checked after use like any other training floor, which is the most ordinary thing about it.

Protected Family Archives.description: The family's own protected archive: sealed cases, controlled light, and records the Castros keep rather than lodge with Ravello Archive House. The room is cool and dim by design, the cases are set in ranks with reading positions between them, and the light comes up only where someone is working. How the two archives divide responsibility has never been set down. Pre-Darkstar politics and Relstaris Core history both leave traces here, in documents nobody offers a visitor unprompted. Family members consult it themselves rather than through a keeper. Requests from outside are heard courteously and usually answered with a suggestion to try elsewhere, which is not quite a refusal and is never quite anything else.

North Terrace Overlook.description: A terrace off the Citadel's upper level, used for the conversations that do not belong in a chamber. Star-glass rail, open air, and a view across part of Solvraxis. It is narrow, unfurnished except for a bench or two, and quiet in the particular way an outdoor space is quiet when the building behind it is not. Elders bring people up here when something needs saying gently, and a student brought up here usually works out they are not in trouble yet. Conversations run at half volume because the space invites it rather than because anything requires it. People lean on the rail and look outward while talking, which makes the difficult parts easier to say.

Valcoro Academy.name: Valcoro Academy
Valcoro Academy.basicInfo: House Valcoro's academy for civic defense, Castro-style movement, non-weapon defense, composure and the ethics of force, taught to students who mostly live out in the city's wards. Training floors, open courts, lecture halls and a scheduling desk in permanent crisis. The grounds are white stone and clear space, built so that a court with open air above it sits a short walk from a hall where people are arguing about when force is justified, and the academy considers those two rooms to be teaching the same subject. Days run on a timetable that is contested from the moment it is posted: halls booked twice, rotations shuffled, visiting examiners arriving on an afternoon that was supposed to be free. Students are corrected in front of each other as a matter of course and recover from it quickly, because everybody's turn arrives. Instructors watch from a balcony above the floors and decide more with a look than they ever say out loud. Beginners start on padding and are told plainly that mistakes are ordinary. The House line is control before force, and the academy is organized to make that true under pressure rather than merely to state it. Disciplined and bright, and considerably funnier than its reputation suggests.
Valcoro Academy.hiddenInfo: The motto, control before force, is a curriculum rather than a slogan, and the academy's real subject is what a person trained to fight owes a city that outlaws weapons. Two things inside it stay unresolved. The Sealed Training Garden is sealed: what is inside, why, by whom, since when, who may enter and what students are told are all deliberately unanswered, and the confident theories circulating in the dormitories are evidence of nothing. And Marcon Valcoro assigned Marea Valcoro her first student group a full year early, on purpose; she has not worked out why and he has not said. Around those, ordinary academy life continues. Tavian Valcoro is always one scheduling crisis behind. Ilaria certifies who may teach the public shape of Castro-adjacent forms. Lioren is patient with students and merciless with parents who push children into flight too early. Instructors settle a term with a glance from the observation balcony. Valcoro sells training and certification that other cities respect, which means its judgements travel considerably further than its students realise.

Main Training Floor.description: The academy's principal training space: a broad sprung floor with movement markers set into it and equipment racked along one wall. The floor gives underfoot in a way that is audible across the room, the markers are inlaid rather than painted, and the light is even enough that nothing casts a confusing shadow. Non-weapon defense and movement drill run here all day, and students are corrected in front of each other as a matter of course. Groups work in sets across the floor while an instructor moves between them, stopping a pair, resetting them and moving on. Nobody stays embarrassed long, because everybody's turn arrives. Water and spare bands live at the rack end, and the floor is wiped down between rotations by whoever finished last.

Open Movement Court.description: An open court with clear air above it, where flight and ground technique are worked together instead of separately. The court is walled to about shoulder height and open the whole way up, with a marked working surface below and nothing overhead to catch anyone who misjudges a descent. Instructors call corrections upward; students land harder than they meant to and pretend otherwise. Drills alternate between the air and the floor so that neither is practised as a separate skill, which is the whole point of the court's design. Training bands catch the light in a way that makes an ordinary drill look briefly choreographed. Sessions end with everyone on the ground and slightly out of breath, and the next group is usually already waiting at the edge.

Composure Halls.description: A run of quiet halls where composure is taught as a trained skill rather than treated as a temperament. The halls are plain, acoustically dead and deliberately unremarkable, with enough space for a group to work without crowding and nothing on the walls to look at. Students are put under pressure on purpose, with noise, provocation and humiliation they can see coming, and drilled until control holds regardless. Knowing what is coming is part of the method and does not make it easier. Instructors escalate carefully, stop cleanly, and talk students through what happened afterwards. Control before force is the House line, and this is the room that has to make it true. Students leave these sessions quieter than they arrive, and the quiet does not last past the corridor.

Civic Ethics Lecture Hall.description: Tiered seating, a speaking floor, and arguments about the justification of force conducted out loud. The hall is bright rather than dim, the tiers are shallow enough that a student in the back row is still in the conversation, and the speaking floor has no lectern to hide behind. Students debate what a weapon-free city asks of people trained to fight, and where the public limits of Castro-style combat sit. Positions are taken, defended and abandoned in the same session, and a student who changes their mind aloud is treated as having done the assignment properly. Instructors rarely settle it; a lecture that ends in agreement is treated as a wasted hour. The arguments continue out of the door and into whatever anyone does next.

Beginner Training Court.description: The smaller court where new students start: padding underfoot, slow drills, and an explicit understanding that beginner mistakes are ordinary rather than shameful. It is enclosed and modest in size, with everything softened at the edges and a floor that forgives a bad landing. Drills are broken down further than they need to be and repeated until they are dull, which is the intention. Lioren Valcoro's first-flight groups pass through here, and the comedy is dependable, because confidence tends to arrive several weeks ahead of competence. Older students drift past the entrance to watch and are moved on. The padding is replaced section by section as it wears, so the floor is always a patchwork of slightly different shades.

Schedule Desk Corridor.description: A long corridor built around the scheduling desk and its permanently contested slate of hall bookings, student rotations and visiting examiners. The corridor is wide enough to queue in and lined with benches nobody sits on for long, and the desk itself carries the current slate on a display that changes several times an hour. Tavian Valcoro works here, one crisis behind and unfailingly polite about it. Students queue to negotiate; staff arrive to renegotiate whatever the students just changed. Conversations overlap, and a good deal of the academy's actual information moves through the queue rather than the desk. A hall freed at short notice is claimed within minutes, usually by whoever happened to be standing there.

Sealed Training Garden.description: A garden inside the academy grounds, sealed. Planting is visible past the seal and that is the limit of what anyone can confirm: what is inside, why it was closed, by whom and since when are not answered by the academy. The seal itself is unremarkable to look at, neither fortified nor hidden, and it is simply there in a place where a way through would otherwise be. Student theories are numerous, confident and mutually contradictory, and none of them count as evidence. Staff asked about it answer briefly and move the conversation on, which students read as significant and which may be nothing more than staff having answered the same question many times. The planting past the seal is green and unremarkable, and it is clearly being maintained by somebody.

Instructor Observation Balcony.description: A balcony set above the training floors where instructors watch and assess. It runs along one side at a height that takes in a whole floor at once, with a rail to lean on and no seating, because nobody is up there long enough to sit. Marcon, Ilaria and Neressa turn up here between sessions, and a look exchanged across the rail decides more about a student's term than most of them realise. Conversations up here are brief and specific, and they end when one of them goes back down to the floor. Whether the students below know they are being watched is never made explicit. The rail is polished dull along the stretch that gives the best view of the main floor.

Ravello Archive House.name: Ravello Archive House
Ravello Archive House.basicInfo:
House Ravello's archive: public records, lineage research, record integrity and the city's cultural memory, kept openly rather than hoarded. A bright atrium, reading steps used for public history lessons, a genealogy hall and a cafe where a fair share of the day's real conversations happen. The building is white stone and high light, arranged so that the public parts come first and the working parts follow, and a visitor with no appointment can get a long way into it before anyone asks what they want. Request desks take records enquiries all day; comparison benches check documents against alteration; lineage registers are read at lecterns by people finding out who they came from. School groups sit on the steps outside the reading rooms and are taught history in the open, which the House regards as its entire argument rather than as outreach. Staff are precise, unhurried and hard to rush. What is refused is refused courteously and without explanation, and there are sealed vaults beneath the public floors that no catalogue mentions. Still, precise, and more socially powerful than it looks: a city that exports verification and trust keeps its memory here, and everyone knows it.

Work on offer here: Solvraxis — The Misfiled Box; Study — The Agreement Nobody Can Find (ask Nessa Ravello).
Ravello Archive House.hiddenInfo: Ravello's position is that peace depends on accurate memory, which makes an archive a civic power rather than a storeroom. That power is contested quietly. Families ask for lines to be removed, records turn up altered, and Maereth Ravello answers every question with a document and every document with a caution, while Eloria argues permanently that access and not preservation is what memory is for. Below the public floors, the Sealed Record Vaults hold old house agreements nobody will itemise; what was altered, who sealed it and who may open it go unanswered. Nessa Ravello keeps finding material the catalogue says does not exist, and Maereth keeps declining to notice how often the difficult requests reach her desk. Veylan's restoration shelf still holds items whose owners never came back. The House handles record integrity and alteration; House Veyth handles notarial work, seals and appraisal from its small premises in the hub. No hierarchy between them is established in either direction, and neither answers to the other.

Public Archive Atrium.description: The archive's bright public face: a tall atrium in white stone, request desks down one side, catalogues reachable from any civic band. The light comes from high above and falls evenly, the floor is pale and quiet underfoot, and the sound of the room is a steady low murmur that never resolves into anything. Scholars and ordinary citizens use it in roughly equal measure, for a records request, a half-remembered name, or a school group being told again not to run. Desk staff take enquiries in the order they arrive and ask the clarifying questions that turn a vague memory into a searchable request. Most archive visits begin here, and a fair number end here too, satisfactorily, within a quarter of an hour.

Chief Archive Steward Chamber.description: Maereth Ravello's chamber, where the hard questions land once the public desks have failed to settle them: a disputed record, a request that ought not be granted, a family who want a line removed. The room is small, well lit and arranged for two people to talk across a table, with shelved reference material behind and nothing decorative anywhere. She answers with a document and then qualifies the document. Appointments are made rather than walked into, and they run as long as they need to. Few people leave with exactly what they came for, and most leave better informed than they wanted to be. The chair on the visitor's side is comfortable, which is a deliberate courtesy and does not change the outcome.

Lineage Records Alcove.description: A recessed alcove of lineage registers, reading lecterns and Sovian Ravello's meticulous cross-references. It is set back from the main floor, quiet, with the registers shelved within reach of the lecterns and light angled down onto the reading surface. People come to find out who they came from, which is usually unremarkable and occasionally not. Most enquiries resolve into a line of names and dates that confirm what the family already said. The cross-references are what make the alcove useful, and they are the work of one person keeping them current. The alcove is small enough that anyone receiving an unwelcome answer has nowhere discreet to put their face, and the staff have learned to look elsewhere when it happens.

Record Integrity Station.description: Benches of comparison equipment where documents are checked against alteration: ink, substrate, seal, hand, and the places where a record has been made to agree with itself. The benches are lit from several angles, the equipment sits within reach at each position, and a document under examination stays flat and untouched while the instruments do the work. Ravello's concern is whether the city's memory is intact. Most of what comes through is sound, and saying so is most of the output. A finding of alteration is written up carefully and passed onward rather than announced. House Veyth's notarial work sits beside it without either House answering to the other, and the two questions are kept clearly apart by the people who do both.

Public History Lesson Steps.description: Shallow stone steps outside the reading rooms, used for open history lessons. They are broad and generous, comfortable to sit on for an hour, and placed where anyone passing can hear what is being said without having to commit to staying. School groups sit in rows, civic classes take the upper steps, and passers-by stop for as long as the subject holds them. Questions come from the steps as often as from the class, and the teaching adjusts to take them. Teaching history in the open rather than behind a request form is, for House Ravello, the entire argument. When no lesson is running the steps are simply somewhere to sit, and they are used that way constantly.

Archive Cafe.description: The archive's cafe: a quiet brewing counter, conversation tables sized for a drink and personal notes, paired window seats and a shelf that keeps bags clear of any spill. The room is warm without being ornamental, with clean-lined furniture and soft light, and it is quiet enough that two people can talk without either of them raising their voice. Cyrra in several preparations, crisp Terva, thin-sliced Korrin. Portions are meant to satisfy real hunger, and a customer who only wants a drink gets the same courtesy as one ordering food. Any research material carried in follows the archive's own handling rules, which the cafe does not relax. Staff notice a cold cup that has been stared at too long and bring fresh water without asking why.

Sealed Record Vaults.description: Sealed vaults beneath the public floors, closed under Ravello authority. They are below the working levels, reached by ways that are not signposted, and the seals are solid, plain and obviously maintained. What is held there, which old house agreements it covers and what was altered appear on no public catalogue, and asking produces a courteous non-answer. The non-answer is consistent enough that it is clearly a policy rather than an evasion by any individual. Staff who know the procedure do not discuss it and staff who do not are genuinely unable to help. The mystery here is document-shaped and quiet; this is an archive, not a conspiracy headquarters, and the vaults sit under a building that spends its days teaching children.

Genealogy Display Hall.description: A long hall where the city's lineages are displayed rather than filed: branching illuminated charts, house lines, names a visitor may recognise as their own. The charts run the length of the walls at a height that can be read while walking, lit from within so the branching carries, with the older lines given no more prominence than the newer ones. Civic pride in its plainest form. Residents bring visiting relatives through it, and children look for their own surname before anything else. It is also occasionally uncomfortable, because a family line shown accurately is not always the version that family tells. Corrections are requested at the desk and handled as a records matter, slowly and on evidence.

Bellovari Market District.name: Bellovari Market District
Bellovari Market District.basicInfo:
House Bellovari's district of markets, galleries, pubs, workshops and festival courts, the liveliest non-Castro place in Solvraxis and the city's public warmth made concrete. Star-glass ornaments, Mirrorwater shards, music on the performance steps, Liora Bellovari's pub and a restaurant that refuses to hurry dinner. The district is built of the same white stone and dark star-glass as the rest of the city and is simply busier with it: stalls under light canopies, a balcony running above the market floor, a workshop where heat and careful hands turn star-glass into ornaments, a vendor court laid out with anchor points for festival ribbons. Trade here is selective and unshouted, which visitors from trade cities find strange and then restful. Goods are checked before they reach the stalls, and the weapon-free law arrives at that check as ordinary procedure rather than as security. Errands and rumour move together, so a purchase takes longer than it needs to. Evenings run on music, exhibitions, shared tables and stories everybody has already heard. Polished, social, and not stiff about it: the district is the argument that peace has to be lived rather than stored.

Work on offer here: Solvraxis — Who Left Whom (ask Viaro Bellovari); Trade — Star-Glass for the Hundred-House Market (ask Darian Bellovari).
Bellovari Market District.hiddenInfo: Bellovari runs the markets and cultural commerce, which means it also runs the city's rumour traffic. A purchase at Starfall Market takes twice as long as it should because of who you meet, and that is the mechanism rather than a side effect. Two pressure points sit in the district. Darian Bellovari's Cargo-Check Station is where the weapon-free law meets imported goods as routine procedure, and a shipment problem here becomes a social embarrassment long before it becomes a civic matter; anyone trying to exploit the law would first have to get past a man who knows every courier by name. And the Corsair Housefront is the careful outsider presence Solvraxis permits, selling travel goods under city rules, deferring to local law, with no named Corsair staff and no claim to being an enclave. Visitor friction is the recurring hook. Elsewhere the district leaves its coincidences unexplained: the Performance Steps share a name with the hub's Starfall Promenade, and the Gallery Salon shares its motif with Mirrorwater Commons in the wards. Canon connects neither pair.

Starfall Market.description: The district's public market: polished stalls under light canopies, selective goods, and none of the shouting a trade city would bring. The stalls stand in ordered runs with clear space between them, the canopies throw a soft light down onto the goods, and the whole floor stays quiet enough for two people to talk across a table of wares. Errands and rumour move together here, so a purchase takes twice as long as it needs to because of everyone met on the way. Traders know their regulars, ask after families, and finish the transaction somewhere in the middle of the conversation. Bellovari commerce is social business first. Stallholders set out and pack down on their own rhythm, and the floor is swept clean between one day and the next.

Market Patron Balcony.description: A balcony running above the market floor, kept for patrons and for anyone content to watch the district work. It runs the length of one side at a height that takes in the whole floor, with a rail, comfortable seating set back from it and enough distance that the market below arrives as a pleasant murmur. Conversations happen up here that the noise below never reaches. Arrangements get made, apprentices get discussed, and a commission is as likely to begin at this rail as in any gallery. Being seen to choose the balcony over the stalls says something in Solvraxis, and the people who choose it generally know precisely what. Refreshment is brought up without being ordered, by staff who have learned who takes what.

Mirrorwater Gallery Salon.description: House Bellovari's art salon: hung work, reflective glass panels, and apprentices hovering near their own pieces while trying not to. The rooms are hung sparely with plenty of wall between works, the reflective panels throw light back across the space, and the seating is arranged so that people talking are still facing the art. Exhibition evenings are as much about taste performed as art shown. Visitors circulate, opinions are offered carefully, and an apprentice's first shown piece is the evening's real event whether or not anybody says so. On ordinary days the salon is quiet and open, and people come in on their way somewhere else. It shares the Mirrorwater motif with a residential commons across the city, and no connection between them is claimed.

Silver Cup Pub.description: Liora Bellovari's pub, lived in through favoured seats and familiar voices: a public counter, small tables, a longer friends' table and a modest performance corner. The room is warm and unfussy, with enough light to read a face across a table, and a staff member collecting empty cups before anybody asks. Kessar drinks beside Cyrra and ingredient-described alternatives, with crisp Terva and dried Nalki for a light supper. Market workers, gallery visitors, off-duty instructors and relatives dropping in after errands make up most evenings. Liora keeps the room, hears a great deal and repeats very little. Most evenings the loudest sound is a story everyone already knows, told again for somebody who has not heard it.

Cargo-Check Station.description: Where incoming goods are checked before they reach the stalls. It is a working bay with unloading space, inspection benches and a manifest station, kept as clean as the market floor because the same district maintains both. Darian Bellovari runs it and knows every courier by name, which is why the weapon-free law lands here as ordinary procedure rather than security theatre. Manifests are read against loads, questions are asked conversationally, and a discrepancy is resolved with the courier rather than over their head. A shipment that fails a check becomes a social embarrassment well before it becomes a civic problem. Couriers wait with their loads and are offered somewhere to sit, which most of them take.

Starfall Promenade Performance Steps.description: Broad tiered steps given over to music and street performance, with room for a crowd that assembles by accident. The steps are shallow and generous, facing a level space at their foot where a performer can work, and they hold an audience comfortably without anyone having to be seated or ticketed. Galen Bellovari can make three minutes on these steps feel like an occasion, and generally does. Between performances people sit on them to eat, wait or talk, and a musician setting up draws a crowd out of that. Nothing is scheduled and nothing is announced. The name echoes the hub's Starfall Promenade; whether the steps stand on it is not something canon states.

Star-Glass Workshop.description: The workshop where star-glass is worked into Bellovari ornaments and gallery shards. It is hot, bright at the working positions and dim between them, with benches set around the heat, finished pieces racked well away from the traffic and a door left open onto the district for anyone who wants to watch. Heat, careful hands, and apprentices who are allowed to ruin a piece long before they are allowed to finish one. Ruined work goes into a bin without comment and the apprentice starts again. Masters talk through what they are doing while they do it, which is the whole of the teaching method. How the material is made and where it comes from, the craft does not explain to anyone watching from the door.

Festival Vendor Court.description: A wide vendor court laid out for celebration: anchor points overhead for light ribbons, stall footings set into the paving, and space enough for the district at its warmest. The paving is pale and level, the footings sit flush when nothing is set into them, and the anchor points overhead are easy to miss until the ribbons are up. Between festivals it is simply a court that vendors use, and it is used most days by somebody. When a festival runs, the court fills with light, food, music and the whole district at once. Solvraxis festivals are elegant and still end with somebody's children badly overtired, being carried home past stalls that are already packing down.

Corsair Housefront.description: The Corsair presence Solvraxis permits: a modest frontage selling travel goods and imports carefully, under city rules rather than beside them. It is one shopfront among the district's others, with goods displayed in the window, a counter inside and no more space behind it than any comparable business has. Outsider etiquette gets tested here more often than anywhere else in the district, because the people who come through it are the most likely to have arrived from somewhere with different manners. Purchases are ordinary, questions about where something came from are answered vaguely and cheerfully, and the weapon-free law applies to the stock exactly as it applies to everything else. It is a shopfront rather than an enclave, and it defers to Solvraxis law without argument.

The Unhurried Table.description: A restaurant off the market, where the crowd outside carries in as a comfortable murmur. A small welcome vestibule, a dining room spaced so a family can be loud in private, an open finishing counter and a quieter alcove. The spacing is the room's whole design principle, and it is why a table can be animated without the rest of the room joining in. Selka-braised Korrin, seared Nalki with chilled Neris, Cyrra to close. The finishing counter is open to the room so diners can watch food leave the kitchen without standing in the staff's way. Walk-ins and reservations both work, and a quiet table is available to anyone rather than reserved for anyone in particular. Lunch is moderate; the evening meal takes longer and costs more because it is meant to.

Orvessa Welfare District.name: Orvessa Welfare District
Orvessa Welfare District.basicInfo:
House Orvessa's district of welfare halls, clinics, counselling alcoves, schoolrooms and a guesthouse for new arrivals. Care is offered here plainly, without ceremony and without turning anybody into a case. The buildings are the city's usual white stone and soft light, arranged low and open with short queues, provided chairs, wide doors and nothing anywhere that looks clinical unless it has to. A welfare hall takes a request without making anyone explain themselves twice. A clinic recovery room keeps its monitoring out of the patient's eyeline. A counselling alcove is small enough that using it implies nothing. Supplies for shelters are counted and rotated on ordinary days by people who will carry too many of them at once. Schoolrooms teach the residential side of the city and field the questions children ask about why nobody carries weapons. Newcomers are met at the Gate district and housed here while the city stops being confusing. It is the warmest district in Solvraxis and the one that best explains what the city thinks protection actually means: not only stopping danger, but being there afterwards, plainly, for as long as it takes.

Work on offer here: Solvraxis — The Reserve Count (ask Renzo Orvessa).
Orvessa Welfare District.hiddenInfo: Orvessa's argument is that safety is proven after fear ends, and the district is built to make that literally true: the recovery court, the counselling alcove and the clinic all exist for the scene that comes after the danger rather than during it. In practice the House also works as the city's early warning system. Families arriving at the support counters bring problems Solvraxis would otherwise never see, and the schoolroom's children ask the questions their parents have learned to leave alone. The Lunar Gate Guesthouse pairs with Calessa Orvessa's reception desk over in the Gate district, so House Orvessa is both the first Solvraxis institution most visitors deal with and the one that houses them afterwards, which makes it unusually well informed about who has just arrived and why. Jovian Orvessa's habit of carrying too many supplies at once is a running joke covering a genuinely well-stocked shelter system. The counts of clinics, schoolrooms and shelter points across the city are not published anywhere.

Civilian Welfare Hall.description: The district's main welfare hall: open, unceremonious, staffed by people who never make anyone explain themselves twice. The room is wide and softly lit, with a run of staffed positions, seating that is actually comfortable and enough space between people that a conversation stays where it is held. Support is arranged the way anything civic is arranged in Solvraxis, plainly and without turning the applicant into a subject. Requests are heard, matched to what exists, and arranged while the person is still in the room wherever that is possible. Staff bring water without being asked. Being unremarkable is the whole of the design intention here, and residents treat coming in as no more significant than any other errand.

Public Clinic Recovery Room.description: A recovery room in the district's public clinic: soft light, low beds, monitoring kept out of the patient's eyeline. The equipment is present and deliberately unemphasised, set behind and above rather than in view, and the room is warm, quiet and arranged so that a visitor can sit close without anyone having to move anything. Care rather than medical machinery. Staff check in often and without fuss, and they let a patient sleep. This is where the conversations after the danger happen, which Solvraxis treats as part of the treatment rather than as something that comes afterwards. Visitors are not limited to fixed hours, and people who simply sit with someone in silence are left to do it.

Lunar Gate Guesthouse.description: House Orvessa's guesthouse for arrivals, where a newcomer stays while they work out how the city fits together. Simple rooms, a communal breakfast, staff who will explain something twice without condescension. The rooms are plain, clean and quiet, the communal table is large enough that nobody eats alone unless they want to, and the whole place is arranged around the assumption that its guests are temporarily lost. Questions about customs, transit, law and where to buy anything are answered at any hour by whoever is on. Orvessa meets visitors at the Gate district reception and houses them here; both ends of that arrangement are deliberate. Guests leave when they are ready, and a fair number come back to say so.

Emergency Shelter Supply Room.description: Shelter stock kept counted, rotated and ready: supply packs, bedding, water, civic lighting. The room is shelved to the ceiling in labelled runs with a working aisle down the middle and a check sheet at the door, and everything in it has a date on it and a place it belongs. On any ordinary day the work is inventory: counting, rotating stock toward its use-by, restacking what the last check disturbed. Jovian Orvessa can reliably be found carrying more of it at once than is sensible, and the resulting logistics comedy is a district fixture nobody has yet managed to prevent. The stock is genuinely ready, which is the point of all the counting, and the drills that use it run without drama.

Quiet Counseling Alcove.description: A small alcove with two chairs, a screen that closes, and nothing in it that looks clinical. The chairs face each other at a comfortable angle rather than across a desk, the light is low and warm, and the screen closes the alcove off from the corridor without sealing it. Emotional recovery is handled here as ordinary care rather than as intervention, with no referral drama and no ceremony. Sessions are arranged easily and end when they end. The modesty is the point: a person can use it without anyone concluding something has gone badly wrong, and people do use it for things that are genuinely small. There is water on the side table and nothing else at all.

Residential Schoolroom.description: A schoolroom serving the residential side of the city: low tables, pale blue classroom-light clips on every slate, and children who still ask the questions adults have stopped asking. The room is bright and cheerfully untidy, with work pinned up wherever there is space and the tables arranged in groups rather than rows. Teachers field the awkward ones, like why nobody carries weapons and what happens if somebody does. The answers given are honest and age-appropriate, and the follow-up questions are harder than the first ones. Lessons run through the ordinary subjects and out into whatever the class has decided to be interested in. How many such rooms the city has is unrecorded.

Family Support Counters.description: A row of counters where families arrange the practical end of welfare: assistance, school support, housing help, the conversation that turns a difficulty into something the city can act on. The counters are low enough to talk across while seated, spaced so conversations do not overlap, and staffed by people who know which help actually solves which problem. Queues are short and chairs are provided. Children come along and are given something to do. Cases are opened, arranged and closed at the counter wherever possible rather than referred onward. This is where a private problem becomes visible without becoming a public one, and the staff handle that distinction carefully every single day.

Soft Seating Recovery Court.description: A courtyard of deep seating and filtered light, the gentlest space in the district and the clearest statement of what House Orvessa exists for. The seating is genuinely soft and set in small groupings rather than rows, planting filters the light across the court, and the whole space is arranged so that sitting for a long time is comfortable rather than merely possible. People sit here once fear has ended, often beside someone who does not need them to talk about it. Staff pass through without checking on anyone. Safety is proven after fear ends, and this is where the House demonstrates it - not by saying anything, but by having built somewhere to sit afterwards.

Lunar Gate District.name: Lunar Gate District
Lunar Gate District.basicInfo: Solvraxis's arrival district: three Lunar Gate platforms serving Relstaris, Korrvane and Helvyra, an orientation hall, a calm waiting court and a peace line where weapons are screened. The platforms sit under white stone and dark star-glass with silver-blue light, generously spaced, and nothing about the district is built to hurry anyone through it. Arrivals step off a Gate, clear a screening line run as hospitality rather than inspection, and are oriented before they go further: city customs, what is socially expected, and the weapons law explained as civic trust. Anyone who would rather not take unfamiliar aerial lanes is pointed toward the Public Transit Rings, which is an ordinary suggestion rather than a concession. House Orvessa keeps a reception desk here and houses guests at its own guesthouse, so a newcomer is met by the same family at both ends. Traffic is steady rather than heavy: Solvraxis is connected without ever having become a thoroughfare, and it uses the network carefully. Sensitive movement is handled quietly at the district's far end. Clean, selective and unhurried, watchful without feeling oppressive. Most visitors form their impression of the whole city here, in about twenty minutes.
Lunar Gate District.hiddenInfo: Solvraxis connects to three cities and no more, which is a standing choice about what the city wants arriving. The district's work is largely social: arrivals are taught the weapons law as civic trust rather than confiscation before anyone has a chance to test it, and after orientation newcomers are pointed at the Public Transit Rings rather than sent straight into unfamiliar aerial lanes. That leaves Restricted Transit Control as the quiet end of the operation, where an arrival needing Castro or Valcoro representation is handled and where Dravon pressure at the city edge is absorbed before it becomes visible anywhere else. What makes a transit restricted, who authorises it and what the procedure involves are not posted and not explained. Secondary pressure accumulates here too: suspicious arrivals, visitors probing the weapon-free law for a loophole, cargo spillover that pulls Darian Bellovari down from the market, and Genesis students off the Korrvane platform who read Castro restraint as weakness and are corrected about it very politely.

Relstaris Gate Platform.description: The platform serving Relstaris, the capital connection and the most consequential civic business the district handles. It is a clean open platform under high light, with boarding space, seating set back from the arch and staff positions where they can be found without being conspicuous. Darkstar Castro resides at the Relstaris Citadel as Core Holder, which gives this arch a political weight the staff never mention aloud. Official parties, civic correspondence and ordinary travellers all use it, and the staff make no visible distinction between them. Departures are called calmly, and nobody is hurried onto a Gate. Anyone who misses a departure is simply put on the next one, which happens often enough that the procedure is entirely routine.

Korrvane Gate Platform.description: The Korrvane platform, where House Genesis arrivals step into a city that outlaws weapons. The platform itself is identical in build and light to the others, and the difference is entirely in who comes through it. The contrast does most of the work by itself: a culture built on public proving meeting one that considers proving largely unnecessary. Arrivals expecting to be challenged are instead greeted and offered directions, which lands differently on different people. Orientation staff are practised at explaining the difference without it sounding like a correction, and they do it several times a day. The prohibition applies to a blade bought anywhere else, and saying so politely at the start saves a longer conversation at the screening line.

Helvyra Gate Platform.description: The Helvyra platform, connecting Solvraxis to the movement and trade hub it uses carefully and selectively. It handles more freight interest than the other platforms and still does not feel like a freight platform: the same pale stone, the same unhurried spacing, goods handled in their own area away from the arriving passengers. Much of what the city does not make itself arrives through here or through Corsair routes. Merchants and couriers are regulars and are known to the staff by sight. Traffic is steady rather than heavy, because Solvraxis is connected without ever having become a thoroughfare. Travellers arriving from a busier city usually notice the quiet before they notice anything else about the district.

Arrival Orientation Hall.description: Where visitors are oriented before they go further: city customs, what is socially expected, and the weapons law explained as civic trust rather than confiscation. The hall is bright and open with seating in groups, staff who come to people rather than waiting to be approached, and displays that answer the ordinary questions so that staff time goes to the unusual ones. Guesthouse orientation cards are handed out here. The explanation is short, friendly and entirely unapologetic, and it covers what to do with something that cannot be brought in. Newcomers who would rather not take unfamiliar aerial lanes are pointed toward the Public Transit Rings instead, which is offered as a convenience and taken as one.

Visitor Waiting Court.description: A calm court with seating, water and clear sightlines, where visitors wait for orientation, for someone meeting them, or for a question to be resolved. The seating is comfortable and spread out, the sightlines mean anyone looking for a particular face can find it from the entrance, and there is nothing anywhere that counts down or hurries a queue along. The waiting is not engineered to pressure anyone, which arrivals from harder cities find disorienting for about ten minutes and restful for the rest of it. Staff pass through, answer what they are asked and move on. Children use the open middle of the court, and nobody suggests that they should not.

Gate Security Peace Line.description: The screening line, run as a peace-line check in the Valcoro manner: courteous, unhurried, and closer to hospitality than to inspection. The line is short, the staff stand on the same side of it as the people they are screening, and the check is explained while it is happening. Weapons are screened because the city is weapon-free by civic trust and the line exists to keep that true. Someone carrying a blade bought elsewhere is told so plainly and helped to make arrangements, without being treated as a problem. Nobody working it is armed, and nothing about it is staged to intimidate. The whole exchange usually takes less time than the explanation that accompanies it.

Orvessa Guest Reception Desk.description: House Orvessa's desk in the arrivals district, where Calessa Orvessa meets guests as they clear orientation. It is a plain staffed desk with chairs beside it rather than in front of it, placed where people arriving from orientation will pass it without having to look for it. Names checked, rooms arranged, a first conversation that is genuinely a welcome rather than a formality. Guests are asked what they need rather than told what is available, and the answer usually includes something practical about the next day. The House receives visitors here and houses them at its Lunar Gate Guesthouse, with the same family at both ends. A guest who arrives with nothing arranged is still sorted out before they leave the desk.

Restricted Transit Control.description: The quiet end of the district, where sensitive movement is handled away from the public platforms. It is a plain working space, deliberately unremarkable, with no signage suggesting what it is for and no view of it from the arrival areas. Castro or Valcoro representatives appear when an arrival needs them, and Dravon pressure reaching the city edge is dealt with here first. Whatever happens here happens calmly and at conversational volume, which is the district's standard for everything else as well. What makes a transit restricted, and who authorises it, is posted nowhere. Staff elsewhere in the district know it exists and know not to speculate about it in front of visitors.

Solvraxis Residential Wards.name: Solvraxis Residential Wards
Solvraxis Residential Wards.basicInfo: The living side of Solvraxis: eight wards of bright, well-kept housing for families, civic workers, shopkeepers, retired defenders and academy students. Garden paths, reflective pools, transit stops built for children, and student houses with curfews nobody quite keeps. The wards are white stone and planting, with shared courtyards, small bridges, rooftop study gardens and evening spaces that people actually use, and the maintenance is constant enough to be invisible. Each ward has its own character: streets of family homes, older hillside terraces above the pools, a livelier commons that runs late, transit-adjacent housing full of people moving across the city, a protected outer ward where drills run without drama, and student housing in two grades of supervision. Movement in and out is half flight and half the Public Transit Rings, and nobody reads either choice as saying anything. Neighbours notice things and say most of them indirectly, which is how gossip travels here and how a household in difficulty is quietly noticed. Safe, lived-in and deliberately ordinary, because a protected city is proven by how ordinary people live inside it, and this is where that proof is kept.
Solvraxis Residential Wards.hiddenInfo: Nothing here is poor, neglected or dangerous, which is exactly why trouble reads so loudly when it arrives. The wards are also where the city's other institutions leak into each other. Second-Year Student Houses sit under both Valcoro and Orvessa oversight, and Third-Year Terrace Housing carries youth overlap across all four Castro-derived minor Houses, Valcoro, Ravello, Bellovari and Orvessa, which makes its quiet debate rooms the fastest route for anything a student is not supposed to know yet. Silverwell Terrace holds families who remember Solvraxis before Castro dominance fully settled, and their observant, indirect conversations circle a question the city core does not ask out loud: whether peace this dependable depends too much on one man. Sunrail Court catches Lunar Gate spillover and the occasional suspicious visitor sighting. Larkglass Commons carries the gossip and most of the student comedy. And Valehome Ward keeps its shelter routes marked and drilled, which is a haven's way of admitting what it is prepared for.

Dawnmere Rows.description: Ordinary residential streets of bright white-stone homes, small garden paths and shared courtyards, lived in by families, civic workers and shopkeepers. The homes sit close without crowding, the garden paths are individually kept and mildly competitive about it, and the courtyards between them are where children end up. Child-safe transit stops connect into the Public Transit Rings so young residents can travel sheltered, with a guardian or alone once they are ready. The stops are a convenience for children still learning to fly rather than a statement about their eventual ability. Neighbourhood routine is the whole texture: school runs, errands, somebody's delivery left with somebody else, a conversation over a garden wall that lasts longer than either party planned.

Silverwell Terrace.description: Older hillside housing above reflective pools: generational homes, long-settled families, and neighbours who notice everything and say most of it indirectly. The terraces step down the slope with the pools below holding the light, the stonework is older than most of the city's and better cared for, and the same families have held some of these houses for generations. People here remember Solvraxis before Castro dominance fully settled, and the quiet conversations circle whether the city's peace leans too heavily on one man. Those conversations happen over tea, at length, and settle nothing. Nothing is said outright about anybody, and everyone understands what has been said anyway.

Larkglass Commons.description: The liveliest residential quarter, with small eateries, music corners, casual shops and student hangouts that run late. The frontages are close together and the light spills out of them, tables get put outside without much ceremony, and the noise stays at a level that the surrounding homes have long since made peace with. Less formal than the city core and quietly proud of it. Gossip circulates faster here than anywhere else in the wards, Galen Bellovari performs when invited, and Nina Castro causes harmless chaos on principle.
